News.title: Missing prisoner, 27, on the run for six months after absconding from jail as public warned ‘call 999 & do not approach’
News.content:
LAG MANHUNT Missing prisoner, 27, on the run for six months after absconding from jail as public warned ‘call 999 & do not approach’

COPS have launched a fresh manhunt appeal for a drug dealer lag who went on the run from an open prison six months ago.

Darnell Smith escaped HMP Springhill, in Buckinghamshire, on January 28 at around 11.30am.



Thames Valley Police have warned he should not be approached.

Police said today the prisoner, 27, is still “unlawfully at large”, and was last seen wearing all black clothes.



They added he fled the prison ‘without the authority or lawful licence to be in the community’.

Smith was serving a six-year prison term for possession with intent to supply a controlled class A drug, having been jailed in 2023.

Cops described him as being around 5ft 8ins tall and of medium build, with links to Surrey, Sussex, Croydon and Plumstead in London.

Investigating officer Police Staff Investigator Evelina Kersyte, Thames Valley Police’s Prison Crime Team, said: “We are appealing for the help of the public to trace Darnell Smith, who is unlawfully at large after escaping HMP Springhill.

“If you see Smith, do not approach him and call 999 instead.”

Cops added that anyone with information on Smith should call 101 or make a report online, quoting reference number 43260045393.



The appeal comes months after another lag absconded from the open prison, after Mamad Elmi, 27, fled the facility on Boxing Day last year.

HMP Springhill, which has more than 320 inmates, is a Category D prison, meaning it has “minimal security and allow(s) eligible prisoners to spend most of the day away from the prison on licence to carry out work, education or for other resettlement purposes.”

News.title: ‘Frankenstein’ killer who butchered young sailors GUILTY of sexually assaulting four men while working in Royal Navy
News.content:
SICK PREDATOR ‘Frankenstein’ killer who butchered young sailors GUILTY of sexually assaulting four men while working in Royal Navy

A “FRANKENSTEIN” killer who butchered two young sailors has been found guilty of sexually assaulting four men while working in the Navy.

Allan Grimson lured two young recruits back to his flat in Portsmouth then brutally murdered them when they spurned his advances.



He first slaughtered Nicholas Wright, 18, on December 12, 1997 – before murdering Sion Jenkins, 20, exactly 12 months later.

The former petty officer – dubbed the “Royal Navy‘s Dennis Nilsen” – is feared to have killed up to 20 people.



He has also been named as the prime suspect in the disappearance of Simon Parkes – an 18-year-old Royal Navy sailor who was last seen in December 1986 in Gibraltar, where Grimson was stationed at the time.

Grimson has now been convicted of sexually assaulting three young men in the Navy and one teenager around the same time as he killed Sion and Nicholas.



Chillingly, he abused the victims in the same flat in Portsmouth where he murdered the pair.

The fiend was also found guilty of 11 counts of indecent assault, one count of rape and one count of taking indecent photographs of a child.



Winchester Crown Court heard he could have been released on parole while serving his life sentence – until he was charged with the historic offences.

Grimson preyed on the victims between February 1994 and November 1999.

He told police one of the men was “lucky to be alive”, before adding: “If you’re going to rape somebody, to get away with it, kill it.”

One of his sex attack victims said he could only open up about the horror after Grimson was jailed in 2001 because he then felt “safe”.

Grimson served in the Royal Navy and in 1999 he was a serving Petty Officer Marine Engineering Mechanic and an instructor at the Royal Navy Firefighting School in Horsea Island, Portsmouth.



The prosecution said that this brought Grimson, a “big, powerful man” into contact with a lot of young men in their late teens.

Hulking Grimson – known as the “Frankenstein” killer – struck fear into the heart of the Royal Navy in the 1990s as he targeted sailors to butcher in a depraved reign of terror.

He first targeted Nicholas, 18, who was bludgeoned with a baseball bat after he rejected Grimson’s sexual advances.

The monster then sliced his ear off with a diving knife.

Once Nicholas was too hurt to defend himself, the brute slit his throat.



The next day, Grimson wrapped his naked body up – later telling police he’d felt a “tingling” sensation while doing so.

He then dumped the naval rating’s mutilated body in a ditch.

Exactly one year later, Grimson attacked and raped Sion in his house of horrors before tying him up and putting him in a bathtub.

As the 20-year-old begged to go home, the killer beat him to death with a bat before dumping his body by the side of the A32.

Grimson confessed to his sadistic crimes in excruciating detail – leading one expert to brand him the most dangerous psychopath of the 250 he had examined.



He was jailed in 2001 at Winchester Crown Court for life with a minimum of 22 years.

Sentencing him at the time, Mr Justice Cresswell told him: “You are a serial killer in nature if not in number.

“You are a highly dangerous serial killer who killed two young men in horrifying circumstances.”

Grimson will be sentenced on November 6.

News.title: ‘Life wasn’t easy for you’: Family pays heartbreaking tribute to Sonia Exelby who ‘paid sadist to violently kill her’
News.content:
TRAGIC SONIA TRIBUTE ‘Life wasn’t easy for you’: Family pays heartbreaking tribute to Sonia Exelby who ‘paid sadist to violently kill her’

THE family of a Brit woman who allegedly paid a sadist to kill her have released a heartbreaking tribute to her, saying: “Life wasn’t always easy for you.”

Sonia Exelby, 32, from Portsmouth, was found stabbed to death and buried in the woods in Marion County, Florida on October 17.



Dwain Hall, 54, is accused of violently ending her life after meeting Sonia on a fetish website two years earlier.

He has pleaded not guilty to kidnapping and murdering her and will stand trial in November.



Sonia’s devastated parents have now released an emotional tribute to their daughter, who they say was a “truly beautiful person, inside and out”.

Their statement continues: “She had the gentlest soul – so gentle that she chose to become vegan, because she couldn’t bear the thought of any animal suffering just so she could eat.

“That was who she was: kind, compassionate, and full of quiet love.

“She was incredibly talented. Sonia could play the piano so effortlessly, and when she sang, she had the voice of an angel.

“Being around her felt special—she brought a calmness and warmth that made everything feel a little lighter.

“Sonia was one of those rare people who made you feel completely safe to be yourself.



“She never judged, never criticised – she simply accepted people as they were and loved them for it.

“That is something so many of us will carry with us forever.”

They say Sonia had an “especially close and special bond” with her sister Sara and was “surrounded by loved everyday”.



One of her friends wrote that they had “never known a soul with a bigger or purer heart, and nobody made me feel seen quite like she did” and her siblings described her as the “softest most gentle soul”.

The tribute finishes: “We know that life wasn’t always easy for you, but your life was so much more than the struggles you faced.

“This is so important to us that the life you lived is what you are remembered for. You were deeply loved, and you will always be deeply loved. We miss you more than words can ever say.

“We love you so much, always, and forever”.

Sonia’s alleged killer, Hall, was denied bail last November, with the judge saying: “There is a large amount of evidence against you.”

Hall described himself to authorities as her mentor who wanted to help her, not let her kill herself.

An autospy revealed Exelby had been stabbed four times – Hall initially claimed not to know the Brit woman, before admitting they had had sex several times.

He also admitted to having violent tendencies, police reports revealed.

The alleged killer told investigators he picked Exelby up from the airport on October 10 and took her to an Airbnb in Reddick, where they had sex multiple times.

And police recovered chilling video that showed Exelby appearing bruised and scared, allegedly filmed by her suspected murderer just days before her death.



In the video, police said the Brit woman cried as her alleged killer asked how she wanted to die.

She hesitated, before telling Dwain Hall, 53, she wanted to be stabbed.

Her alleged killer replied: “This is how you wanted to die, right?”

The haunting video, filmed on Hall’s phone, was obtained by police following his arrest for her murder.

On the same day the video was taken, Exelby expressed doubts about the situation to a friend and said Hall had given her a rundown on how to use a gun, it is alleged.



“He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him. I was questioning it last night,” Exelby wrote to her friend on Discord.

“I thought he’d do it quick and not give my mind time to stew and realize this is the last thing I’ll ever day [sic] to anyone if I don’t take his offer of shooting him.

“I’m so so scared I’m so broken and in so much pain all I can do is lay here and doing what gee [sic] wants makes him respect me enough not to do the things I really hate.”

Investigators said the messages “showed that Hall was controlling her, that she was afraid, and had made a mistake”.

News.title: Tributes to ‘selfless’ family including baby girl killed after car crashed into trees on way home from footie tournament
News.content:
A FAMILY including a seven-month-old girl died in a horror crash on their way back from a football tournament.

Abu Camara, 36, his wife, 30, their baby and an 18-year-old woman believed to be a cousin died on Saturday when their car left the road and crashed into trees.

Abu and the two women were declared dead at the scene, with the baby girl rushed to hospital – but she tragically couldn’t be saved.



Cops have arrested a 33-year-old man on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving, and took him to hospital with serious injuries.



Emergency services were called to a stretch of road between the A50 Toyota Island and the A516 in Derby at around 11pm on Saturday.

Cops said all five people were from Leeds in West Yorkshire, and their family members are being supported by specialist officers.

Today the Gambia Welfare Society, Leeds, paid tribute to Abu, saying he was returning from a football tournament in Birmingham when they crashed.



It added: “Our community in Leeds, especially the Sarahuleh community, has been struck by a devastating tragedy.

“Abu was a dedicated servant of his community, passionate about his Deen, supporting the new mosque, and mentoring young children through football.

“He will be remembered for his kindness, humility, and selfless service.”

The society wished the families of those involved “strength and patience during this heartbreaking time” and said it was “grateful” the driver had survived the incident, adding that it was “praying for his full and speedy recovery”.



Cops said: “The relatives of those involved are aware and are receiving support from specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this difficult time.

“We are continuing to appeal for anyone who witnessed the crash to come forward.

“Officers are also keen to hear from anyone who has any dash cam footage which may have captured the incident.”

News.title: Beachgoer, 22, pushes pregnant fiancée to safety during ‘bloody’ shark attack in waist deep water on Florida beach
News.content:
BEACH BLOODSHED Beachgoer, 22, pushes pregnant fiancée to safety during ‘bloody’ shark attack in waist deep water on Florida beach

A BEACHGOER shoved his pregnant fiancée to safety before battling a shark in waist-deep water during a terrifying attack.

Jacorey High was left with severe injuries after the predator clamped onto his leg as the couple enjoyed a swim.



The hero, from Henry County, Georgia, only realized the full extent of the attack once he made it back to shore.

Jacorey had been vacationing with family in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Saturday evening when the medium-sized shark struck in shallow water.



The 22-year-old said his first instinct was to protect his pregnant fiancée as the animal lunged at him.



“I realized right away it was a shark because of the way it bit down on my foot, but I was more worried about getting my fiancé out of the water,” he said.

Jacorey said the shark refused to back off after sinking its teeth into his left foot.

“Then it came up to try to get my arm, so I had to push it away from me. I ran, and it tried to get my other leg,” he added.

He described the shark as grey on top and roughly reaching from the size of his leg up to his waist.



“Then it came up to try to get my arm, so I had to push it away from me. I ran, and it tried to get my other leg,” he added.

After dragging himself from the surf, Jacorey saw blood pouring from his foot before medics rushed him to hospital.

He later underwent surgery after doctors found the shark had caused extensive damage to his foot.

“I didn’t really feel it until I got to the hospital when they started giving me medicine for it,” Jacorey explained.

Doctors have warned his recovery could take around three months, although it remains unclear whether he has suffered permanent damage that could affect his ability to return to work.



“Hoping that it didn’t really mess up anything important in my foot so that I can go back to work,” he said.

A GoFundMe set up to support Jacorey High says he suffered extensive ligament and tendon damage and is expected to remain hospitalized for at least another week.

Organizers said the dad-to-be now faces “multiple treatments, rehabilitation, and an extended time away from work with no clear timeline for his return”.

The campaign has so far raised $535 toward its $100,000 goal to help cover medical bills, lost income and living costs.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

According to marine life experts at the Georgia Aquarium, unprovoked shark attacks are rare, with only around 60 to 65 recorded worldwide each year.



Officials have not confirmed what species of shark attacked Jacorey.

News.title: Woman in 20s dragged into building & sexually assaulted in horror early hours attack as CCTV released in hunt for man
News.content:
A WOMAN was dragged into a building and sexually assaulted in a horror early hours attack as police launch a manhunt for the attacker.

The attack took place in Islington, north London, between Essex Road and Northchurch road at around 3am on Friday, July 4.



The Met Police said the woman – who is in her early 20s – was approached by an unknown man who began harassing her.

He then dragged her into the entrance of a building on Northchurch Road where he physically and sexually assaulted her.



The man is then said to have fled in the direction of Angel before two members of the public heard the woman shouting for help and came to her aid.

She continues to be supported by specialist officers.



Police are now appealing for witnesses who were in the area between 2.45am and 3.30am and have released CCTV images of a man they wish to identify.

Following the attack, the suspect is believed to have entered a shop on Essex Road but left without making a purchase.

He is described as being of average build and approximately 5ft 8ins to 6ft tall.

The man is also thought to have short hair or a shaved head and was wearing a distinctive tie-dye T-shirt featuring blue and pink streaks.



Detective Chief Inspector Paul Ridley, who is leading the investigation, said: “We take reports of this nature incredibly seriously and are committed to supporting victims and putting those responsible before the courts.

“This was a deeply distressing attack on a young woman, which we are investigating as an attempted rape. My officers have been working tirelessly to identify the suspect as quickly as possible.

“CCTV shows a man fleeing along Essex Road, running past a bus stop towards Angel. There were a number of vehicles on the road at that time.

“Please get in touch with us if you recognise the man or if you have CCTV or dashcam footage that could help our investigation. No piece of information is too small, and what may seem insignificant to you could prove vital to our investigation.

“Two members of the public bravely came to the woman’s assistance. While officers have spoken to a woman who intervened, we are yet to speak to man who also stepped in. He is described as a white male in his late teens or early 20s, with an athletic build and curly, ash-blonde hair.



“I would like to make a direct appeal to him to get in touch with officers. He may have crucial information to support the investigation and would ask that you contact us as soon as possible.”

News.title: Check out the bizarre new ‘human refrigerator’ built to help beat heatwaves – but would you pay the eye-watering price?
News.content:
COLD HARD CASH Check out the bizarre new ‘human refrigerator’ built to help beat heatwaves – but would you pay the eye-watering price?

A BIZARRE new “human refrigerator” has hit the market to help those feeling the heat keep cool this summer.

Set at a chilly 15C, the freezing cold box on wheels has been created just in time to beat the heatwaves sweeping across Europe as temperatures could reach above 40C.



Japanese technology whizzes have crafted a so-called personal cooling box for the human body dubbed the Do Hiemon Box.

But it comes at a hefty price.



A single Do Hiemon Box is available to buy for 1.5m yen – or £6,862 – and it requires extra cash to make the electrical cooling pump work.

The wacky new invention has been created by two companies – a specialist vending machine manufacturer and steel toolbox company.

Each Do Hiemon Box comes in at 7ft tall and almost 4ft deep allowing for easy and comfortable access for all.

The user sits on a built-in chair inside the stainless steel box and faces out through a tall glass panel – much like being inside a vending machine.



Powerful jets then blast chilled air to the head, neck, shoulders and back to help rapidly lower body temperature within just five minutes.

The unit is maintained at around 15C and is programmed to shut down automatically after 20 minutes of use.

There are three settings in total which change up the airflow and cooling angles and temperatures.

It costs 16 yen or 7p-an-hour to operate, according to manufacturer SDRS.

This makes it more energy-efficient than the average air conditioner in Japan.



The box was first created after Japan was hit by 38C heat earlier in the year as the government issued heatstroke warnings.

SDRS say after just 10 minutes inside the box, users may feel less tired too due to the temperature shock.

As it sits on wheels, the box can be moved around despite its weight and can even be used outside.

The product went on sale in April, according to its supplier Trusco.

One unit was donated to Maebashi City Hall in Gunma Prefecture for visitors to use free of charge during opening hours if they need to cool down.



The cool boxes are yet to make their way over to Europe, where several nations are currently battling wildfires and expecting heatwaves.

Several major wildfires are raging across France with mass evacuations continuing across the country as officials battle the “apocalyptic” flames.

The fires are now less than seven miles away from Bordeaux with over 850,000 residents being warned the city is at risk of being reduced to ashes in the coming days.



The Gironde wildfire has been scorching huge swathes of land as it continues to grow as the Biscarrosse fires also rage on in France.

Across in Spain, “monster” flames are casting doubt over summer holiday travel plans as Madrid and Avila are under national emergency warnings.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The UK is also set for a fourth heatwave this week as wildfires continue to rage across the country and drought is officially declared.

Brits saw temperatures cool over the weekend but they are set to soar again, reaching highs of 33C in some areas.

News.title: I took autistic son away in term time – it’s the only way he can enjoy a holiday but now I’m struggling with huge fine
News.content:
FINE HELL I took autistic son away in term time – it’s the only way he can enjoy a holiday but now I’m struggling with huge fine

A MUM thought taking her autistic son on holiday during school term was the ‘best idea’ until she was slapped with a £320 fine – and says she’ll stick to UK caravans in future.

Emily Allman jetted off to Malaga, Spain, with her husband Tony Allman, 35, nine-year-old autistic son Miles Allman, Samantha Allman, five, and her in-laws on May 7.



The 32-year-old thought going away in term time was ‘the best idea in the world’ as Miles struggles with big crowds and noisy ‘popular’ places due to his condition.

The mum-of-two said it was cheaper to pay the fine for their £4,000 stay than pay £10,000 for the same holiday during the school summer break.



Emily said she submitted a holiday request to the school a week-and-a-half before the travel date and assumed it had been approved after not hearing back.

When the modelling agency agent returned home a week later on May 14, she discovered a letter stating the holiday request hadn’t been approved and was slapped with a £320 fine.

Emily posted a video online with the caption: “I knew it was coming. But my point is, he can’t travel during school holidays. It’s far too overwhelming for him.

“The school still decided it wasn’t a good enough excuse. Goodbye wages.”



A resigned Emily said the family will now have to settle for UK and caravan holidays in future.

Emily, from Ashington, Northumberland, said: “We put in a request to the school. My son, having autism and ADHD, struggles with really popular places.

“Even around our home town he struggles with big crowds if it’s too loud or if it gets too hot.

“We thought going in the term-time would be the best idea in the world. My mother-in-law said if we went two weeks after, it went from £4,000 to £10,000.

“We knew even if we did get fined it would be cheaper than having to pay that.



“I sent the form to school and rang the educational welfare office and told them about the situation with my son, they said it was down to the discretion of the head teacher.

“They have worked with my son since reception and know how he is and what he struggles with, I thought ‘they’ll probably accept it’.

“I didn’t hear anything back up to the point of us going on holiday so I thought ‘it’s been accepted’. We had the most incredible holiday.

“When we came home, as we arrived through the front door of the house, there were these letters waiting saying it hadn’t been approved.

“I knew the fines were coming two weeks later. It was £80 per person, per child, so it was £160 each for me and my husband.”



Emily said it was her kids’ first time going abroad but they won’t be able to go again due to the the fines increasing.

Now, Emily claims children should be able to have ‘some’ days off in the year during term time to allow for holidays.

Emily said: “The circumstances are different for each child.

“The money was a pain in the a** but when it comes to his needs, I’m not going to push him to go to a place where he is not going to enjoy it. That would be a complete waste of money.



“It was the first time my kids had been on a plane to go abroad. He [Miles] was able to get on the plane first and see the airplane.

“Even that was difficult for him. It was busy, it was on a weekend, the airport was full. I would love for there to be a week or so that the child is able to be given throughout the school year.

“Adults get holidays given that they can take. If we book a few months in advance, it would be a lot easier.

“This is the first time we’ve ever done it. I think the fine goes up if you do it again within three years, we won’t be able to do it again for a while.



“It will have to be a case of staying in the UK and going to caravan parks just to get them away.”

The viral video Emily shared, which racked up more than 20,000 views, had mixed reactions from people.

Emily said: “Lots of people were shocked we were fined and others said they had been accepted for the same reasons.

“I think there should be something put in place to understand the child as a person and not just another number.

‘I’ll pay the fine, I knew it was coming, but it’s the principle. It’s had many mixed reviews with people arguing among themselves.



“It’s one of those things you unfortunately have to deal with as a parent, not that I think it’s fair. I don’t think I’ll ever be able to get away during school time.”

Some commenters empathised with Emily while others said that there is no excuse to miss school.

One wrote: “It isn’t a good enough excuse though…like no matter your intentions you are still pulling the kid out of school for something that is not necessary.”



A second commented: “If you can afford the holiday, you can afford the fine.”

A third wrote: “Well let’s be honest it’s not a good enough excuse.”

Another commented: “Let it go to court, explain it to them.”

But one wrote: “I’m 100% homeschooling, ain’t no way I am being told when to go on holiday.”

Northumberland County Council referred the enquiry to WISE Academies.



Louise Hall, Executive Headteacher at WISE Academies, said: “We understand that this is a difficult situation for the family, and we do not take the decision lightly to refer cases to the local authority to issue a penalty notice.

“WISE Academies is committed to supporting all students with special educational needs and disabilities and we work closely with families to create tailored support plans.

“However, consistent school attendance is a legal requirement and remains vital for every child’s social, emotional and academic progress.

“Department for Education guidelines make it clear that the DfE ‘does not consider a need or desire for a holiday or other absence for the purpose of recreation to be an exceptional circumstance’ enabling authorisation of absence.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“While we recognise the unique challenges faced by some parents, a family holiday during term time does not meet the threshold for an exceptional circumstance so cannot be authorised.



“The policy is applied consistently to ensure equity across our entire school community. We remain committed to working constructively with the family to support their child’s ongoing welfare and education within the school environment.”

News.title: Lloyds and Barclays down: Hundreds 'can't make payments' as Halifax also hit
News.content:
Lloyds, Barclays and Halifax customers are all experiencing issues which include problems with the app, bank transfers and online banking

Lloyds and Barclays down: Hundreds 'can't make payments' as Halifax also hit

Thousands of Lloyds, Barclays and Halifax customers have reported major problems with their banking this afternoon.

Customers say they are unable to make payments or transfer money, while others have received messages warning them payment had failed but later realised the money had actually gone through.

Lloyds Bank said it is investigating an issue affecting Faster Payments, which "may cause delays".

The bank also urged customers who have attempted to send money not to send it again as this may result in duplicate payments.

Hundreds of Barclays customers say they have been unable to receive external payments, while the majority of Halifax users reporting issues today said they were struggling to transfer funds.

News.title: English football set to trial new law THIS WEEK to stop goalkeeper tactical timeouts
News.content:
English football set to trial new law THIS WEEK to stop goalkeeper tactical timeouts

Football fans have grown tired with opposition goalkeepers going down supposedly injured and forcing the referee to pause the game, but lawmakers are attempting to stamp it out

View 2 Images Tactical timeouts could soon be a thing of the past (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

A new law which aims to prevent goalkeepers feigning injury and forcing a tactical timeout could be trialed in English football as soon as this weekend. The much-maligned timeouts have become increasingly common in recent seasons, with keepers going down supposedly injured and giving the referee no choice but to stop the game as per the current rulebook.

‌



A physio would then enter the field and treat the goalkeeper before the match restarts at a different phase, stopping the flow of the game while allowing players to speak with their coaches during the break in play. This isn't the case for when an outfielder receives treatment, as they have to wait on the sidelines after the play has restarted until the referee signals that they can return.

‌



But the new law will change that. According to BBC Sport, if a referee signals that the physio can come on to treat a goalkeeper, the team's manager must nominate an outfielder to leave the pitch for one minute. If the manager doesn't choose a player within 10 seconds, the team's captain will automatically be selected.

‌



The Football Association, Premier League, English Football League, National League and Women's Super League have all agreed on the law. First, though, permission is needed from the International Football Association Board (IFAB).

Should they give the green light in England, the law could be seen in action for the first time during Saturday's Carabao Cup preliminary round tie between Tranmere Rovers and Rochdale at Prenton Park.

‌



In November, Leeds United manager Daniel Farke accused Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma of feigning injury in order to 'bend the rules' during their clash at the Etihad Stadium. "Everyone knows why he went down," Farke claimed post-match.

"It is not the elephant in the room. Why he went down it was obvious. It is within the rules. It is smart. If I like it? If it's within the sense of fair play?

What do you think of the new law? Have your say in the comments section.

‌

"If it should be like this I will keep to myself. It is up to the authorities to find a solution. I ask the fourth official at this point if you want to do something. Our hands are tied.

"If we don't educate our players in football what to do in terms of fair play and sportsmanship and whatever and if we just try to bend the rules and even do a fake injury in order to do an additional team talk, it is not what I like personally. But if it is within the rules I can't complain."

News.title: France wildfires live: Inferno threatens Bordeaux as tourists told 'stay away'
News.content:
More than 220,000 people in south-west France's Gironde region have been evacuated as raging wildfires approach Bordeaux

Fierce wildfires are raging seven miles from the French city of Bordeaux and its airport, with more than 220,000 people evacuated from their homes in the south-west of the country.

Firefighters are struggling to contain the flames, which have burned 42,000 hectares - an area four times the size of Paris - leaving two firefighters dead and 88 injured. Volunteers, including local farmers, are helping by towing huge water tankers to the scene.

President Emmanuel Macron held a crisis meeting today as shifting winds and arid conditions have made the blaze difficult to control. The main fire has generated a huge fire thunderstorm, fuelled by its own winds and lightning, the National Firefighters Federation of France said.

Local official Sophie Brocas said: "We urge tourists not to come to this region, at least until the situation is under control. I encourage tourists who are already here to consider another destination."

Meanwhile in Spain, 25,000 people have been ordered to evacuate and almost 40,000 have been told to stay indoors. Wildfires near Madrid "slowed their advance" overnight but remain active, the regional government said today.

News.title: UK weather maps show when temperatures peak in heatwave as 20 areas face 30C or more
News.content:
UK weather maps show when temperatures peak in heatwave as 20 areas face 30C or more

The Met Office has warned temperatures could hit 35C on Wednesday, with weather maps showing that up to 20 counties could see 30C temperatures or above

View 2 Images Temperatures could climb to 35C in parts of south-east England on Wednesday (Image: Met Office)

The Met Office has warned temperatures could soar to 35C on Wednesday as a fourth heatwave hits the UK with weather maps showing that up to 20 counties face 30C or above.

‌



Tuesday will bring increasingly hot conditions, particularly across south-east England, where temperatures are forecast to climb to 29C or 30C, before reaching a peak on Wednesday.

‌



A Met Office forecast map for 4pm on Wednesday shows scorching highs of 34C in Cambridge and parts of Norfolk and Suffolk, along with 33C in London and parts of the Home Counties.

‌



The soaring temperatures are expected to push conditions beyond the threshold needed to make it the UK's fourth heatwave of the year. Amber heat health alerts have been issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for the South East, the East Midlands, East of England and London.

An amber alert means "significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures, including a rise in deaths, particularly among those aged 65 and over or with health conditions", the UK Health Security Agency warned

View 2 Images Heat heath alerts issued by the UK Health Security Agency - the green shading indicates no alerts (Image: UKHSA)

‌



Yellow heat health alerts have been issued for the South West, West Midlands and Yorkshire and the Humber. The alerts will be in place from 9am on Wednesday, July 29, until 9am on Thursday, July 30. As yet, there are no alerts in place for the North East or North West of England, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland.

Counties set for 30C on Wednesday:

Bedfordshire

Berkshire

Buckinghamshire

Cambridgeshire

Essex

Greater London

Hampshire

Hertfordshire

Kent

Leicestershire

Lincolnshire

Norfolk

Northamptonshire

Oxfordshire

Rutland

Suffolk

Surrey

Warwickshire

Wiltshire

Worcestershire

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



The Met Office has said that, if temperatures rise high enough to meet local thresholds for three consecutive days, a fourth UK heatwave of the year could be recorded. So far, 2026 has seen three defined heatwaves, in May, June and July.

Gregory Wolverson, deputy chief forecaster at the Met Office, said: "This is a short-lived spell of heat, but temperatures will climb quickly through the first half of the week, particularly in the southeast.

"By Wednesday, some areas could see temperatures in the mid-30s, and while the heat will not be widespread across the whole of the UK, it will be enough for parts of the southeast to likely meet official heatwave criteria by Thursday.

Article continues below

"Elsewhere, the weather will be more changeable, and the change to cooler, more unsettled conditions will arrive sooner from the north and west, with a mix of sunshine and showers. Across northern areas, it is possible there will be heavier showers with a small risk of isolated thunderstorms through the week."

News.title: Newquay deaths: Man and his daughter drown after 'fall from rocks' at Fistral Beach
News.content:
Beachgoers bravely tried to rescue a man and woman after they reportedly fell from rocks and died in the choppy sea at Britain's most popular surfing spot.

Newquay deaths: Man and his daughter drown after 'fall from rocks' at Fistral Beach

Scene at Fistral beach where witnesses say man and woman fell into water

A father and his daughter, in their 60s and 30s. have tragically died after rescue crews pulled them from the water at Britain's most famous surfing beach in Cornwall.

People at Fistral Beach, in Newquay, bravely attempted to rescue the pair - reportedly a father and daughter - with witnesses suggesting they had fallen from rocks.

Witnesses said nine emergency vehicles and a helicopter rushed to the 750-metre long sands, known as the 'home of British surfing' , last night. Police, the coastguard and the ambulance service were deployed at around 9.30pm. Images from Fistral last night showed people crowding on the sands trying to help with the rescue effort.

The area is well-known for having extremely strong and dangerous rip currents, particularly during outgoing tides. Locals said the sea currents were "very strong" last night.

The beach has regular lifeguard patrols but, tragically, the incident happened after they had finished for the day.

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Government prepared to consider major change to pregnancy scans - Monday, July 27 update
News.content:
Government prepared to consider major change to pregnancy scans - Monday, July 27 update

It follows calls for a third trimester ultrasound scan to become routine under the NHS

View 2 Images NHS hospitals in England typically offer at least two ultrasound scans during pregnancy

The Government is prepared to consider implementing a routine third trimester pregnancy ultrasound scan if experts advise them to, it has announced in a major health update. Currently, NHS hospitals in England offer at least two ultrasound scans during pregnancy - one at 11-14 weeks, and a second between 18-21 weeks.

‌



Ultrasound scans, which last usually between 20-30mins, are used to assess the health of the baby while in the womb. It is your choice whether to have one or not. There are no known risks to the baby or the mother from having an ultrasound scan.

‌



But the Government has now confirmed that it is open to the idea of a routine third scan, should it be suggested by the UK National Screening Committee. The update comes after a petition launched on the Government website on March 23, 2026 reached 10,000 signatures, prompting a response.

‌



The petition, entitled 'Require NHS to offer routine third trimester pregnancy ultrasound scan', was launched by Louise Thornton and now has 10,072 signatures. The Government is obliged to respond once it reaches 10,000 signatures.

She said: "As a mother of a baby born via emergency c-section due to missed foetal compromise I urge the Government to require the NHS to offer a routine third trimester ultrasound scan. I think this could reduce emergency c-sections, stillbirths and lifelong disabilities due to missed foetal complications.

"Currently the NHS offers two routine scans, one at 12 weeks and one at 20 weeks. After this the baby's health is relied upon fundal height, parent blood pressure, dipstick urine tests, and a minutes-worth of doppler use every 2-4 weeks. I believe that not only are these methods outdated, but can also miss growth restrictions, reduced foetal heart rate and placental issues. I therefore call for the NHS to offer routine third trimester scans, which could detect issues earlier, medical intervention can be involved sooner and emergency c-sections reduced."

‌



The Government responded: "The Government would consider a routine NHS third trimester ultrasound scan in the event of an evidence-based recommendation from the UK National Screening Committee. A call for new proposals is open.

"National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) antenatal care guidance recommends offering two routine ultrasound scans: one in the first trimester, and one at around 20 weeks. For pregnancies classified as low-risk, NICE advises that additional routine scans after 28 weeks do not provide significant benefits and should not be offered as standard practice. Instead, NICE recommends targeted scanning based on clinical need.

"Antenatal and newborn screening programmes are offered to women during pregnancy and to the baby after birth. The NHS offers screening for over 30 conditions during this time, including a 20-weeks scan for women, which screens for 11 physical conditions identifiable at this stage in development. Screening and treatment of babies prevents deaths and disabilities and improves quality of life in more than 1,000 children per year.

‌



"Mandating a routine ultrasound for all women in the third trimester when there are no specific clinical symptoms would be considered a screening programme. The Government is advised on all screening matters by the independent UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC), which consists of leading medical and screening experts.

"Screening can cause harm, so the UK NSC will only recommend screening if it is confident that there is robust evidence that offering screening will do more good than harm. We have not asked the UK NSC to look at providing a routine third ultrasound scan in the third trimester of pregnancy to identify medical issues.

View 2 Images The Government said it 'would consider a routine NHS third trimester ultrasound scan in the event of an evidence-based recommendation from the UK National Screening Committee'

‌



"Recent studies, such as the IRIS study, have explored routine third trimester ultrasound combined with biomarkers which suggest improved detection of small babies but there remains insufficient evidence that universal screening alone reduces stillbirth. However, the UK NSC welcomes any new evidence which suggests the case for a new or modified screening programme via its open call, which opened on 1 July and closes on 30 September 2026.

"The NHS has multiple initiatives in place to support fetal, neonatal and newborn safety, such as the Saving Babies Lives Care Bundle (SBLCB) and the Avoiding Brain Injury in Childbirth Programme.

"The SBLCB is a package of evidence-based interventions to support staff to reduce stillbirth, neonatal brain injury, neonatal death and pre-term births. This includes guidance on managing multiple pregnancies to ensure optimal care for the woman and baby. Element 2 of SBLCB focuses on fetal growth risk assessment, surveillance and management. Implementation of the SBLCB is supported through NHS Resolution’s Maternity Incentive Scheme, which provides a strong financial incentive to encourage its adoption and consistent use. As part of Safety Action 6 in Year 7 of the Maternity Incentive Scheme (2025/26), NHS trusts were required to demonstrate they were on track for full implementation of SBLCB v3.2. The results from Year 7 show that, as at April 2026, 117 out of 119 (98% of) trusts were compliant with Safety Action 6.

‌



"Fetal and maternal wellbeing are continuously risk assessed during labour. The Avoiding Brain Injury in Childbirth Programme, backed by £7.8 million in funding, is working to improve maternity outcomes by enhancing the identification and management of fetal distress during labour and the obstetric emergency of impacted fetal head at caesarean birth. NHS England is leading on national implementation. Through this programme we will seek to improve clinical practice, communication and care for women and families, resulting in better outcomes and experiences. The project will help maternity staff improve clinical practice in detection and response to suspected intrapartum fetal deterioration and management of impacted fetal head at caesarean birth. The programme will be fully implemented by March 2027.

"Baroness Amos published her final report and recommendations of the national independent investigation into NHS maternity and neonatal care on 30 June. Her investigation found that women and families are not being listened to, accountability is not being delivered when things go wrong, and that racism and discrimination are driving inequalities in outcomes.

"The National Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce, which is comprised of family representatives, clinicians and other experts, and chaired by the Secretary of State, will develop a new national action plan. We will publish the action plan by the end of the year. Once published, the Taskforce will hold the system to account for implementing the action plan and improving outcomes and experiences for women, babies and families, as well as staff.

‌



"Michelle Welsh MP, as the government’s first Maternity and Neonatal Adviser, will continue to work directly with families, the government, the NHS and maternity organisations to push for better, safer care for mothers, babies and families."

Ultrasounds during pregnancy

The first routine scan normally takes place after 12 weeks, and is called a 12-week scan. This is when you are given a due date, as well as your baby's size. It can include a nuchal translucency (NT) scan, which is part of the combined screening test for Down's syndrome, if you choose to have this screening.

The second scan is known as a 20-week screening scan, and usually takes place between 18 and 21 weeks of pregnancy. It is also known as the anomaly scan or mid-pregnancy scan as it checks for 11 different physical conditions. You can usually learn the results of the scan immediately.

‌



Finding out the sex of your baby is not offered as part of the national screening programme, but you may be able to during your 20-week scan. It depends on the policy of your hospital.

A growth scan, or third trimester scan, can take place at any time between 24 and 41 weeks gestation. They are often recommended if your are defined as a 'high-risk pregnancy'. Urgent Growth scans are sometimes required for the following reasons:

Recurrent episodes of reduced fetal movements

Diagnosis of a medical condition

Slowing measurement or small measurement when the midwife measures the symphysis fundal height (the measurement of your bump)

Slowing growth on a serial growth scan

Article continues below

The sonographer will take several measurements which will give us a representation of your baby’s wellbeing. Assessing these factors can tell us if a baby is growing well or may need further intervention.

At the end of the scan, the sonographer will plot the estimated weight of your baby on the electronic chart (Intergrowth 21st Chart). This will tell us if your baby’s weight and the pattern of growth is perceived to be normal for you.

If the growth of your baby is slowing down or your baby measures below the 10th centile or above the 97th on your GROW chart, you may need some extra scans and appointments to keep a closer eye on your pregnancy.

News.title: 'I advise lottery winners on how to spend jackpot – there's simple reason some marriages end'
News.content:
'I advise lottery winners on how to spend jackpot – there's simple reason some marriages end'

The National Lottery has made more than 8,000 millionaires, handing out a staggering £103billion in prize money - but it hasn't been a happy ending for all jackpot winners

View 3 Images Gillian and Adrian Bayford won the jackpot - but things quickly turned sour (Image: SWNS.COM)

The National Lottery has created more than 8,000 millionaires or multi-millionaires since its first draw in November 1994.

‌



Its various games, including EuroMillions and Set For Life, have made some people rich beyond their wildest dreams. But there are downsides to striking it lucky.

‌



Britain's youngest winner Callie Rogers and bin man Michael Carroll, notoriously nicknamed the 'lotto lout', were declared bankrupt after squandering their winnings.

‌



Roger and Lara Griffiths, and Adrian and Gillian Bayford, were among those couples who won the lottery but saw their marriages later come crashing to a halt.

Winners adviser Andy Carter has passed on his wisdom to more than 2,500 people for the last 20 years. One of his main tasks is making sure people don't ruin their lives after coming into money.

View 3 Images Andy Carter has advised lottery winners for decades (Image: PA)

‌



He spends his time speaking to lucky winners after they scoop anything from £50,000 to £195,000, and he says there is one simple reason why some marriages end.

Andy told the Daily Mail that coming into money will just shine a spotlight that are already present in a relationship.

He said: "Sudden wealth will exaggerate how you are. So if you are very happy in your marriage, you'll have a lovely time. And if you are having a difficult marriage, it gives you something else to be difficult about."

‌



Adrian and Gillian Bayford were among those to split after winning a huge jackpot. Former postman Adrian won a staggering £148million, the second biggest lottery jackpot in UK history at they time it was won in 2012.

The couple split after nine years of marriage just 15 months after their life-changing win.

Adrian and Gillian are just one of three couple in the UK's top 10 jackpots who have gone public - and two of those marriages did not last.

‌



Colin and Chris Weir, from Largs, North Ayrshire, in Scotland, won an incredible £161million in July 2011. They split eight years later, after almost four decades together, and Colin died less than a year after that.

View 3 Images Chris and Colin Weir called time on their marriage after almost four decades (Image: SWNS.COM)

According to Andy, the biggest mistake winners can make in the days and weeks after a payout is "trying to be too generous" with friends and family.

‌



It is natural for people to come cap in hand if someone they are close to has just come into a large sum of money.

National Lottery operator Allwyn now provides a financial planning service with experts who help winners make calculations for the future.

Andy explains that while winners might want to give a large sum of money to a son or daughter, a solicitor might advise them to consider whether this is a wise move.

Article continues below

He also suggests that many people who had their lives ruined by hitting the jackpot probably didn't have the support that is available now.

The National Lottery has handed out a staggering £103billion in prize money.

News.title: Tragedy as two women, 24 and 26, dead after afternoon swim in Loch Fyne
News.content:
Tragedy as two women, 24 and 26, dead after afternoon swim in Loch Fyne

Two women, aged 24 and 26, have died while swimming in Loch Fyne, in Argyll and Bute, on Sunday afternoon

View Image Emergency services attended Loch Fyne following reports of concern for two drivers (Image: Google)

Two women, aged 24 and 26, have died while swimming in a Scottish loch.

‌



Police Scotland said officers were called to a "report of concern for two female divers" at Loch Fyne, in Argyll and Bute, at about 3.30pm on Sunday.

‌



The 26-year-old woman was pronounced dead at the scene, while the body of the 24-year-old woman was found in the water after further searches.

Article continues below

HM Coastguard and rescue teams from Crinan, Dunoon, Kames and Inveraray were involved in the operation. Lifeboats from Tighnabruich, Campbeltown and Largs were also dispatched to the scene

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "The deaths are being treated as unexplained and a post-mortem examination will take place in due course."

News.title: How wildfires in France and Spain might affect your travel plans
News.content:
The UK government has not specifically warned against travel to anywhere in France or Spain, but it does advise caution.

In France, it says access to affected areas may be restricted and roads may close at short notice. It adds that further evacuations may take place.

It has also issued a general warning about the high risk of wildfires in France during the summer season from April to October.

For those in an affected area in France or Spain or planning to travel there, the UK government recommends following instructions and updates from local authorities and emergency services at all times.

Those needing emergency help in France or Spain can call 112.

Travellers should also bear in mind the UK government's advice can and does change in response to moving events.

Anna-Marie Duthie, travel insurance expert at financial rating firm Defaqto, says that if this happens after you have booked your trip, "you may be covered for cancellation or curtailment".

"You may also be covered for additional travel and accommodation costs should your trip be disrupted due to a catastrophic event, if your insurer offers this cover or you've paid to include it," she adds.

To know if this applies to you, check your policy.

News.title: NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform, PM tells BBC
News.content:
Andy Burnham has told the BBC "the NHS will collapse" if social care is not reformed but said he could not put a timeline on changes.

In his first major interview since becoming prime minister, Burnham said he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system.

The prime minister also suggested making it harder to claim benefits, saying the country had to get serious about getting the welfare bill down.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has meanwhile written to the prime minister, saying he should rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to fund social care reform.

Burnham told the BBC that if the government did not reform social care, the NHS would "collapse under the weight of trying to care for people who've really not needed to end up in the NHS system".

But pressed on whether he would create a new system before the next election, he said he "couldn't put a timeline on it right here, right now", though he would put "whatever political capital I have into fixing broken social care".

Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care in England in 2009 when he was health secretary under Gordon Brown and pursued the idea of a compulsory levy to fund it.

That Labour government also floated the idea of allowing people to defer the payment until after they died, which led to the Tories branding it a "death tax".

Burnham is due to make a speech on adult social care on Wednesday.

The BBC understands the PM will stop short of unveiling plans for a new system in this speech, instead announcing he is speeding up the Casey Commission, an independent review that has been considering possible solutions for social care.

Baroness Louise Casey is not expected to give her final recommendations until 2028, but Burnham wants to bring her schedule forward.

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Sarah Woolnough, chief executive of healthcare think tank the King's Fund, said the current "punitive system" meant that "quite a lot of people go without care that they need", with one in seven paying in excess of Â£100,000 for social care.

While Burnham has not yet outlined any plans, Woolnough told the BBC Radio 4's Today programme that reforms could range from making social care free at the point of need to placing a cap on the amount people spend.

"The PM has for a long time mooted the idea of a social care system similar to NHS," she said.

"It would be expensive but on the scale of what we spend on other public services - around Â£200bn on the NHS - we are talking for some of these options low billions per year."

Adult social care has proved a complex issue to tackle for successive governments.

Two years ago Sir Keir Starmer was criticised when Labour scrapped plans for an Â£86,000 cap on the amount people in England would spend on social care in their lifetime.

Badenoch wrote in her letter to Burnham that "any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".

Layla Moran, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the Health and Social Committee, told the Today programme: "We do need to discuss where the money is going to come from but also we need to all be putting our political capital into this."

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said he was ready to do "whatever I can to find a real and lasting consensus on social care".

"Family carers must be at the heart of any new system, everyone must get the care they need and no one should lose their home as a result," he said.

Reform Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said social care needed fixing but warned the party would fight any proposal for a "universal death tax".

He said: "It's not fair to raid people's life savings and drags hundreds of thousands more families into paying tax when their loved ones pass away."

News.title: Man jailed for abduction and rape of girl, 15, in Edinburgh basement
News.content:
A masked rapist who abducted a 15-year-old girl from an Edinburgh city centre bus stop has been jailed under a lifelong restriction order.

Aaron Strachan, 21, pulled a knife on the girl on the city's Princes Street in May last year, before marching her to a basement storage area and raping her.

The High Court in Edinburgh heard that he also attacked a man with a hammer days later, and had a criminal record of violence, robbery and possession of weapons.

Strachan was jailed for a minimum of five years with an order for lifelong restriction (OLR). It means a parole board must decide if he is ever safe to be released.

Judge Michael O'Grady described Strachan's crimes as the "stuff of nightmares".

Strachan admitted raping the girl and charges of serious assault against two male victims in December last year.

The judge said he expected Strachan to be in custody or under supervision for the rest of his life.

News.title: UK's iconic Jodrell Bank telescope faces axe in science cuts
News.content:
The Jodrell Bank Observatory, which has housed the UK's largest telescope for nearly 70 years, has lost its funding and could now close, the BBC understands.

The observatory and its network of telescopes have been pivotal to the country's study of distant galaxies and training future astronomers. Scientists have described the decision as "heartbreaking" and "scientifically misguided".

All scientific observations at Jodrell are expected to cease on the 1 April 2028 unless alternative funding can be found.

The funding body, the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, said it had to focus investment on projects that deliver "the greatest long-term impact".

Prof Brian Cox, professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester - which hosts Jodrell Bank Observatory - described the cuts as "hasty and ill-considered".

"The damage to the UK's science base has already been substantial. I am astonished that UKRI are still ploughing ahead and not working with the Burnham government to find a solution," he said.

The site was first established in 1945 and pioneered radio astronomy and the study of galaxies beyond our own.

It was also pivotal during the Cold War, when it was used to monitor Soviet missiles during the height of nuclear tensions between the USSR and Nato powers.

Its contribution to global scientific efforts earned it Unesco World Heritage status in 2019.

But the UKRI, which has an annual budget of just under Â£10bn, says it has had to cut the observatory's annual Â£2.8m budget because planned research costs for physics and the running of its labs had escalated.

The announcement is part of broader cuts to astronomy, nuclear and particle physics research over the next four years which will also impact on other projects.

The UK will no longer participate in research at the James Clark Maxwell Telescope in Hawaii, which scientists are using to image supermassive black holes at the centre of galaxies.

UKRI has also cut funding for the UK's involvement in two instruments on the Extremely Large Telescope which is being built in Chile to search for signs of life on other Earth-like worlds.

And a number of upgrades to improve experiments at the Large Hadron Collider will not be paid for by the agency.

Prof Michele Dougherty, executive chair of the science and technology branch of UKRI, said: "After listening to our community we have protected core discovery research. However, the situation does require some tough, but necessary, decisions.

"These are never easy choices, but we have made what we feel are the right decisions to bring... a sustainable financial position by 2029/30."

News.title: Amber heat health alerts for parts of UK ahead of next heatwave
News.content:
Amber heat health alerts have been issued for much of eastern England for later this week as temperatures rise again.

The East Midlands, East of England, London, and the South East are all under the amber alerts from 9am on Wednesday until 9am Thursday.

With the temperature forecast to peak in the mid-30s Celsius on Wednesday, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), which issues the alerts, warns that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures.

Yorkshire and the Humber, the West Midlands, and the South West are all under less severe yellow alerts for the same period.

This latest heatwave comes after some of the driest regions of the UK missed their chance of rain over the weekend.

Parts of the northern and western UK saw some rainfall on Saturday and Sunday, with further showers and unsettled conditions expected over the next few days.

But southern parts of the country - where the least amount of rain has fallen - are set to see temperatures climb once again, with more dry and sunny weather in the forecast.

It comes as parts of Wales have officially entered drought status, while parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in "prolonged dry weather", the final stage before drought is declared.

The coming days will only exacerbate dry conditions as another heatwave is expected to be declared, with temperatures peaking around 34-35C (93-95F) in south-east England or the East of England.

News.title: Very strong tide led to West Mersea drownings, relative says
News.content:
A mother and daughter who drowned off the Essex coast were swept out to sea by a "very strong" tide, a relative has said.

Shahin Ahmed said six members of his family were paddling at West Mersea beach when they were knocked off their feet on Wednesday afternoon.

Shelina Rahman, 41, and 15-year-old Sameeha, died in the tragedy, while Ahmed's seven-year-old son Musa was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.

Ahmed said his son, who is from east London, remained on a life support machine at a hospital in London.

Three others were also taken to another hospital by ambulance after the incident. Ahmed said 12 of them were visiting West Mersea that day.

"This was 20 minutes before we were going to go home. The whole day, alhamdulillah (praise be to God), was really nice," Ahmed told Bangladeshi newspaper Surma News.

News.title: TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85
News.content:
TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie has died at the age of 85, his agent has said.

Oddie became a household name in the 1970s as part of zany TV comedy trio The Goodies, before concentrating on his love of wildlife, as one of the original hosts of BBC TV's Springwatch and other shows about birdwatching.

In a statement, David Foster said: "It is with deep sadness that I announce the passing of Bill Oddie, the country's best-loved birder.

"Bill was a multi-talented celebrity â wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist. Yet it was never fame that he valued. Instead he encouraged us to respect and protect the environment."

News.title: Bill Oddie: Comedian who found nature a welcome refuge from mental illness
News.content:
Bill Oddie, who has died at the age of 85, was one of Britain's best known comedians and naturalists.

A product of the Cambridge Footlights, the cradle of so much post-war British comedy, he shot to fame in the 1970s as a member of the anarchic Goodies.

Bird watching was a lifelong passion and he moved into presenting nature programmes, including the BBC's Springwatch.

But his life was plagued by bouts of acute depression which caused repeated admissions to psychiatric hospitals - where Oddie suffered from severe lithium poisoning as a result of his treatment.

News.title: Laura Kuenssberg: Our exclusive behind-the-scenes access at No 10 as Andy Burnham became PM
News.content:
Listening carefully during our interview, it seemed Burnham had distinct gears. He was fluent and passionate on his familiar ground: his desire to sort out social care, his track record in Manchester, his desire to run a government that feels relevant and effective where you live, local leaders eager to make many more decisions and able to spend taxpayers' money more freely without permission from Whitehall.

Those are his core beliefs, arguments he's made hundreds, if not thousands of times.

But when it comes to how he'll apply what he thinks in principle to what he does in practice, that was not always so clear. On social care for example, he's long believed there ought to be a National Care Service, like the NHS. But in a speech on Wednesday, that's not likely to be what he unveils.

Instead, he told me he'd "brought it straight forward", understood to mean speeding up the government review by Baroness Louise Casey of what ought to be done, not saying, "here's the plan".

When it came to questions that are on his desk for the first time, there was a contradiction. Burnham told us all many times that he will stick to the manifesto the country voted for in 2024.

But he's also vowed his arrival in office will usher in the biggest change in four decades. You don't have to be a student of political history to find a mismatch there - he's going to stick broadly to Sir Keir's plan, yet shift the government more fundamentally than leaving the EU, or the financial crash? Really?

And beyond the rhetorical tension in several areas, Burnham gave clear indications that he will apply "new eyes". Will he stick to the home secretary's plans to make migrants wait 10 years or more before they can permanently stay in the UK? He's looking at that again he told me, and hinted that care workers could possibly be exempt.

News.title: Funeral boss who lied about burying dad has shown no remorse, daughter says
News.content:
A woman whose dead father was discovered at an undertaker's three months after his funeral says her hellish ordeal has "crucified" her.

The body of Peter Moody, 65, was found by police alongside 34 others and more than 100 sets of ashes at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024. One of the bodies had been there for a year.

Former funeral director Robert Bush, 48, of Otley, West Yorkshire, will appear at Hull Crown Court later for sentencing. He previously admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.

Peter Moody's daughter Joanne Moody, 48, who is expected to join other families wronged by Bush in the court's public gallery, said: "It's broke me, it's crucified me."

News.title: 'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
News.content:
Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.

Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.

"That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said.

"You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"

Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.

Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless".

"I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said.

"I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back.

"Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."

Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.

Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.

Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".

It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and they have "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.

It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.

News.title: Girlguiding unveils first major redesign of uniform range since 1990
News.content:
Girlguiding has unveiled the first major redesign of its uniform range in more than 30 years, with the aim of allowing its members the "freedom to express themselves".

Under the new, pared-back approach, members will only be required to wear a top from the new range to be considered "in uniform".

The new range has been inspired by feedback from thousands of Guides, Rainbows, Brownies and Rangers that suggested they valued choice and the ability to express their own style.

Girlguiding chief executive Felicity Oswald said "practicality, comfort and sustainability" were at the centre of the redesign, which is the first overhaul of all sections' uniforms since 1990.

The organisation said the uniform combines the charity's heritage with modern colours and prints.

The range is made up of 30 items of clothing, 15 accessories and neckerchiefs - with prices starting at Â£12 for a T-shirt.

Design features include hidden pockets in waist bands, thumb holes and badge sashes which double as cross-body bags.

"It's really comfortable," Isy, 12, who is in the Guides, told BBC Breakfast. "It doesn't feel like the old ones and it's practical to move in."

Poppy, a seven-year-old Brownie, said she wanted "loads of pockets, because I always lose badges, so I wanted somewhere to put them".

She also showed off the new Brownies gilet, which doubles as a pillow. "It has another secret pocket," Poppy added.

News.title: Teens in court accused of murder after stabbing
News.content:
Three teenage boys have appeared in court charged with murder after a fatal stabbing in Luton.

Bedfordshire Police were called to reports of violent disorder at Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 BST on Friday, where a 17-year-old boy was found with stab wounds. He later died in hospital.

A 16-year-old and two 17-year-olds, who cannot be named because of their age, appeared at Luton Magistrates' Court charged with murder, violent disorder and possession of a bladed article.

They were remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.

Another 17-year-old boy arrested over the weekend has been released on bail pending further inquiries, while a further 17-year-old who was arrested on Friday, and who was being treated in hospital for serious injuries, remains in police custody.

Det Ch Insp Nick Gardener said: "We understand this was a shocking incident for the local community and we would like to reassure them that we have had detectives working tirelessly on this case throughout the weekend.

"High visibility patrols and an increased police presence in the area will continue."

News.title: Teen denies record Channel migrant dinghy crossing
News.content:
A teenager accused of endangering the lives of more than 160 migrants by allegedly piloting a record-breaking dinghy crossing of the English Channel is to stand trial.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, originally of Sudan, appeared at Margate Magistrates Court earlier, where he denied endangering lives at sea during the attempt which set off from France last Thursday.

He appeared with the aid of an Arabic interpreter and when asked how he wished to plea, denied having piloted the dinghy.

Atak was then remanded into custody and will next appear at Canterbury Crown Court on 24 August.

Prosecutor Lucie Fish told the court that, on Thursday, a rigid hulled inflatable boat departed the French coast headed towards Dover carrying the migrants.

The vessel was intercepted by Border Force and Atak is alleged to be one of two people controlling its speed and travel.

The boat was poor quality, overcrowded and "appeared to be deflating upon interception", the prosecutor added.

Pictures of Border Security Command towing the dinghy into Dover showed to be about the same size as a standard bus, at 13m (42ft) long.

Endangerment at sea is a new offence that was created by the government under Sir Keir Starmer to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the English Channel.

In June, two men were the first to be jailed for the crime, each receiving sentences of more than two years.

The previous record arrival in a single vessel was 128 people.

Home Office figures show that while the overall number of arrivals this year is down by about 45% on 2025, the number of migrants per boat has gone up.

News.title: Teenager found guilty of murdering drug dealer
News.content:
A teenage boy has been found guilty of murdering a drug dealer, who he robbed at knifepoint with another boy.

The 16-year-old, who cannot be named because of his age, fatally stabbed Hamid Erfani, 46, in a Cheltenham alleyway on 16 December 2025, after allegedly taking cash, drugs and a mobile phone off him.

He was found guilty by a jury at Bristol Crown Court earlier.

The boy, who was 15 at the time of the attack, denied murdering Erfani and claimed he acted in self-defence.

The 16-year-old and a second teenager previously admitted to robbing Erfani.

The court was previously shown CCTV footage of the defendant and the other boy arriving at the scene in Larput Place.

Erfani arrived by car shortly after, parked and walked into the alleyway.

Although the site of the attack was not covered by CCTV, Anna Vigars KC, prosecuting, told the jury witnesses saw that the pair "cornered" Erfani with large knives, to which he "unsurprisingly" did not resist.

News.title: Two women dead after diving trip at Scottish loch
News.content:
A HM Coastguard helicopter and rescue teams from Crinan, Dunoon, Kames and Inveraray joined the search.

Lifeboats from Tighnabruich, Campbeltown and Largs were also sent the scene.

Loch Fyne extends 40 miles (65km) from the Sound of Bute and is the longest sea loch in Scotland.

It is a popular diving location and known for its oysters and seafood.

Keith Waugh, from a local diving club, said it was usually "incredibly safe" and many divers use the area as a training site.

He said the water near St Catherines, known as Seal Reef, has a reef near the surface and a small speedboat at the bottom.

Waugh, who has been diving for decades, said: "We usually explore the reef and see what fish might be there, and zig-zag to the surface.

"The reef starts really close to the surface so it's ideal as a training experience."

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "The deaths are being treated as unexplained and a post mortem examination will take place in due course."
