World.title: The men’s World Cup is over, now Mexico’s women are ready for their moment
World.content:
With the 2026 edition of the men’s World Cup behind us — in which Mexico became the first country to host the sporting event on three separate occasions (1970, 1986 and 2026), leaving an indelible impression on fans worldwide who openly celebrated Mexico’s culture, gastronomy and spirited fandom — the “summer of North American soccer” is coming to a close. Well, sort of. It’s not completely over.

Luckily for fans of fútbol (also known as fút or balompié in Mexico), on-pitch action will resume with a different set of national heroes, as Mexico and the rest of the globe prepare for the upcoming 2027 Women’s World Cup.

World Cup qualifying has already begun

View this post on Instagram A post shared by FOX Sports MX (@foxsportsmx)

Though the tournament won’t actually take place until next summer — hosted in Brazil, marking the first time the FIFA women’s edition will take place on Latin American soil since debuting in 1991 — the race for the trophy is already underway.

Last winter, World Cup qualifying games began; this fall, North American qualifiers, which determine which teams from the region will compete in the World Cup, will conclude.

Here’s a look at Mexico’s national women’s squad and how they have fared so far on their historically arduous journey for sporting glory.

A history of women’s professional soccer in Mexico

Like all women’s sports around the globe, Mexico’s Liga MX Femenil is relatively new and lags behind its male counterpart league in terms of financial support, national investment, media coverage and, as a result, fandom. Despite those barriers, it has been celebrated as a highly successful effort.

The league was announced in late 2016 and officially played its first game in 2017. Since then, it has quietly developed into one of the world’s leading women’s leagues, with the Associated Press reporting that “women’s pro soccer is thriving in Mexico” and The New York Times citing it as the most-watched women’s league on the planet.

That said, it hasn’t been a path without systemic and cultural resistance. Instances of gender bias, sexism and a massive gap in pay and resources have endured. Last summer, Mexican men’s national team legend and former superstar Javier “Chicharito” Hernández was fined by the Mexican Football Federation for demeaning comments on social media that portrayed women as “failing” and “eradicating masculinity,” prompting a response from President Claudia Sheinbaum. In 2023, former Club América Femenil player Scarlett Camberos chose to leave the team and country due to excessive sexual harassment and cyberstalking.

Liga MX Femenil and the birth of the FIFA Women’s World Cup

Though Liga MX Femenil — both its successes and its accentuated reminder of Mexico’s machismo — is relatively nascent, pro women’s soccer in Mexico can be traced back to 1970. Before FIFA’s involvement, an unofficial Women’s World Cup existed as a series of international events independently sponsored by various nations. In those times, Mexico finished in third place at the 1970 World Cup in Italy and ended as runner-up in the largely erased 1971 World Cup in Mexico. It is estimated that the 1971 final at Estadio Azteca drew 110,000 fans. Unofficial tournaments continued throughout the 1980s under non-FIFA-sanctioned entities like the Chinese Taipei Football Association.

Pressure for an official FIFA Women’s World Cup mounted, crescendoing in 1986 when Norwegian delegate Ellen Wille famously urged FIFA to legitimize a women’s tournament in a speech that “changed the course of women’s football,” according to the BBC. In 1988, FIFA organized a trial tournament, the FIFA Women’s Invitation Tournament in China. Overwhelming success resulted in the debut of the official Women’s World Cup in 1991 in China.

Surprisingly, since the FIFA era of the World Cup began, Mexico’s women’s team hasn’t shown much promise. That is finally changing.

The road to the 2027 World Cup is off to a perfect start

In February, Mexico’s women’s team kicked off its World Cup campaign in the preliminary qualifying rounds of the Concacaf W Championship. Concacaf is the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, representing one of FIFA’s six continental governing bodies, which divides competition into regional tournaments that funnel teams into the World Cup every four years. Under this format, all North American, Central American and Caribbean teams face off, with the four quarterfinal winners earning direct berths to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Currently, Mexico is among the remaining eight North American countries with a chance to secure a World Cup ticket this year. It can do so by defeating Haiti on Nov. 28 at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium in Texas.

Mexico’s women haven’t reached a World Cup since 2015. Unlike the Mexican men’s national team — which has qualified 18 times dating back to 1930 — the women have appeared only three times (1999, 2011 and 2015). While the Women’s World Cup has taken place only nine times compared to 23 for the men, El Tri Femenil has struggled to assert regional dominance, holding a 33.3% qualification rate compared to the men’s nearly 80% rate over a much longer period.

A thus-far ‘flawless’ qualifying journey

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Concacaf W (@concacafw)

However, this World Cup cycle is proving to be different: Mexico’s women have been perfect in their qualifying run, an unprecedented feat. In 2023, Mexico also went undefeated for the first time at the Pan American Games in Santiago, Chile, en route to claiming its first gold medal, proving this current team’s success is no fluke.

El Tri has topped Group A of the Concacaf W Championship qualifiers with a flawless 12 points — going unbeaten in four matches and scoring 36 goals while conceding zero. That places them among the continent’s strongest units and makes them favorites to advance. While they have primarily played lower-ranked competition — such as Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, which Mexico defeated 14-0, and Puerto Rico — the core of the 2023 Pan American Games roster remains intact, leading many to consider this the best women’s team Mexico has ever fielded.

‘The Sorceress’ and other Mexico stars to watch

The roster is headlined by Lizbeth “La Maga” Ovalle (whose nickname translates to “The Sorceress”). Having debuted professionally in 2017, the winger — originally from Aguascalientes, who gained fame as one of Mexico’s top scorers with Tigres UANL — set a record in 2025 by signing a US $1.5 million contract with the Orlando Pride of the National Women’s Soccer League, making it one of the most lucrative deals in women’s soccer history. That same year, Ovalle won the FIFA Marta Award for “Best Goal of the Year” at The Best FIFA Football Awards ceremony for her spectacular “scorpion kick” goal.

Behind Ovalle, Mexico boasts a depth of experience and skill with team captain Rebeca Bernal and the formidable striker Charlyn Corral, one of Mexico’s all-time leading goal scorers. Complementing the veteran leadership is “Concacaf Best Young Player” award winner Alice Soto, a 19-year-old dynamic midfielder who debuted professionally at age 13 and has been scoring in Liga MX Femenil ever since.

Why upcoming qualification matters

Against Haiti, Mexico can automatically claim a direct spot in the 2027 World Cup. A loss would send the team to a playoff round for a second chance.

Haiti is coming off its inaugural appearance in the 2023 Women’s World Cup in Australia and New Zealand. Les Grenadières, as they are known, are a rising team led by attacking duo Melchie Dumornay and Nérilia Mondésir, supported by a defense that has allowed only one goal during qualifiers.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mente Mujer (@mentemujer_)

Though the Women’s World Cup does not begin until next June, the matches will stream on Netflix for the first time, with Mexico’s women primed for their deepest run in tournament history. Furthermore, the 2031 Women’s World Cup will be co-hosted by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica, marking the first time Mexico will host the FIFA women’s event.

Until then, El Tri Femenil hopes to deliver the nation its first World Cup trophy — regardless of gender.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: US crimes against Mexico from an immigrant’s perspective
World.content:
There is nothing like living outside of your native country to make you reflect on the meaning of its actions, especially if your native country happens to be the United States of America.

Living in Mexico, of course, makes you an automatic representative of your country. This is not a fair position to be in, but it is the story of immigrants everywhere. For the most part, I benefit from my country of origin: whereas plenty of people in the U.S. might look down on an immigrant from Mexico, here it is the opposite. Most people expect me to be cool and interesting, and maybe a little sneaky, scary or both.

We may all be individuals, but the human brain only has so much capacity to think of people as individuals. Gather too many foreign individuals into the same place, and the borders between us blur and blend until we are collectively “others.”

Proud and ashamed

Many things about the U.S. make me very, very proud to be from there: like jazz music, the advancement of civil rights and feminism. First in flight. Customer service agents who are mostly empowered to actually help you. Clean public restrooms with toilet paper, for free!

Other aspects of my home country, however, make me feel deeply, deeply ashamed. A less-than-stellar record when it comes to genocide and enslavement, for example. And oh, Lord, influential religious leaders who would love to send us back to those “good old days.” Deliver us!

When it comes to current events, our treatment of immigrants is at the top of my list right now.

In case you have been protecting your peace more than I have and have abstained from the news, here is a sad summary: Donald Trump returned to office with as much of a mandate as you could suppose to reduce the “out of control” immigration in the U.S.

The killing of innocents and deportation of US citizens

More Latinos in the U.S. than ever voted for him. Strangely, they seemed to believe his promise that he would only target and deport “the criminals” among them. Who would not get behind that?

As it turns out, there are a lot fewer “immigrant criminals” than most people thought. So, unfortunately for the law-abiders, the net was pretty much immediately cast much, much wider to meet detention quotas set by the administration. It caught mothers and fathers taking their children to school. It caught lots and lots of people here legally, papers be damned. It caught those who were brought as children and have known no other life than that of an American.

On top of the generalized horror of being torn from one’s life, there is the very suspicious fact that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been extremely cagey, caught in lies more than once. It is a fight every time a local official wants to enter a (privately run) detention facility. Those who have come out of them have described the places as unfit for human beings. Rotting food, freezing temperatures and medical needs that are ignored. It is not hard to imagine how over 50 people have died since detentions were ramped up upon Trump’s return, some by suicide. Seventeen of these deaths have been of Mexican nationals (14 in custody, three during “operations”).

A lack of institutional control

Then, of course, there are the vehicle stops and shootings under extremely suspicious circumstances. One of the latest, of course, was that of a Mexican national, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who turned out not to even be ICE’s target. ICE’s story is that he tried to “weaponize his vehicle” against them. Witnesses say it was quite the opposite. The feds had to be blocked from deporting the witnesses. Weird behavior from an institution that has nothing to hide, right?

In short, things are truly out of control.

The U.S. and Mexico are supposed to be allies. What is going on here?

‘A general lack of accountability’

The main thing that is going on, I believe, is that the wrong people are in charge. Unhappy people voted them in, believing their lies about what the source of their unhappiness actually stemmed from. A threadbare social safety net paired with barely-there labor laws that are happy to let people simply fall through the net and onto the concrete pavement? Nah, that cannot be it … transgender people and immigrants, that is who is hurting you!

Social media — what was supposed to bring us together — and a general lack of accountability to the truth that the internet age has wrought have been excellent at getting people all riled up for stupid reasons.

The U.S. is really pushing it with Mexico right now.

Can Mexico do anything about it?

I personally think that is doubtful, but who knows? I have been wrong before. But if ICE cannot even be held accountable for its on-camera killings of U.S. citizens, who is going to put a boot on its neck over immigrant killings?

And when the offending country has been essentially in charge of international justice for decades, it is hard to tap the brakes. After all, who do you go to for help when the police themselves are corrupt?

Mexico, of course, understands this conundrum in a literal sense. But Mexico also does not claim to be the distributor of justice for the world, either.

Of all the words I might use to describe Mexicans, “proud” would be in the top five. While it seems that a few insults here and there will always be tolerated because of the particular power dynamic the two countries have, you cannot just start letting its citizens die and not even apologize for it.

Mexico files criminal complaints

Claudia Sheinbaum, thankfully, is not letting this go. Criminal complaints, cease-and-desist letters to the private companies in charge of detention, the United Nations. They are going at it from all angles.

The Secretariat of Foreign Affairs is “filing a criminal complaint against whoever is responsible.”

But, gosh. “Whoever is responsible.” Hmm. There is our first issue right there.

Would that be the president, for insisting that as many immigrants be tossed out of the U.S. as possible? Stephen Miller, the architect of the whole thing? Agency heads? Those who hire and “train” (or don’t) ICE officers? The private companies who feel no need to provide adequate living conditions? The offending/negligent immigration officers themselves? It truly is a long list of candidates.

The known reality, of course, is that in the end, it is unlikely anyone will be held to account. I mean, we cannot even get the U.S. to acknowledge that it dropped a bomb on an Iranian girls’ school, killing hundreds of children. Sanctity of life, indeed.

‘The twin monsters of incompetence and cruelty’

How are we supposed to get anyone who has been given “free rein” to carry out the president’s signature plan to play fair?

One of the biggest crimes that humans commit against each other is allowing the twin monsters of incompetence and cruelty to go on … and right now, those twin monsters have the full backing of the U.S. federal government.

This is what happens when you remove the shackles of accountability from institutions filled with the kinds of people who see the world as a fight between those who hunt and those who get hunted.

And many people who work in ICE fancy themselves hunters; they like to prey on people who are running or scared, or just trying to stay out of trouble’s way. They are hunted by the same types of people who used to catch (and torture) runaway slaves. They sniff out fear and relish the capture.

So here we are, many of us, living in a country that has welcomed us in ways that the U.S. would not dream of welcoming our neighbors. It is a strange and sad position to be in. It is also worth remembering that the tables could always turn.

We are the “others” here, after all.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: World Cup glow fades as tariffs and security challenges take center stage
World.content:
This week marked the end of the 2026 FIFA World Cup and the conclusion of Mexico’s third turn as a host country. The week opened with President Sheinbaum’s attendance at the World Cup final in New Jersey, where brief exchanges with Trump, Carney and other officials set the tone for USMCA review talks that resumed in Mexico City. Sheinbaum later called the tournament a diplomatic success, and world leaders had high praise for Mexico’s performance as a host nation.

As World Cup excitement faded, security stories dominated elsewhere. Zacatecas authorities linked the multihomicide of 10 people, including a former mayor, to extortion and official collusion, while a Sinaloa Cartel kingpin, “El Mayo” Zambada, was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. While El Mayo’s court case has run its course, infighting within the cartel he once led prompted 900 more troops to deploy to Mazatlán, Sinaloa. The week ended with the annoucement of sweeping U.S. sanctions against an opposing organized crime syndicate, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

On the economic front, inflation fell to its lowest level since 2020 and a new round of U.S. tariffs largely spared Mexico.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Security: Homicides fall, but high-profile violence persists

México state’s homicide rate has dropped to its lowest level in 19 years, officials said Wednesday, citing a “unified command” strategy that cut daily killings by 58% since September 2024. In Morelos, Governor Margarita González’s administration touted a 54% homicide drop alongside improving public perceptions of safety, even as the state investigated the murder of a mayor with alleged ties to organized crime.

That progress contrasted with events in Sinaloa and Oaxaca. The Zacatecas multihomicide, which included a former mayor of Sombrerete and two Fresnillo officials, is being investigated as a possible case of extortion and collusion between criminals and public officials. In Mazatlán, a string of targeted attacks over the past two weeks left at least a dozen dead, prompting the arrival of 900 additional troops, bringing the security deployment to more than 1,300 personnel. Authorities attributed the violence to the ongoing feud between Sinaloa Cartel factions that intensified after Zambada’s 2024 arrest. Separately, journalist Alejandro Leyva was shot dead in Oaxaca on Wednesday, the second journalist killed in Mexico in less than a week. Federal prosecutors took over the case at the request of state officials.

On Thursday, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned 39 individuals and 16 companies linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, including the CJNG’s new leader, Juan Carlos Valencia González, a.k.a. “El Pelón.” The U.S. called it the largest action ever taken against the group, and Mexico’s financial intelligence unit blocked the same accounts.

El Mayo’s sentencing and its aftermath

Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, Sinaloa Cartel co-founder, was sentenced to life in prison and ordered to forfeit $15 billion by a U.S. federal judge on Monday. In court, Zambada urged young people to avoid a life of crime. President Sheinbaum said she agreed with the sentiment but declined to explicitly endorse a message from a convicted trafficker. Mexican officials said Wednesday it remains unclear whether Zambada could ever be transferred to a Mexican prison, a decision that depends on whether the Attorney General’s Office pursues extradition.

Trade and economy: Inflation eases, tariff fights continue

Mexico’s annual inflation rate fell to 3.10% in the first half of July, the lowest for any comparable period since December 2020, driven largely by falling produce prices. Meanwhile, the tariffs Mexico implemented this year on countries without free trade agreements — chiefly targeting China — cut affected imports by 23.2% between January and May, even as overall imports from Asia rose on surging Taiwanese semiconductor purchases.

On the U.S. side, President Trump’s re-imposed tariffs took effect Friday on dozens of countries, but Mexico avoided major new costs: About 80% of Mexican exports remain tariff-free under the USMCA, according to Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard. While dozens of other countries faced increased tariffs, Mexico’s rate remained at 10%. The U.S. gave Mexico a heads-up before the announcement, as U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer visited Mexico City this week to meet with Sheinbaum and press for stricter automotive rules of origin in the ongoing USMCA review, citing a growing U.S. auto trade deficit with Mexico.

Health, migration and infrastructure

Deputy Health Minister Eduardo Clark reported that 30 public hospital projects have been completed since October 2024, adding 1,474 beds toward a goal of 9,000 by 2030, with 33 more projects due this year. Health officials also moved to calm fears over a U.S. Cyclospora outbreak initially attributed to lettuce from Guanajuato: After the FDA retracted a positive test result, Mexican authorities said there was no evidence of contamination in Mexican-grown produce.

A new report from the Migration Policy Institute found the Mexican-born population in the U.S. has fallen to 11.1 million, down more than 500,000 since a 2007 peak, a decline researchers said could accelerate amid stepped-up immigration enforcement. On infrastructure, the government launched the second construction phase of its passenger rail program, which will link central Mexico to Saltillo and the Pacific coast, while separate data showed Mexico is drawing more international tourists but earning less per visitor as land-crossing traffic outpaces higher-spending air arrivals.

Also this week, the federal government joined Jalisco state officials in announcing a joint effort to rehabilitate Guadalajara’s aging water infrastructure and curb industrial contamination of the Lerma River, while Mexico City announced three regional forums to debate social media and AI regulation for minors.

Looking ahead

USMCA negotiations are set to continue following this week’s talks with Greer, with both sides aiming for interim agreements before year’s end even as the review process stretches toward 2036. Security officials face pressure to build on regional and national homicide declines while containing the Sinaloa Cartel factional violence driving unrest in Mazatlán and elsewhere. Investigations into the Zacatecas multihomicide and the killing of journalist Alejandro Leyva remain open, with federal authorities now involved in both cases.

Energy Finance · Jamaica

Key Facts —The loan. IDB Invest is arranging an US$80 million financing package for Jamaica Public Service, the country’s main electricity utility. —The structure. It splits into an A Loan of up to US$50 million and a second tranche of up to US$30 million in blended finance. —The purpose. The larger tranche refinances debt-service due over three years and funds capital spending through 2029; the blended tranche funds grid hardening. —The trigger. JPS faces heavy costs from storm restoration, including work after Hurricane Melissa. —The history. JPS previously signed a US$100 million IDB financing package in February 2024 for network upgrades.

Jamaica’s main power utility is turning to a development lender to steady its finances after a run of destructive storms. IDB Invest is arranging an US$80 million package to help Jamaica Public Service refinance debt and harden its grid.

Jamaica Public Service is the island’s main electricity utility. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

The financing package

IDB Invest, the private-sector arm of the Inter-American Development Bank, is lining up an US$80 million loan for Jamaica Public Service, known as JPS. The Jamaica Gleaner reported the plan on July 24, 2026.

The package is structured in two parts. An IDB Invest A Loan of up to US$50 million would refinance debt-service payments falling due over the next three years and cover additional capital spending through 2029, while a second tranche of up to US$30 million in blended finance would fund further grid hardening and infrastructure upgrades.

Why JPS needs the money

The utility has been battered by successive storms, including hurricanes in July 2024 and October 2025 and restoration tied to Hurricane Melissa. Those events left JPS with unplanned expenditure exceeding US$300 million for repairs and recovery.

Refinancing near-term debt service eases pressure on the utility’s cash flow while it rebuilds. The blended-finance tranche is aimed at making the network more resilient to future storms.

Building on earlier support

The new package builds on a US$100 million financing deal JPS signed with the IDB in February 2024. That earlier program funded transmission and distribution upgrades, reductions in energy losses, and digital and technology investments.

Together, the deals underscore the development bank’s role in financing Caribbean grid modernization. Small island utilities face rising costs from stronger storms and the need to integrate more renewable power.

What it means for Jamaica

A more resilient grid matters for households and businesses that bear the cost of prolonged outages after storms. Reliable power is also central to Jamaica’s tourism-heavy economy and its push to add renewable capacity.

The financing does not by itself lower electricity bills, but it supports the investment JPS says is needed to keep the lights on. Final terms remain subject to the lender’s approval process.

World.title: Peru El Niño Costero 2026 Pushes Global Food Prices Higher
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Climate & Economy · Peru

Key Facts —The alert. Peru’s ENFEN commission activated an El Niño Costero alert on February 13, 2026. —The forecast. The event is expected to run from around March into November, mostly weak with possible moderate intensity around mid-year. —The duration. Recent studies suggest the warming could last into early 2027. —The crops. Agricultural activity fell 2.06% in March, with mangoes, coffee and cacao among the hardest hit. —The fish. Anchovy fishing restrictions have pushed fishmeal prices up more than 75% from a year earlier.

Peru is bracing for a long stretch of unsettled weather along its Pacific coast. The country’s El Niño monitors say the current coastal warming will persist into late 2026, pressuring both farms and fisheries.

Peru’s anchovy fishery is highly sensitive to El Niño warming. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A long, mostly weak event

Peru’s multi-agency study commission ENFEN activated an El Niño Costero alert on February 13, 2026. It projected that the event would begin around March, persist until November and remain mostly weak, with a chance of moderate intensity around the middle of the year.

More recent assessments suggest the warming could last into early 2027 and may intensify toward the end of 2026. El Niño Costero refers to warming concentrated near Peru’s coast, distinct from the basin-wide Pacific pattern.

ENFEN, which stands for the Multisectoral Commission for the National Study of the El Niño Phenomenon, brings together oceanographers, meteorologists and fisheries experts. Its job is to translate sea-temperature data into practical warnings for government agencies and the public.

The distinction between a coastal event and the larger El Niño–Southern Oscillation matters because a localised warming can still deliver heavy rains and disrupt marine life even when the broader Pacific looks unremarkable.

For readers outside Latin America, it helps to think of El Niño Costero as a warm patch that hugs the shoreline rather than stretching across the entire ocean. That concentrated heat can supercharge local storms and push fish into cooler, deeper water, creating economic headaches that are felt well before any global climate headlines appear.

Pressure on coastal crops

The stakes are high because many of Peru’s most valuable export crops grow in the coastal valleys that El Niño Costero hits hardest. Agricultural activity fell 2.06% in March, with mangoes, coffee and cacao among the crops most affected.

Analysts warn that if sea-surface temperatures climb beyond weak levels, damage to farming could deepen. Shifts in rainfall and heat can disrupt flowering, harvest timing and crop quality in sensitive valleys.

Peru’s coastal agriculture relies on a delicate calendar. Mango trees, for instance, need a dry period to trigger flowering, and unseasonal rains can slash yields.

Coffee and cacao, often grown on hillsides just inland, are vulnerable to both excessive moisture and temperature swings that encourage fungal diseases. When output drops, the effects travel quickly through export channels to buyers in North America, Europe and Asia who count on Peruvian shipments to fill supermarket shelves.

A hit to the anchovy fishery

El Niño also disrupts the cold, nutrient-rich waters that sustain Peru’s anchovy, the backbone of its fishmeal industry. Fishing restrictions tied to the warming have driven fishmeal prices up more than 75% from a year earlier.

Peru is one of the world’s top suppliers of fishmeal, a key ingredient in fish and shrimp feed. Higher prices ripple through global aquaculture supply chains far beyond Peru’s shores.

The anchovy fleet operates under a strict quota system that is adjusted as ocean conditions change. When warm water pushes anchovy schools deeper or farther south, the government often shortens the fishing season or reduces the allowable catch to protect the stock.

That conservation logic is sound, but it immediately tightens the global supply of fishmeal, raising costs for salmon farmers in Norway and Chile and for shrimp producers in Southeast Asia.

A mixed outlook

Not all effects are negative. Forecasters at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts have flagged that parts of Peru could see wetter conditions, which in some areas can help replenish soil moisture and reservoirs.

The balance of risks will depend on how strong the event becomes and how long it lasts. Authorities continue to monitor coastal temperatures for signs of intensification into 2027.

What to watch next is whether the moderate-intensity window around mid-year widens or stays narrow. Another open question is how quickly the anchovy biomass recovers if the warming eases, because that will determine whether fishmeal prices stay elevated through the end of the year.

On land, the key unknown is whether the extra rainfall arrives at the right moment for crops that have already suffered a dry spell, or whether it comes too fast and causes flooding in the narrow coastal valleys. The answers to those questions will shape Peru’s economic trajectory well beyond 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long will El Niño Costero last in Peru?

ENFEN projected it would run from around March into November 2026, and recent studies suggest the warming could persist into early 2027.

Which crops are most affected?

Agricultural activity fell 2.06% in March, with mangoes, coffee and cacao among the crops hit hardest along the coast.

Why are fishmeal prices rising?

Anchovy fishing restrictions tied to the warming have pushed fishmeal prices up more than 75% from a year earlier, affecting global feed markets.

Investigations · Brazil

Key Facts —The step. Brazil’s Federal Police will investigate businessman Daniel Vorcaro’s dealings with Cemig Sim, according to a report published on July 26, 2026. —The figure. Vorcaro is the controlling shareholder of Banco Master, the private bank at the center of a major fraud investigation. —The backdrop. The Central Bank liquidated Banco Master in late 2025, and Vorcaro was arrested in November 2025. —The company. Cemig Sim is the retail energy arm of Cemig, the power utility controlled by the state of Minas Gerais. —The status. The matter is an investigation; no charges related to Cemig have been confirmed and those involved are presumed innocent.

Brazil’s sprawling Banco Master investigation is reaching into the energy sector. Federal Police plan to examine banker Daniel Vorcaro’s business dealings with Cemig Sim, the retail arm of Minas Gerais utility Cemig.

Cemig is the power utility controlled by the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What the report says

According to a report published on July 26, 2026, Brazil’s Federal Police will investigate the business dealings between Daniel Vorcaro and Cemig Sim. The step widens an investigation that has already touched banking, politics and a web of companies linked to the businessman.

Cemig Sim is the retail energy-services arm of Cemig, the electricity company controlled by the state of Minas Gerais. The reported focus is on Vorcaro’s dealings; the utility itself has not been accused of wrongdoing.

The Banco Master scandal

Vorcaro is the controlling shareholder of Banco Master, a mid-sized private bank whose collapse became one of Brazil’s largest banking scandals. The Central Bank moved to liquidate the institution in late 2025, and the Federal Police launched an operation into alleged financial fraud.

Vorcaro was arrested in November 2025 as part of that operation. Investigators have been mapping a network of companies connected to him and his associates, examining flows of money and corporate control.

Why the Cemig angle matters

Extending the inquiry to a dealing with a state-controlled utility raises the profile of the case and its potential political dimensions. Brazilian authorities have signaled interest in understanding companies tied to public officials and candidates as the 2026 electoral cycle unfolds.

For Cemig, one of Brazil’s largest listed utilities, the reported scrutiny concerns a counterparty rather than the company’s own conduct. The distinction is important, and no finding of wrongdoing by Cemig has been reported.

What happens next

As an investigation, the process may take months and could proceed without producing charges related to Cemig. Everyone involved is entitled to the presumption of innocence under Brazilian law.

The case continues to unfold across multiple fronts, from the banking failure to the businessman’s corporate holdings. Further steps will depend on what investigators find as they examine the reported dealings.

Cut flowers are among the goods affected, alongside some apparel, foods and cosmetics. —The exposure. In 2025 the United States took about 80% of Colombia’s flower exports by value. —The jobs. Colombia’s floriculture industry sustains roughly 130,000 jobs, most held by women. —The cost. Colombia’s flower growers, who supply a large share of the bouquets sold in the United States, are pushing back against a rising US tariff. A duty on affected Colombian goods climbed to 12.5% on July 24, squeezing one of the country’s signature export industries.

Colombia is one of the world’s largest exporters of cut flowers. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A higher duty on flowers

A US tariff on a specific set of Colombian products rose from 10% to 12.5% on July 24, 2026. Cut flowers sit among the affected goods, together with some apparel and textiles, candies and chocolates, certain processed foods, cosmetics and select manufactured items.

The increase compounds a 10% duty first imposed in 2025, the first US tariff on Colombian flowers in more than a decade. That earlier move reversed the near zero-tariff access Colombian growers had long enjoyed under the US-Colombia trade agreement.

Why the stakes are high

The United States accounted for about 80% of Colombia’s flower exports by value in 2025, making the market difficult to replace. Colombia is one of the world’s largest suppliers of cut flowers, shipping hundreds of millions of stems for peak dates such as Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day.

The industry sustains roughly 130,000 jobs, the majority held by women, many in rural areas around Bogotá and Medellín. Growers warn that higher duties could erode margins and pressure employment across the supply chain.

A broader trade dispute

The flower tariff is part of a wider strain in US-Colombia trade. The industry group ANDI estimates that about US$5 billion of Colombian exports to the United States is at risk across all affected sectors, roughly 30% of the country’s shipments to that market.

Exporters have urged both governments to resolve the dispute and restore predictable access. For now, growers face higher landed costs in their most important market at a time of thin margins and intense global competition.

What changed for Colombian flowers?

A US tariff on affected Colombian goods, including cut flowers, rose from 10% to 12.5% on July 24, 2026, on top of a 10% duty first imposed in 2025.

How dependent is Colombia on the US flower market?

The United States took about 80% of Colombia’s flower exports by value in 2025, so the market is hard to replace.

How many jobs depend on the sector?

Colombia’s floriculture industry supports roughly 130,000 jobs, most of them held by women.

World.title: Colombia’s Colectora Transmission Line to Finish in 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Energy Infrastructure · Colombia

Key Facts —The project. Grupo Energía Bogotá’s Colectora line will connect wind and solar parks in La Guajira to Colombia’s national grid. —Progress. The government said the project reached about 90% completion by June 2026 and is due to finish in 2026. —Scale. The 228-kilometer line runs between the Colectora and Cuestecitas substations and requires 1,027 towers. —Capacity. It is designed to carry about 1,050 megawatts from 15 wind parks and one solar park. —Investment. The project represents an investment of close to US$300 million.

A transmission line four years in the making is finally nearing the finish in Colombia’s windy northeast. The Colectora project would unlock more than a gigawatt of stalled wind and solar capacity in La Guajira.

Wind turbines in La Guajira, the focus of Colombia’s renewable-energy push. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A long-delayed line nears completion

Colombia’s Energy Ministry and Grupo Energía Bogotá said the Colectora transmission project had reached about 90% completion by June 2026 and would be finished this year. The line had faced roughly four years of delays tied to permitting, the pandemic and more than 235 prior-consultation processes with local communities.

The 228-kilometer line connects the Colectora and Cuestecitas substations, with 1,027 towers projected across its two sections. It is one of the largest transmission works underway in the country.

Prior consultation is a right enshrined in Colombian law and international conventions that requires project developers to engage with Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities before work can begin on their lands. In La Guajira, home to the Wayúu people, this meant hundreds of individual dialogues that had to be completed before towers could rise or cables could be strung.

The sheer volume of these processes, layered on top of pandemic-era restrictions, explains much of the four-year wait.

Why La Guajira matters

The Colectora line is designed to carry about 1,050 megawatts from 15 wind parks and one solar park in La Guajira, a peninsula with some of the strongest and most consistent winds in South America. Without the line, those parks cannot deliver their output to Colombia’s National Interconnected System.

The project carries an investment of close to US$300 million. Officials describe it as a backbone linking the country’s renewable frontier to demand centers elsewhere in Colombia.

La Guajira’s geography makes it uniquely valuable for wind generation. Trade winds sweep across the flat, arid peninsula with speeds that are unusually high and steady compared with most inland sites.

That translates into capacity factors—the percentage of time a plant actually produces power—that can far exceed those of wind farms in less exposed regions. For a country that has historically leaned on hydroelectric dams, tapping this resource represents a structural shift in how electricity is sourced.

What completion would mean

Finishing the line would remove a key bottleneck that has held back Colombia’s wind build-out for years. Enlaza, the Grupo Energía Bogotá unit running the works, said the connected wind parks would enter operation one and a half to two years after construction is completed.

The rollout is central to Colombia’s goal of diversifying an electricity mix long dependent on hydropower, which leaves the grid exposed during dry spells and El Niño. Adding Guajira wind is meant to improve reliability and lower emissions over time.

A diversified grid matters because hydropower, while clean and cheap, is vulnerable to weather cycles. During strong El Niño events, rainfall drops and reservoir levels can fall sharply, forcing the country to fall back on more expensive thermal plants that burn gas or coal.

Wind from La Guajira tends to blow most strongly during the dry season, which means it can act as a natural hedge, filling the gap precisely when hydro output dips.

What to watch next is whether the wind parks themselves stay on schedule. Even with the transmission line in place, each park must complete its own financing, turbine installation and grid-connection tests.

Another open question is how the Wayúu communities, who participated in the prior consultations, will experience the project’s operational phase and whether the promised social investments materialize as expected. Finally, observers will be watching whether the Colectora line’s completion encourages regulators to approve additional transmission corridors in the region, which could multiply La Guajira’s contribution to the national grid.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Colectora project?

It is a 228-kilometer transmission line built by Grupo Energía Bogotá to connect wind and solar parks in La Guajira to Colombia’s national grid.

How far along is it?

The government said the project reached about 90% completion by June 2026 and is expected to be finished during 2026.

How much capacity will it carry?

The line is designed to move about 1,050 megawatts from 15 wind parks and one solar park.

World.title: De la Espriella to Close Embassies in Cuba, Nicaragua
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Foreign Policy · Colombia

Key Facts —The plan. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella says he will close about 14 Colombian embassies after taking office on August 7, 2026. —The list. Missions named for closure include those in Cuba, Nicaragua, Hungary, Romania, the Czech Republic, Azerbaijan, Vietnam, Malaysia, Algeria, Ghana, Senegal, Ethiopia, Haiti and Barbados. —The break. He also announced plans to cut diplomatic ties with Cuba and Nicaragua to what his team calls a minimum. —The additions. De la Espriella said he would reopen Colombia’s embassy in Israel and open a mission in Nigeria. —The rationale. His team frames the cuts as reducing spending and shifting resources toward national security, followed by an audit of remaining missions.

Colombia’s incoming government is preparing a sharp reset of the country’s diplomatic map, aiming to concentrate its overseas presence on strategic allies. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella says he will close about 14 embassies and dramatically downgrade ties with Cuba and Nicaragua from his first days in office.

The Palacio de San Carlos in Bogotá, seat of Colombia’s Foreign Ministry. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

The announced closures

De la Espriella, who is set to assume the presidency on August 7, 2026, confirmed plans to shut roughly 14 of Colombia’s diplomatic missions, a move that would sharply prune its foreign network. The list of posts earmarked for closure spans three continents and includes embassies in Cuba, Nicaragua, Hungary, Romania, the Czech Republic, Azerbaijan, Vietnam, Malaysia, Algeria, Ghana, Senegal, Ethiopia, Haiti and Barbados, touching every major geopolitical theater from Central Europe to Southeast Asia, West Africa and the Caribbean.

The incoming president framed the measure as a fiscal discipline tool designed to reduce public spending and re-channel savings toward pressing national security needs at home. His team added that the closures would be followed immediately by a technical audit of Colombia’s remaining missions during the administration’s first 100 days, with the aim of streamlining operations and reassessing diplomatic footprints.

A turn away from Havana and Managua

De la Espriella singled out Cuba and Nicaragua, announcing he would reduce Colombia’s engagement with their governments to a minimum, a stance his incoming administration described as a principled refusal to extend political legitimacy to regimes it labels dictatorships. The decision effectively ends high-level bilateral diplomacy with Havana and Managua, leaving only the barest consular and humanitarian links in place.

The clean break marks a stark departure from the outgoing government of Gustavo Petro, who cultivated notably warmer relations with Havana and other left-led states, often positioning Colombia as a mediator between ideological camps. It quickly realigns Colombia’s incoming foreign policy with conservative governments in the region that share a deep distrust of leftist authoritarianism, reinforcing a broader rightward shift in Latin American diplomacy.

New priorities

Alongside the downsizing, De la Espriella said he would reopen Colombia’s long-shuttered embassy in Israel and open a new mission in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous nation and largest economy. The twin moves signal a deliberate pivot toward deeper security and economic partnerships with key Middle Eastern and West African players that the incoming government views as high-potential allies.

Omar Bula, the designated foreign minister, will oversee the entire overhaul, which is expected to reshape where Colombia maintains a resident diplomatic presence and how it delivers services to its citizens abroad. Consular support for the affected countries would typically be reassigned to nearby embassies or handled by honorary consuls, ensuring that Colombians in the shuttered jurisdictions still have access to essential documentation and assistance.

What to watch

Closing embassies is an executive prerogative, but the scale of the proposed cuts would be unusual for a country that has traditionally maintained a broad, if thinly stretched, diplomatic network across the globe. Analysts will watch how quickly the changes are enacted, whether affected countriesu2014many of them long-standing partnersu2014respond with reciprocal measures or diplomatic protests, and how the move affects Colombia’s influence in multilateral forums.

The announcements remain pledges until the new government takes office and issues formal decrees following the inauguration on August 7, 2026. Their final scope may shift as the promised audit of missions proceeds and as political opposition or logistical challenges prompt adjustments during the transition period.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many embassies would close?

President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella says he plans to close about 14 Colombian embassies after taking office on August 7, 2026.

Which relationships would be downgraded?

He announced plans to reduce diplomatic ties with Cuba and Nicaragua to a minimum, citing opposition to governments he considers dictatorships.

Is Colombia opening any new missions?

Yes. De la Espriella said he would reopen the embassy in Israel and open a new mission in Nigeria.

In the first quarter of 2026 the terminal handled 411,000 TEUs, a 3% year-on-year rise and a record for that period. —Scale. The container terminal at Paranaguá has opened 2026 at a record pace. TCP moved 835,000 TEUs in the first half, extending its lead as the busiest box terminal in southern Brazil.

The Port of Paranaguá in Paraná state, southern Brazil. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A record first half

Terminal de Contêineres de Paranaguá, known as TCP, said it handled 835,000 twenty-foot equivalent units in the first six months of 2026. That marked a record for the period and a 4% increase over the 803,000 TEUs moved in the same span of 2025.

The first-half result built on a strong opening quarter, when TCP handled 411,000 TEUs between January and March. That figure was 3% higher than a year earlier and itself a record for the quarter.

Southern Brazil’s busiest box terminal

TCP moved a record 1.663 million TEUs across all of 2025, consolidating its position as the largest container terminal in southern Brazil according to the national waterway regulator ANTAQ. The terminal serves export-heavy supply chains in Paraná and neighboring states.

Vessel traffic also set a mark in 2025, with 1,019 ship calls, the first time the terminal exceeded 1,000 berthings in a single year. Reefer cargo, used for chilled and frozen goods, passed 70,000 containers for the first time.

Investment and outlook

TCP has highlighted rail expansion and infrastructure upgrades as it seeks to move more cargo inland by train rather than road. The terminal presented those plans at the Intermodal South America 2026 logistics fair earlier this year.

Sustained growth in agricultural and industrial exports has underpinned the terminal’s volumes. Continued gains would depend on harvest cycles, global freight demand and the pace of Brazil’s port and rail investments.

TCP moved a record 1.663 million TEUs in 2025 and is the largest container terminal in southern Brazil, according to regulator ANTAQ.

São Paulo’s water utility Sabesp is moving to fold power company EMAE fully into its structure. Shareholders vote on July 30 on a merger that would delist EMAE and make it a wholly owned subsidiary.

Sabesp, the São Paulo state water and sanitation utility. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

The merger on the table

Sabesp and Empresa Metropolitana de Águas e Energia, known as EMAE, executed a merger protocol in June 2026 under which Sabesp will absorb every EMAE share it does not already hold. Extraordinary general meetings of both companies are scheduled for July 30, 2026 to vote on the plan.

If approved, EMAE would become a wholly owned subsidiary of Sabesp and its stock would be removed from B3’s Traditional listing segment. Sabesp has estimated the transaction costs at roughly R$4.45 million (about US$0.8 million).

How Sabesp got here

Sabesp acquired control of EMAE in January 2026, purchasing about 74.9% of its voting capital for roughly R$682 million (about US$126 million). It followed with a mandatory tender offer for remaining common shares priced at R$49.46 (about US$9.20) each.

In March 2026 Sabesp bought the Oceania investment fund, which held a strategic EMAE stake, for R$171.6 million (about US$32 million). Those steps lifted Sabesp’s direct and indirect holdings and set the stage for a full merger.
