World.title: Ministry of Health & Wellness welcomes return of Vital Statistics Unit to KHMH
World.content:
Ministry of Health & Wellness welcomes return of Vital Statistics Unit to KHMH

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Health & Wellness announced the reopening of the Vital Statistics Unit (VSU) Office at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital (KHMH), marking a significant advancement in providing easier access to essential birth and death registration services for the people of Belize.

The Ministry says that the unit is conveniently positioned at the primary entrance within the Admissions & Billing Unit, thereby reducing the need for unnecessary travel and enhancing the efficiency of this crucial public service.

Minister of Health & Wellness Kevin Bernard, is optimistic and enthusiastic about this new development.

He believes that “The reopening of the Vital Statistics Unit at Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital is a significant achievement for our country and, more importantly, for the families we serve. Birth and death registration are essential services and making them available where they are needed most reflects our commitment to delivering more accessible, efficient, and people-centred healthcare and public services. I thank my colleague, Hon. Anthony Sylvestre, the Ministry of the Attorney General, and the management of KHMH for their partnership and shared commitment to serving the people of Belize. This is an excellent example of what we can accomplish when ministries and public institutions work together with a common purpose.”

The Ministry also extended gratitude to the Board of Directors, Chief Executive Officer, Management, and staff of the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital Authority for their support in making the new office a reality. The Ministry also congratulates the Vital Statistics Unit personnel managing the KHMH office.

The Ministry reaffirmed its ongoing commitment to bolster interagency partnerships within the Government to deliver more efficient public services and further enhance the welfare of all Belizeans.

World.title: Belize’s Population reaches 428,644 in 2026, World Population review estimates
World.content:
Belize’s Population reaches 428,644 in 2026, World Population review estimates

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s population has reached an estimated 428,644 people as of January 1, 2026, according to data published by World Population Review, placing the country 177th among the world’s most populous nations.

The figure represents a 1.63 percent annual growth rate, with Belize accounting for less than 0.01 percent of the global population.

The population estimate shows continued growth from 422,924 people recorded in 2025 and 390,812 in 2020.

Belize City remains the country’s largest urban centre, with an estimated 66,409 residents, followed by Belmopan with 22,956 and San Ignacio-Santa Elena with 22,157. San Pedro Town has an estimated population of 16,453, while Orange Walk Town has 14,910.

Overall, about 40.75 percent of Belize’s population lives in urban areas, a share that continues to increase annually.

The data also highlights Belize’s relatively young population, with a median age of 28.3 years, compared with a global median of 31 years.

Males account for 50.43 percent of the population and females 49.57 percent, while life expectancy at birth is estimated at 74.1 years.

The figures compiled by World Population Review draw on United Nations population estimates and projections, as well as data from the Statistical Institute of Belize.

World.title: International News: Shooting at Seattle Food Festival claims 3 lives, several injured
World.content:
International News: Shooting at Seattle Food Festival claims 3 lives, several injured

By Zoila Palma: Three people were killed and several others wounded, including a 2-year-old child, after two people allegedly exchanged gunfire at the Bite of Seattle food festival near the iconic Space Needle on Sunday evening.

The shooting sent hundreds of festivalgoers fleeing the Seattle Center grounds as authorities responded to reports of gunfire shortly after 6 p.m, CNN reports.

Two victims were pronounced dead at the scene, while four others, including the toddler, were transported to Harborview Medical Center. A fifth victim later arrived at another hospital with a gunshot wound, and one of those hospitalized subsequently died, according to Seattle police.

Witnesses reported hearing multiple gunshots as crowds ran for safety, with videos showing people knocking down a fence to escape the area.

Police said two people were believed to have been shooting at each other, and two weapons were recovered. One suspect, described as a young person, was taken into custody, while authorities continued searching for a second person believed to be involved.

The motive remains unknown, but police said there was no ongoing threat to the community and urged witnesses to provide information.

World.title: More Belizean teachers teaching in the U.S. through Participate Learning
World.content:
More Belizean teachers teaching in the U.S. through Participate Learning

Participate Learning continues to accept applications for its international teaching Program in the United States of America. The organization has assisted many Belizean teachers, who after their time teaching abroad, return to Belize to share their experiences and the new knowledge they have garnered in the education sector. Thirty Belizean teachers have joined the program so far this year and have been participating in orientation sessions since June 20th through August 13th in the United States (US).

This is a dedicated induction and support program designed to help ensure the best possible transition and experience in the United States. “Many educators dream of having an international experience, but they also have questions about how the process works, what they need to prepare, and what life in the United States would be like. Our goal is to support them from the very beginning with clear and practical information so they can evaluate this opportunity with confidence,” said Ronald Ramírez, Recruitment Manager for Latin America at Participate Learning. Up-to-date, more than 85 teachers have taught in American schools through this prestigious program.

Teaching in a U.S. public school can represent an important opportunity for both professional growth and personal development for Latin American educators. Through Participate Learning, teachers can apply for positions in public schools in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Virginia.

Belizean educators interested in pursuing this professional experience abroad need to know that applying to the program is free. Participate Learning does not charge an application fee. Interested candidates can review the requirements and, if they meet the profile, begin the online application process at no cost by visiting the website https://www.participatelearning.com/international-teachers/apply/.

The successful applicant is provided with airfare and health insurance is subsidized. Participate Learning purchases the one-way airline ticket for selected participants after visa approval. In addition, health insurance has an estimated monthly cost of $99.69 for the teacher, as part of it is subsidized by Participate Learning.

In regard to the salary selected teachers receive an annual salary equivalent to that of U.S. educators, typically ranging from approximately US$42,000 to US$70,000, depending on experience, academic qualifications, and school district. These salaries are generally expressed as an annual gross amount before taxes and deductions. As a result, one of the most common questions is how much a teacher actually takes home each month. Using the lower end of the published salary range as an example, a salary of US$42,000

per year translates into a gross monthly income of US$3,500. After estimated federal and state tax deductions, as well as Social Security contributions, the approximate monthly net income would be US$2,700, depending on the state.

When it comes to the cost of living, it depends on personal circumstances and the state the teacher will be living in. Participate Learning shares the following estimated monthly cost ranges for a teacher traveling alone:

Housing rent: between $650 and $1,800, depending on housing type, number of

bedrooms, and location.

Vehicle purchase and ownership: between $500 and $1,100, depending on the

vehicle and financing terms. This estimate includes the monthly loan payment,

insurance, and fuel.

Utilities: between $100 and $175.

Cell phone and internet: between $75 and $150.

Food: between $200 and $300.

Certain education-related expenses paid out of pocket, such as classroom materials, books, supplies, computers, or software, may be tax-deductible when filing an annual tax return.

The program also allows family members to accompany participants. These include the spouse and children under the age of 18 to accompany the teacher. In addition, a spouse may apply for work authorization after arriving in the U.S. The processing time for this authorization is approximately three months. Participate Learning supports selected teachers throughout different stages of the process, including guidance on visas, housing options, transportation, arrival logistics, and preparation for working in a U.S. school.

To apply, candidates must have an advanced level of English, at least two years of full-time teaching experience after obtaining their university degree (Bachelor’s degree), be currently employed, hold a valid driver’s license, and be available to live in the U.S. for a minimum of two years.

Interested candidates can begin their application today. Once again, the link to apply can be found at https://www.participatelearning.com/international-teachers/apply/.

World.title: Argument ends with a piece of wood to the head in Douglas
World.content:
Argument ends with a piece of wood to the head in Douglas

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A verbal altercation between two Douglas Village cane cutters turned violent, leaving a 54-year-old man bleeding from the head, and a younger villager now formally charged with wounding and threat to death.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Friday, July 24, 2026, at about 1:40 p.m., the injured man was brought to the Trial Farm Police Station with injuries to the head. He told police that he and another man had become involved in a verbal altercation, during which the man struck him with a piece of wood, causing his head to start bleeding.

Police issued the injured man medico-legal forms and escorted him to the hospital for medical treatment. The other man was detained pending investigation and taken to the station.

At the station, the detained man was identified as 23-year-old Adriel Zapata, a cane cutter of Douglas Village, Orange Walk Town. He was issued a suspect’s rights in custody acknowledgement form and a custody record, which were read and explained to him before he signed voluntarily.

On Saturday, July 25, the injured man returned to the Trial Farm Station and gave his official statement as the investigation continued.

That same day, police obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged Zapata with the crimes of wounding and threat to death. Cautioned once more, he chose to remain silent.

World.title: Morning patrol search turns up 76 grams of suspected cannabis
World.content:
Morning patrol search turns up 76 grams of suspected cannabis

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 57-year-old man is facing a charge of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply, after police say a search of his bag during a morning patrol in Orange Walk Town produced more than 76 grams of suspected cannabis, in a case where officers brought in a sign language interpreter to ensure the man, who cannot speak, understood every step of the process.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Saturday, July 25, 2026, at about 8:30 a.m., officers on mobile patrol along Staines Alley observed a man with an orange nap sack bag on his back behaving in a manner they found suspicious. An officer stopped him and informed him that a search would be conducted for illegal drugs or firearms.

While speaking with the man, the officer noticed he could not speak. A search of his person found nothing incriminating, but a further search of the orange bag produced a green transparent plastic bag containing a green leafy substance suspected to be cannabis. He was shown the find, informed of the offence, cautioned, and escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station.

At the station, police secured the services of a sign language interpreter, through whom the man was identified as Sergio Betancourt, a 57-year-old Guatemalan labourer of Douglas Village, Orange Walk District. The suspected cannabis was weighed in the presence of both Betancourt and the interpreter, amounting to 76.1 grams, then sealed and labelled as evidence. He was informed of his constitutional rights through a suspect’s rights form in the language he understands, and signed and received his copy.

On Sunday, July 26, police formally arrested and charged Betancourt with possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply to another. Cautioned once more, he chose to remain silent.

World.title: Stepson charged with stealing bicycle and recado from family home
World.content:
Stepson charged with stealing bicycle and recado from family home

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A San Jose Palmar Village woman’s bicycle and a batch of recado she had prepared for sale were taken from her home, and her own stepson has been formally charged with the theft.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 39-year-old woman of the village reported on Saturday, July 25, 2026, that on Tuesday, July 21, at about 3:30 p.m., she returned home after picking up her daughter from work and was informed by a family member that her stepson had taken her purple Kenton brand beach cruiser bicycle, valued at $150, along with five pounds of black recado, valued at $60, which she had prepared for sale.

The total value of the missing items stands at $210. The woman, who has known her stepson for about five years, requested court action, and her statement was recorded in Spanish and translated into English.

Police detained a man in connection with the report, identified at the Orange Walk Police Station as 19-year-old Sotero Samuel Cantun, a Belizean labourer of San Jose Palmar Village. He was issued his rights in custody in a language he understood and signed the acknowledgement willingly.

On Saturday, July 25, police obtained a warrant and formally arrested and charged Cantun with the crime of theft. Cautioned once more, he chose to remain silent.

World.title: Police pull 11.5 pounds of suspected weed from village bushes
World.content:
Police pull 11.5 pounds of suspected weed from village bushes

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A major drug stash lasted less than an hour in its hiding spot, after Special Branch intelligence led police straight to 11.5 pounds of suspected cannabis concealed in a bushy area of August Pine Ridge Village, Orange Walk District.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Saturday, July 25, 2026, at about 10:32 a.m., Special Branch received information of a man in the village in possession of a big black plastic bag, apparently hiding or stashing it somewhere in a bushy area before leaving empty handed.

By 11:12 a.m., police were at the location. A search of the bushes led to the discovery of a black plastic garbage bag concealed behind the dried roots of a fallen tree and covered with small dried palm leaves. When opened, the contents revealed a leafy substance suspected to be cannabis.

No one was observed in the immediate area, and the suspected drugs were retrieved and taken to the Orange Walk Police Station for processing.

At the station, the full scale of the find emerged. The garbage bag held five packages, three rectangular parcels sealed with transparent tape, one square vacuum-sealed transparent plastic bag, and a green plastic bag tied closed. Weighed on a gram scale, the packages amounted to a total of 11.5 pounds, or 5.22 kilograms, of suspected cannabis.

The bags were sealed and labelled pending handover to the exhibit keeper. No arrests have been made, and the matter remains under police attention.

The seizure ranks among the larger drug finds in the district in recent months, and the professional packaging points to product destined for distribution rather than personal use. Anyone with information is urged to contact the Orange Walk police or Crime Stoppers anonymously at 922.

World.title: Sitting duck
World.content:
The 10 per cent General Consumption Tax that had softened the blows suffered by tourism activities is expected to move to the standard 15 per cent, effective next year April

ATTENTION will turn this Wednesday to a crucial meeting between the finance ministry and anxious tourism leaders fearing that a General Consumption Tax (GCT) increase being proposed for the sector will badly hurt its viability for the immediate future.

Nervously awaiting the outcome of the discussions also are sectors like domestic agriculture and manufacturing — broken down into produce, poultry, dairy, juices, sauces, water, electricity, packaging, furniture, uniforms, amenities, and transport and services, for which tourism is the anchor customer.

The tourism industry and its spin-off entities have been fretful in recent years over its future profitability after a series of financial shocks, mostly stemming from natural weather events, left the sector reeling.

Sector leaders interviewed by the Jamaica Observer for this story said Hurricane Melissa caused more than US$8 billion in physical damage, pointing out that rebuilding room stock, restoring attractions, and repairing the infrastructure that moves visitors around the island is not a one-season exercise. Much of that work is still under way.

Industry-wide, it was accepted that the Andrew Holness Administration was bound to ask the sector to help carry the burden of funding the expansive post-Hurricane Melissa recovery, as has always been the approach by governments after major disasters.

But when Finance Minister Fayval Williams tabled revenue measures in this year’s budget, she shook the tourism sector by announcing that the 10 per cent GCT, that had softened the blows suffered by tourism activities would move to the standard 15 per cent, effective next year April.

Williams said the one-year notice would give the tourism sector itself more time to recover from Melissa. What the finance minister’s calculations did not factor in, however, was the flow of earnings from the sector.

Notably, most rates were already negotiated and inked with overseas partners like tour operators. Jamaica’s tourist entities were, therefore, being asked to pass off a 50 per cent rate increase where other sophisticated tourism markets are fighting for the same global tourism traveller.

Passing on GCT increases would, at best, be impossible without doing further critical damage to the sector and leaving it naked and exposed to its overseas competitors, the leaders concurred.

“For the most part, hotel room sales are contracted often 18 months to two years in advance with tour operators and wholesalers in source markets,” said new Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) President O’Brien Heron when queried by the Observer.

“It means that a contract signed with a tour operator or wholesaler in 2026 involves a significant share of the room nights that will be sold in the 2027 season [and beyond] at the current 2026 room rates, inclusive of GCT.

“…Those contracts cannot be reopened just because Jamaica’s tax rate changed, which means that the local hotel or attraction will have to absorb the difference between the old and new GCT rate through to the end of the current contract period,” he added.

Moreover, industry leaders insist recovery is not the only pressure that has intensified since the measure was announced. Energy costs have soared, exacerbated by war in the Middle East that has pushed up global oil prices from roughly US$60 a barrel in December 2025 to near US$100 by March 2026.

Jamaica generates much of its electricity from imported fuel, so that increase passes almost directly into the cost of running a hotel.

“It lands on an industry that was already paying among the highest electricity rates in the hemisphere,” added the JHTA head. “Business electricity in Jamaica runs well above the global average — a structural disadvantage that has nothing to do with how well any individual property is managed.

“For a resort, electricity is not overhead at the margin. Air conditioning, refrigeration, laundry and water production run 24 hours a day, every day, whether the room is occupied or not,” he explained.

Heron roundly disagreed with government number crunchers’ description that it was “a five-percentage-point increase”, reiterating that it was a 50 per cent GCT increase — from 10 to 15 per cent.

“What is at stake here is the economic fabric of tourism, and tourism is the engine that drives Jamaica’s economy,” he said. “When you compress this sector you do not compress one industry. You compress the farmer who supplies it, the manufacturer who packages for it, the transport operator who moves its guests, and the worker whose household depends on it.”

Speaking for the small hotels, JHTA past President Evelyn Smith stressed the struggles facing the sector after being hit by significant disasters like the COVID-19 pandemic, hurricanes Beryl and Melissa; a northerly that threw up angry waves that badly damaged some Negril beachfront properties; and the recent water problem that “forced us to pay huge sums of money to have water trucked to the properties”.

“During these disastrous events, some properties had to shut down altogether; others remained open but retained staff at tremendous sacrifice,” said Smith.

“Negril is well known as having the largest collection of small hotels. We have kept the life of Negril going during these many shocks, especially after Melissa, the worst hurricane to hit Jamaica. We kept our doors open even as cash depleted.”

Smith said she strongly disagreed with the Government that the industry has matured.

“Tourism is an export industry, so our competition is overseas, and we can’t just pass on any increase. Our rates are already set. Our revenues are already very thin, and now we are being asked to absorb further increases. Something is going to have to give.

“This significant increase will hit what we have to do in order to simply remain alive,” she reasoned.

The JHTA’s present leadership is also worried about the dim prospects facing the allied sectors, such as ground transportation and attractions, said Nadine Spence, the 4th vice-president.

“While we fully appreciate the Government’s responsibility to generate revenue to fund national development, timing is critical. The transportation, attractions, and allied sectors are still recovering from Hurricane Melissa and a challenging tourism environment,” Spence pointed out.

“A 50 per cent increase in the GCT applied to hotel accommodation risks weakening Jamaica’s competitiveness at a time when every visitor matters. We depend directly on hotel occupancy, and any decline in arrivals or visitor spending flows immediately through our sector, affecting jobs, investment, and small businesses across the island,” she argued.

“If higher taxes reduce arrivals or visitor spending, transportation and attractions businesses immediately feel the impact. A tax on hotels inevitably becomes a tax on the wider tourism value chain.

“Furthermore, this tax proposal comes at the worst possible time,” she suggested. “An industry facing this level of compounding strain requires temporary relief, incentives, and structural support to rebuild, not an aggressive tax hike.

“Taxing local businesses into submission during a recovery period will only push more players out of the formal market and exacerbate the very revenue shortfall the Government is trying to solve.

“If Jamaica wants a sustainable, high-yielding tourism sector… we need policies that nurture Jamaican-owned ground transport and attraction businesses, enabling them to build domestic wealth that stays right here in the economy.

“An increase in GCT at this critical time is not good for a sector on the rebound, especially when arrivals are down 30 to 40 per cent… Lower pricing will increase volumes which will increase traffic and that means additional revenue,” said Spence.

Martin Zsifkovicks, co-chair of the association’s linkages and agriculture committees, cautioned about the indirect harm threatening agriculture.

“The GCT increase will not automatically damage agriculture fruits, vegetables, as most agricultural inputs remain GCT-free, which is fundamentally important. However, the mechanism runs through hotel profitability rather than the tax code directly,” he suggested.

“When hotels come under margin pressure, procurement is historically one of the first places operators look to cut, precisely because it’s a variable cost that can be scaled up or down quickly, unlike staffing contracts, utilities, or debt service. We have already seen how directly that plays out for farmers: During COVID, when hotel demand collapsed, Government had to step in with a buy-back scheme because produce already planted for the hotel trade had nowhere to go.”

Zsifkovicks agreed that the timing of the increase was bad, saying that close to 5,000 rooms remain off stream since Hurricane Melissa hit in October 2025, and hurricane recovery of this scale typically takes years, not months.

“That means the industry is already absorbing pressure on revenue and cash flow before the GCT increase even takes effect. Layering a tax increase on top of a sector that hasn’t yet returned to full inventory only adds to that strain, and procurement is likely to be one of the first places it shows up.

“A GCT-driven margin squeeze is a different kind of shock than a pandemic shutdown, but the transmission line is the same — pressure on hotel revenue shows up quickly in what and how much hotels are willing to commit to buying from local farmers. That’s the risk worth watching, even though the produce itself isn’t being taxed,” he said.

President Heron also warned that absorbing a tax increase does not simply reduce profit but reduces the cash available for everything that sits below the operating line, like debt service, refurbishment, and reinvestment.

“Most properties in this market are carrying storm-related capital expenditure and, in many cases, related borrowing. Compress operating earnings and the first casualties are not investor dividends. They are the deferred room refresh, the delayed energy-efficiency retrofit, the postponed hire.

“An industry that defers reinvestment does not announce a crisis. It simply becomes gradually less competitive, and the consequences arrive later, when they are far more expensive to reverse,” charged Heron.

He said that when hotel margins compress, procurement is one of the first places operators look to trim costs. And the path of least resistance begins with buying harder. That means suppliers will feel the squeeze through both rate and volume pressures. Not out of any lack of national commitment, but because a buyer under margin pressure buys on price.

“This is where the policy tension becomes difficult to ignore. The Government’s own Tourism 3.0 and Local First agenda commit to prioritising Jamaican farmers, artisans, manufacturers, and micro-entrepreneurs as first suppliers to hotels and attractions. That is a genuinely good policy, and the industry supports it.

“… There is also a principle worth stating plainly. Under Jamaica’s own GCT Act, exports are zero-rated. Tourism is an export industry — it earns foreign exchange and it is consumed primarily by non-residents. By that logic, the tax code, fairly applied across all exporters, tourism services should also be zero-rated.

“Successive government administrations have repeatedly accepted this fact and, while some adjustments have been made to the GCT rate differential, the principle supporting tourism having a lower rate than the national rate is well documented and, up ’til now, was assumed a settled matter,” he added.

Heron said that what the industry is asking for is to be in a position to show the Government the disastrous implications expected to tourism businesses by the proposed change.

Heron confirmed that the JHTA would be meeting with the finance minister this week and that work is under way to put independent evidence in front of Government.

“Tourism’s bottom lines to watch is not only about the hotel’s. It is also the farmer’s, the manufacturer’s, the worker’s, and the country’s. That is precisely why the timing, and the terms of this increase are worth getting right — together,” he said.

World.title: The spy, the specialist and the thief
World.content:
For the second time in a week, police cordoned off Horseshoe Curve on Caledonia Road in Mandeville on Saturday.

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Police here say they are determined to dismantle a network of criminals, particularly those involved in the robbery of bars, during which poker boxes are mainly targeted.

This follows Saturday’s triple fatal shooting by cops on Caledonia Road in Mandeville, involving three suspects with connections to criminals in neighbouring parishes who police said targeted bars across Manchester.

“The group that was involved in the shoot-out, we have been tracking them for some time and, based on intelligence, we even recovered stolen items, including poker box parts at three premises two Fridays ago, tied to these three people,” a police source said.

Police named those fatally shot as Lester Morris, Travis Baker and Sutania Boothe, otherwise called Chun Chun. Two firearms were reportedly seized during Saturday’s alleged shoot-out.

Police said about 4:00 pm they were alerted to a robbery spree and subsequently intercepted a vehicle near Horseshoe Curve.

A highly placed police source said the occupants of the intercepted vehicle opened fire on cops, who returned gunfire. A shoot-out ensued resulting in a prolonged stand-off.

Boothe, Morris and Baker, according to the police, were taken from the intercepted vehicle and rushed to hospital where they were pronounced dead on arrival.

The incident happened in proximity of last Saturday’s double murder in which nursing student Deenekia Pounall and Sadefa Henry were gunned down in a taxi by a gunman posing as a passenger.

Baker and Morris were well known to the police, having both been previously arrested and charged for several offences, including praedial larceny and robbery.

Police described Baker as a third-generation thief in February 2024, when he was arrested a week before his father, Neville, was detained. At that time, the younger Baker was among three men arrested and charged with praedial larceny offences following a high-speed chase in Newport, Manchester. A ram goat was recovered from the trunk of a Toyota Axio in which Baker was travelling.

The elder Baker was subsequently arrested when police caught him and two other men with more than 600 pounds of stolen carrots and Irish potatoes in Kingsland near Mandeville.

A year later, on March 2, 2025, Neville Baker was gunned down in his car at the entrance to the community of Hatfield in Manchester. He had also previously served prison time for firearm offences.

In relation to Morris, police described him as “a poker box specialist” in robbing and dismantling the popular gaming equipment.

In 2022, police in neighbouring St Elizabeth said upscale gaming boxes, including those with touch screen technology, were worth as much as $500,000 each and were in demand, while older versions can be sold for up to $300,000.

Police accused Boothe, the woman killed in the triple fatal shooting, of being integral in robbery sprees.

“She would be the lookout and the spy for the group. She would go into bars and scope out the place and then call in her cronies,” a senior police source alleged.

“These criminals are not just based in Manchester, it is a network of them spanning multiple parishes. We have reason to believe [that] this team may be connected to the multimillion-dollar robbery heist in Red Bank near Junction, St Elizabeth, last month, in which two of their cronies perished in a fiery crash while trying to elude the highway patrol team,” added the police source.

Police theorise that a Toyota Noah motor vehicle, which burst into flames killing its two occupants when it crashed on the Williamsfield highway in the wee hours, was used as the getaway vehicle by thieves who had targeted the St Elizabeth establishment on June 27.

Police said they will continue to pursue criminal suspects linked to a series of robberies.

“There are others of them out there and we will not relent until the criminal network is dismantled,” said a senior police source.

World.title: Families abandon relatives in hospital while occupying their homes
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton addressing a media briefing at Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover on Friday. Photo: Anthony Lewis

WITH hundreds of medically discharged patients continuing to occupy public hospital beds across Jamaica, Health Minister Dr Christopher Tufton says the Government is looking at the law to determine how relatives who abandon loved ones in hospital can be held accountable.

He also revealed that some relatives continue to live in homes owned by the very people they have neglected.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer after last Thursday’s Health Hurricane Response Programme (HHRP) working breakfast, Tufton said social cases currently account for between five and 10 per cent of the country’s roughly 4,000 public hospital beds.

He said the problem has become particularly acute in western Jamaica, where he believes the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa may have worsened an already strained situation.

He warned that the growing number of patients who no longer require medical treatment but remain in hospital is reducing bed availability for people awaiting admission.

“We’re doing another census, because it’s a moving target, and I’ve asked for that information to be granted, but we are really under pressure when it comes to social cases. Like I said at Savanna-la-Mar Hospital [last] week, I checked, there were 26. Now, when you have a hospital with 150, 160 beds and you have 26 [social cases], and you have 30, 40 people waiting for a bed, you understand that problem would have been much less,” Tufton said.

However, the minister said the challenge extends well beyond Savanna-la-Mar Public General Hospital.

“The truth is that the infirmaries seem to be crowded… [and] what is happening is that there’s a gradual creep that is taking place, where health now is becoming a provider of social [services] for the infirm. We’re already doing it unofficially, but practically, yes, in the hospitals; because I think we have, in western region alone — and this could be wrong — in western region alone, maybe because of Melissa, I think we have in excess of 100 social cases.

“And when you contact the families, they say they’re not willing to take the person because they can’t manage them and all of that, while some of them don’t even respond,” he said.

Social cases are individuals who have been medically cleared for discharge but remain in hospital because they have nowhere suitable to go or because family members are unwilling or unable to care for them. Health officials have long argued that these cases place additional strain on an already stretched public health system by occupying beds needed for acutely ill patients.

During a media briefing following a tour of Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover last Friday, Tufton provided a breakdown of social cases currently occupying beds across the island’s four regional health authorities:

* Southern Regional Health Authority currently has 44 cases: 12 at Mandeville Regional Hospital, seven at Percy Junor, Black River has one, Lionel Town has four, and May Pen Hospital has 20;

* South East Regional Health Authority has 89 beds taken up with social cases: Bustamante Hospital for Children and Linstead Hospital have eight each, Spanish Town has 37, Sir John Golding has two, Kingston Public Hospital has 22, and Princess Margaret has 12;

* ​North East Regional Authority, which is the smallest region, currently has 29 social cases: Port Maria Hospital has four cases, Port Antonio has six, St Ann’s Bay Regional has nine, and 10 are at Annotto Bay Hospital.

* Western Regional Health Authority has 98 cases on record. The 360-bed Cornwall Regional Hospital currently has 62 cases while Savanna-la-Mar has 27, and Falmouth and Noel Holmes hospitals have four cases each.

Last Thursday, Tufton told the Observer that the ministry is pursuing several approaches to reduce the numbers, including engaging social workers to reunite patients with relatives, training unpaid caregivers to care for incapacitated family members at home, and expanding community support.

However, he indicated that legal intervention is also under consideration following advice from the Attorney General’s Chambers.

“The third is to look at the laws, which I have spoken about, but our laws don’t currently give us that authority and we are told by the AG to literally take people to court when they have abandoned their loved ones, and there’s clear evidence that they can take care of them because, in some cases, some of these social cases own homes and homes are occupied by relatives,” he said.

Pressed on that assertion, Tufton maintained that some relatives continue living in properties owned by patients who remain in hospital.

“When they die, people come to claim the death certificate in order to get the benefit, so that’s not all the cases but there are some of those cases. So what is happening is that we are really plagued by that, and it puts added pressure on the system and prevents the people who really need a bed from benefiting from a bed,” he said.

According to the health minister, the impact is felt most sharply in hospital emergency departments, where patients often wait hours or days for admission because in-patient beds remain occupied by people who no longer require acute medical care.

Meanwhile, at the media briefing last Friday, Tufton pointed out that the primary role of the Government is to finance public health-care facilities, cover staff salaries, and supply medication, but the social cases crisis has forced his portfolio ministry to step outside its original mandate.

In response, the ministry has partnered with the Ministry of Local Government, providing more than $100 million to fund the build-out of additional space at the St James Infirmary.

“Health [Ministry] has had to commit, not just to building, but also to committing to staff and meals, I believe, for two-plus years. And normally the parish councils are just not able, or that’s the word, to take the additional social cases. So, you know, we really have a problem,” stated Tufton.

When asked by Deputy Mayor of Lucea Andria Dehaney Grant whether Hanover could get similar help, Tufton said, while this is not the norm, the ministry is willing to provide help.

“We have done it because we really have a crisis and we have to try and correct the crisis. That’s not to say we mustn’t work together, and that’s what we’re doing. Where there is a need, and we can help, then we are more than willing to help. If the mayor has an issue and we think we can provide some support, we’re willing to look at it and we’d be happy to discuss it,” assured the minister.

World.title: Blvk H3ro, Yungg Trip embrace Phemomenal
World.content:
Blvk H3ro and Yungg Trip shoots some visuals.

Following a run of standout releases, Jamaican artiste Blvk H3ro returns with Phenomenal, a high-energy anthem produced by Yungg Trip that radiates confidence, resilience, and pure feel-good energy.

Built around an irresistible hook and infectious groove, Phenomenal blends modern reggae with dancehall swagger, delivering a bold celebration of self-belief and unstoppable momentum.

Blvk H3ro’s sharp lyricism keeps it authentic, while the song’s driving rhythm makes it one that seems set to move crowds.

Produced by Yungg Trip, the track pairs powerful messaging with massive festival-ready energy, making it one of Blvk H3ro’s most explosive releases yet.

As his global profile continues to rise, Phenomenal proves once again that Blvk H3ro knows how to balance substance with undeniable vibes; creating music that hits just as hard on the stage as it does in your headphones.

Blvk H3ro is at the forefront of Jamaica’s new wave of reggae, blending roots foundation with dancehall and global influences into a sound that feels both authentic and forward-thinking.

Hailing from Portmore, he’s built a growing international presence, performing across North America, Europe, and Africa while delivering music rooted in discipline, growth, and real-life experience.

A Grammy-nominated artiste and recipient of the Dennis Brown Award for Most Promising Entertainer at the International Reggae and World Music Awards (IRAWMA), among his releases are On A Mission and Winnah.

World.title: Golding denies leaked audio reflects PNP policy
World.content:
A screen grab of People’s National Party President Mark Golding taken from the video released by the Opposition party after its National Executive Council meeting at the University of the West Indies, Mona, in St Andrew, on Sunday.

People’s National Party (PNP) President Mark Golding on Sunday sought to distance the Opposition party from controversial leaked voice notes discussing strategies against the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA), insisting the recordings reflected the personal views of individuals and not official party policy.

However, the party’s explanation came only in a recorded video statement after a highly anticipated opportunity for the PNP to answer questions from the media vanished when it cancelled its planned post-National Executive Council (NEC) press briefing on Sunday.

Speaking in the video released following the NEC meeting, Golding said the party had withheld comment until it had completed its own review of the matter.

“Our review is now complete and it established three things,” Golding said.

“Firstly, the conversation in which those leaked recordings took place did not happen in any official party forum. Secondly, no party officer, no officer of the party participated in that discussion, and thirdly, the PNP has no official NEC or executive WhatsApp group. That doesn’t exist, and certainly not where party policy is made,” he said.

He further maintained that the conversations were not representative of the Opposition’s official position.

“This was a WhatsApp group formed by individuals within the party, and the views expressed were their personal views. So those recordings do not represent the official position of the PNP or any policy of the PNP,” Golding said.

“The PNP takes responsibility for its official positions. Those are set by our constitutional organs, such as this National Executive Council or the Executive Committee of the party, and those that are communicated by our authorised representatives and shown through our public actions or through our public media outlets, social media outlets, and so on,” he added.

The video statement came after journalists arrived at The University of the West Indies (UWI), Mona, for what had been billed as a post-NEC media briefing featuring Golding, party Chairman Dr Angela Brown Burke, General Secretary Dr Dayton Campbell, and other senior leaders. The briefing had been scheduled for 3:30 pm following the executive council meeting.

Instead, members of the media were informed of a two-hour delay and were advised that the planned press briefing had been cancelled, with the party indicating that a video statement would be issued instead.

The cancellation meant the Opposition missed what many had viewed as its first major opportunity to directly answer questions about the leaked recordings that have dominated the political landscape for much of the past week.

The recordings, which have circulated widely on social media and whose authenticity has not been independently verified, allegedly capture two members of the PNP discussing political strategies surrounding NaRRA, the agency established by the Government to coordinate Jamaica’s recovery and reconstruction following Hurricane Melissa.

One of the recordings appears to suggest that the authority should be viewed through a political lens because of the electoral benefit it could bring to the governing Jamaica Labour Party (JLP), while another discusses ways to undermine public confidence in NaRRA Chief Executive Officer Major General (Ret’d) Antony Anderson despite acknowledging his credibility.

The recordings have prompted sharp criticism from the governing JLP, which accused the Opposition of placing partisan interests above the country’s recovery efforts. Civil society groups have also weighed in, with Jamaicans for Justice urging the PNP to distance itself from any suggestion that politics should interfere with national reconstruction.

Against that backdrop, Sunday’s NEC meeting had been expected to provide clarity on the party’s position and whether it intended to investigate the circumstances surrounding the leaked conversations.

Ahead of the meeting, the PNP had advised that the post-NEC briefing would provide “updates from the NEC and address recent reports circulating in the public domain”, adding that members of the media would have an opportunity to pose questions to the party’s leadership on those matters and other issues.

World.title: INTO THE SPOTLIGHT!
World.content:
Jamaica’s Romaine Beckford (Photo: AFP)Photo: AFP

Jamaica’s medal chase in track and field at the Commonwealth Games will start at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland, with the finals of two events — the 110m hurdles and men’s high jump — scheduled to be contested.

National champions Demario Prince, in the hurdles, and Romaine Beckford, in the men’s high jump, are expected to lead the medal chase.

Technical leader Maurice Wilson said all was well in the camp except the withdrawal of men’s sprinter Nishion Ebanks, a loss which could have repercussions for the relays.

“We are settled in and expectations are high despite the cold weather,” Wilson said. “However, we had a late pull out, Nishion Ebanks, which affects the 4x100m relay pool.”

Ebanks was set to contest the individual men’s 100m, along with Ackeem Blake and Rohan Watson. He was expected to form part of the sprint relay team.

Watson will be the only Jamaican competing in the first round of both the men’s and women’s 100m, with the rules allowing the top eight to advance to the next round. Blake and women runners Jonielle Smith and Jodean Williams will sit out the first rounds as a result.

Prince is the leader in the Commonwealth Games 11om hurdles rankings with his personal best 13.01 seconds set at the Prefontaine Classic two weeks ago, while Jerome Campbell is ranked ninth. Both will hope to qualify for the final.

Beckford, who was eighth at the Commonwealth Games four years ago, is ranked third in the men’s high jump. He is to face off against top-ranked Kimani Jack of England and Sarvesh Anil Kushare of India, both of whom have cleared 2.31m this season.

Two-time World Athletics Indoor Championships bronze medallist Raymond Richards of Jamaica and defending champion Hamish Kerr of New Zealand are also down to compete.

Also on Monday, Adelle Tracey, who switched allegiance from England to represent Jamaica four years ago but was not allowed to compete at the 2022 Commonwealth Games because required documentation had not been completed, will make her debut in the women’s 800m. She is to be joined national champion Kelly-Ann Beckford in the first round.

The women’s 800m will be one of the most anticipated events, at least on the opening day of track and field, since a number of top athletes, including England’s Georgia Hunter-Bell, Scotland’s Jemma Reeki and Shafiqua Maloney of St Vincent and the Grenadines, are expected to be in the medal hunt.

Former world champion and Olympic Games medallist Tajay Gayle will hope to improve on his fourth place at the 2018 Commonwealth Games when he takes part in the first round of the long jump. Jordan Turner is also down to compete.

They will go up against top-ranked Sreeshankar of India, Liam Adcock of Australia, Kelsey Daniel of Trinidad and Tobago and Stephen McKenzie of Scotland.

Six-time national champion Nayoka Clunis, a medal contender in the women’s hammer throw, is expected to advance from the first round.

Clunis, who extended her national record to 72.03m this year, is ranked fifth. She is to face top-ranked Canadian Camryn Rogers, New Zealand’s Lauren Bruce and England’s Charlotte Payne.

World.title: Failing the boys
World.content:
Chairman, Education Transformation Oversight Committee (ETOC), Dr Adrian Stokes, gives an update last Thursday, during the ETOC Press Conference for year four, quarter one, at The University of the West Indies Regional Headquarters in St Andrew. Photo: JIS News

DESPITE steady improvements in overall Primary Exit Profile (PEP) performance, Jamaica remains without a clear solution to the long-standing underachievement of boys in schools, prompting Education Transformation Oversight Committee (ETOC) Chairman Dr Adrian Stokes to warn that “a lot more” must be done to close a gender gap that continues to favour girls.

Stokes issued the warning at ETOC’s quarterly press conference at The University of the West Indies’ Regional Headquarters last week.

He argued that one of the country’s most persistent education challenges remains unresolved — boys continue to trail girls in key areas despite years of research into the problem.

This year’s mathematics results underscored the disparity. While 64.9 per cent of girls achieved the “proficient” level, compared with 57.2 per cent of boys, girls also edged boys at the highest achievement level, with 8.3 per cent classified as “highly proficient” compared with 7.7 per cent of boys. Boys, meanwhile, accounted for a larger share of students in the lower achievement categories.

Stokes said the gap could no longer be viewed as simply another statistic.

“The girls continue to outperform the boys in statistically significant ways. It’s not even close. The [Orlando] Patterson report highlights this issue, and indeed, all the entities that have taken a deep dive looking into the Jamaican education system — like the UNICEF report, the 2022 report — point out that Jamaica is one of the few places globally where girls outperform boys in mathematics, for example,” he said.

He noted that the Orlando Patterson-led education review had carefully examined the issue and identified several social and psychological factors affecting boys, but said Jamaica has yet to develop targeted interventions capable of reversing the trend.

“The Patterson report argued that the root cause was not favouritism. It’s not like girls are being given some advantage, knowingly. Rather, what the report highlights is that our boys, through social circumstances, or their abusive upbringing, cultural norms, but generally, let’s say, psychosocial issues that are putting our boys at a disadvantage… So the bottom line is, we have more work to do to find solutions that can close the gender performance gap,” he added.

Although the Ministry of Education recently announced plans to establish a committee to examine how boys are educated, Stokes suggested that would not, on its own, be enough.

“We need to do a lot more than that… Let’s say that’s a first step, hopefully, to something meaningful… We need real initiatives. We need to pilot different ideas. As I said, I am not certain that anyone has a full slate of answers… The question is, how do we respond? Or, how do we modify or evolve the education system to accommodate these psychosocial issues that are playing out in society? So, hopefully, it’s a step in the right direction, but I’m not expecting, just from that committee, to see significant change, a lot more needs to happen,” Stokes noted.

Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information Dr Kasan Troupe agreed that the education system must now adopt more targeted approaches for boys, arguing that biological and social differences influence how they learn.

She said the ministry has already begun examining changes to teaching methods, classroom environments and teacher training.

“So, particularly, we have been talking about how we socialise our boys. Boys learn differently, boys like competition, and so that means our teachers have to be retooled. They have to be trained — we need the bingos, we need the dominoes, we need movements. There’s a whole raft of measures that we have to look at as it relates to how we are going to support our boys,” she said.

State minister Rhoda Moy Crawford struck a more optimistic tone, expressing confidence that the proposed committee would produce tangible results, pointing to the work already undertaken by ETOC since its establishment.

She also argued that the latest PEP results showed there was reason for hope.

“I know this committee that will be put in place to examine what we can do differently to benefit our boys, I know it will be a solid committee…and I’m also motivated by the fact that when we look at our recent PEP results, our top 10 students, out of those 10 students, seven were boys. So all is not lost,” she said.

World.title: Dr Maria Myers-Hamilton
World.content:
Dr Maria Myers-Hamilton.

“I’VE always believed that technology should never be an end in itself. Its true purpose is to improve lives, create opportunities and remove barriers.” For more than three decades, that philosophy has shaped every stage of Dr Maria Myers-Hamilton’s career.

From leading complex banking technology transformations to shaping regional telecommunications policy, her career has been defined by one consistent goal: Using technology to improve people’s lives. Today, as managing director of Spectrum Management Authority (SMA), she is helping to position Jamaica at the forefront of spectrum management and digital innovation. Her leadership has also earned regional and international recognition through roles with the Caribbean Telecommunications Union (CTU) and the Inter-American Telecommunication Commission, where she contributes to shaping the future of global radiocommunications policy.

Yet titles have never been what motivated her.

“When I started my career, I wasn’t chasing titles or recognition,” Myers-Hamilton reflects. “I was fascinated by solving problems. Every role presented a new challenge and another opportunity to learn. Looking back, I realise those experiences were preparing me for leadership — not simply because of the technical knowledge I gained, but because they taught me resilience, adaptability, and the importance of making decisions that affect people’s lives.”

Long before entering telecommunications regulation, Dr Myers-Hamilton built her career in Jamaica’s financial sector, where technology had to be dependable, secure and resilient.

She helped lead the integration of four commercial banks into Union Bank of Jamaica before serving as chief information officer at RBTT Bank (Jamaica), overseeing technology operations across several Caribbean territories. Those formative years, she says, shaped the leader she is today.

“When you’re responsible for systems people depend on every day, you quickly learn that technology is about trust. People may never see the infrastructure behind the scenes, but they rely on it to work every single day. That sense of responsibility has stayed with me throughout my career,” she says.

Since taking the helm of SMA in 2018, she has led an ambitious programme of regulatory modernisation. Under her leadership, the authority has introduced artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced licensing, expanded Jamaica’s spectrum monitoring network, and strengthened disaster resilience and advanced policies that improve broadband access, particularly for underserved communities. These initiatives have helped establish Jamaica as a regional leader in spectrum regulation and digital innovation.

While much of her work is highly technical, Dr Myers-Hamilton measures success differently.

“People often think of spectrum as something highly technical and invisible, but it touches almost every aspect of modern life. It enables communication, supports emergency services, powers innovation, and connects communities. For me, managing spectrum has always been about ensuring every Jamaican, regardless of where they live, has the opportunity to participate in our digital future.”

As one of the Caribbean’s leading women in information and communications technology, Dr Myers-Hamilton is equally passionate about ensuring more women see technology as a place where they belong. Through her roles as chair of the CTU Task Force for the Network of Women and incoming vice-president of the European Union-Latin America and Caribbean Foundation network of women leaders in digital policy, she continues to champion greater female participation in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics while mentoring young professionals across the region.

“Women don’t belong in technology because someone decided to make room for us. We belong because our ideas, perspectives and leadership make technology better. Diverse teams ask different questions, identify different risks and ultimately build solutions that work for more people. That isn’t just good for women — it makes technology better for everyone,” she says.

Her advice to young women considering careers in technology is equally straightforward.

“Don’t let the absence of someone who looks like you become the reason you don’t pursue your ambition. Sometimes you have to become the person others will one day look to.”

Today, Dr Myers-Hamilton continues to represent Jamaica in international discussions shaping the future of telecommunications.

At home, she also serves on several national education and public service bodies, reflecting a career grounded in service beyond technology. Whether advocating for greater digital inclusion, mentoring future leaders or helping develop policies that will shape the next generation of innovation, her focus remains firmly on improving lives.

When asked how she hopes to be remembered, she says: “If people remember me simply as someone who helped move technology forward, I’ll be grateful. But I hope they also remember that I never lost sight of the people technology was meant to serve. I want my legacy to be one of service, inclusion and creating opportunities for others.”

World.title: Poland asks US to extradite its ex-justice minister
World.content:
The request for provisional detention and extradition was delivered through diplomatic channels via Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek, the National Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

The extradition request covers 19 of the 26 alleged offenses for which prosecutors want to charge Ziobro.

The charges include leading an organized criminal group inside the justice ministry, abuse of power, rigging grant competitions to benefit government-friendly organizations, and deploying Pegasus spyware against political opponents.

The former government of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, which was politically allied to the former PiS government in Warsaw, had granted Ziobro asylum but the new Budapest government under Péter Magyar promised to hand him over.

Pre-empting trouble in Hungary, Ziobro flew to the U.S. in May where he was hired by TV Republika, a PiS-friendly Polish broadcaster, as a political commentator. “The United States is freedom. Freedom you can actually fight for,” Ziobro said at the time.

Ziobro has called the charges “fabricated” and accused Tusk of pursuing a political vendetta against him.

He has also vowed to take legal steps against Tusk and his ministers should PiS come back to power after an election slated for the fall of 2027.

However, that electoral landscape has become more complicated after a group of nearly 40 MPs, led by former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki, split from PiS last week. Still, polls suggest that a Tusk-led coalition would fall short of the support needed to secure a majority in the next parliament.

World.title: Commission eyes changes to big business tax to unlock budget deal
World.content:
As EU budget negotiations pick up pace, the issue of new EU-wide taxes — known as own resources — is emerging as one of the hardest problems to solve.

The Commission proposed five new own resources last year to generate fresh revenue to cover soaring defense and competitiveness spending, as well as repayments on its post-pandemic debt, without relying entirely on higher contributions from national governments.

However, the so-called Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE) — which charges an extra 0.1 percent tax on companies that operate in the EU with a net turnover exceeding €100 million — attracted the most scrutiny.

Critics, including business lobbies, the center-right European People’s Party and, crucially, the EU capitals that must unanimously approve any new EU taxes, have argued that CORE runs counter to the EU’s broader goal of enhancing competitiveness.

There are also lingering concerns that taxing revenues — as opposed to profits — is unfair as it would impose the same burden on companies with different profit margins.

Under CORE, companies with higher net turnover pay larger annual lump sums, but those with turnover exceeding €750 million all pay the same fixed amount.

World.title: What will Burnham really change?
World.content:
Andy Burnham came into office promising the biggest change in Britain for 40 years. But one week into his premiership, is Britain seeing transformation—or just a different style of politics?

As Burnham unveils plans on social care, devolution and welfare, Sam and Anne ask just how big the policies announced by Burnham actually are. Is this just a continuation of Starmer with a new face?

They also discuss Burnham’s foreign policy as he prepares to welcome Volodymyr Zelenskyy later today at a British naval base.

World.content:
Icelanders begin voting on whether to restart accession talks with the European Union, reopening a debate shaped by security fears, economic uncertainty and the question of who controls the country’s fishing waters.

Zoya Sheftalovich and Kathryn Carlson also examine Donald Trump’s threat of new tariffs after the EU fined Google €890 million, and what that could mean for the fragile Turnberry trade deal.

World.title: Cold calculation or plucked from thin air? How the EU determines those big fines against Big Tech
World.content:
On the Digital Markets Act, which is a regulatory law but works differently from traditional antitrust law — the fines are intended less to penalize a firm than to incentivize compliance. They also come with less of a sticker shock.

When the Commission started issuing multi-million euro fines under the DMA in 2025, to the opprobrium of some 'Big Tech' opponents, it pointed to the short duration of the conduct as one reason why the fines come far below the 10 percent of global turnover the regulation threatens. The most recent Google fine came in at a very modest 0.22 percent of the annual revenue of parent company Alphabet.

Though revenue is always considered a ceiling and enforcers always consider the same factors like how serious the infringement was, it's difficult to avoid the conclusion that the penalties are to some extent arbitrary — and not immune to political considerations.

The Google fine was actually the sum of two penalties (€460 million for Google’s favoring its own results in search, and €430 million for unfair practices in how the Play Store is installed on smartphones) that conveniently arrived just under the €1 billion mark in a moment of fraught transatlantic trade relations.

Trump has lashed out at the fine, threatening to place a “substantial” new tariff on the European Union. He said the bloc use of fines is “robbing” American companies, pledging to initiate a trade investigation after the EU fined Google for illegal trade practices.

European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier denied that politics is part of the fining process. The EU "always follows due process," he told POLITICO. Regnier said numerous objective criteria — the seriousness and length of the breach, mitigating factors and threshold keeping the penalties under a certain percentage of revenue — help "ensure that fines remain proportional under all circumstances."

World.title: Iceland opposition chief to Europe: Don’t meddle in our referendum
World.content:
The Nordic country will vote on Aug. 29 on whether to resume accession talks with Brussels, with early voting beginning Monday. The referendum will not decide whether Iceland joins the EU — any eventual membership agreement would require a second public vote.

Polls suggest the question of reopening discussions is finely balanced, although a clearer majority remains opposed to membership itself. “We are divided into nearly equal groups for yes and no” on the former, Hafsteinsdóttir said in a phone interview from Vatnajökull, Iceland’s largest glacier. “The referendum will be very tight.”

The vote fulfills a pledge made by Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir’s three-party coalition when it took office in late 2024. The alliance — dubbed the “Valkyrie government” because all three parties are led by women — includes a party that supports EU membership. Frostadóttir has said the referendum is intended to settle “a debate that has hung over the Icelandic nation.”

Several prominent European figures have sounded positive about the prospect of renewed talks. French MEP and Renew Europe leader Valérie Hayer traveled to Iceland in June and called for the EU to make accession easier. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos welcomed the vote and said the bloc “will be ready” if Iceland chooses to join, while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Reykjavík had “nothing to lose” by restarting negotiations.

The warm tone comes as Brussels seeks to revive enlargement as a geopolitical project, drawing Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans closer while showing the EU can still attract new members amid strained relations with Washington and growing competition with China.

Iceland’s case is different from those of most current candidates. The North Atlantic nation of around 400,000 people is already closely integrated with the bloc through the European Economic Area and the Schengen zone, and conducts most of its trade with the EU.

World.title: French politicians can’t get enough of ‘De Gaulle’
World.content:
The epic tale of a solitary, dogged patriot fighting to save his country from annihilation while standing up to an overbearing ally across the Atlantic captures the zeitgeist of French politics today.

As France again faces questions about the future of its alliance with the United States, French people find themselves forced to choose between various leaders portraying themselves as national saviors ahead of the presidential election next year.

So presidential hopefuls from across the political spectrum, including those from parties that view De Gaulle less favorably, are hailing the film’s portrayal of the wartime general’s brilliance in times of trouble — and, in thinly veiled casting attempts, trying to portray themselves as France’s next providential leader.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu last week said the movie’s success spoke to the French need of “meaning” and “perspectives” in a rare interview with glossy magazine Paris Match.

Perhaps the most surprising endorsement came from anticapitalist firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose party France Unbowed opposes conservative movements that have claimed to carry on De Gaulle’s legacy, despite the general himself equally despising all political parties.

During his Bastille Day address in the western city of Paimpont, the left-wing leader, one of the top contenders in next year’s election, strongly encouraged his supporters to watch a “magnificent movie,” drawing parallels between De Gaulle’s uphill battle to build up the country’s free forces during the war and his own campaign.

World.title: You can visit every bridge on the back of euro banknotes – and they’re all in one town
World.content:
Social media is aflutter with the vote for the new eurozone banknote design, which was announced last week.

 

Netizens are fiercely debating which of the 10 finalists is their favourite, and the discourse has inevitably put the original notes back in the limelight.

While you’ve no doubt seen the designs while handling cash over the years, there’s a good chance you’ve never stopped to actually look at them properly.

Unlike euro coins, which have different designs on the front depending on which country produced them, the euro notes are identical across the bloc.

Every note has a window or doorway on the front, which is meant to “symbolise the European spirit of openness and cooperation”, while the backs have bridges, which “symbolise communication between the people of Europe and between Europe and the rest of the world”, according to the European Central Bank (ECB).

The banknotes were meant to depict architectural styles from periods in history – for example, the €10 note is Romanesque – rather than actual monuments or bridges.

That was until the town of Spijkenisse in the Netherlands decided to make the latter a reality.

The Euro Banknote Bridges

Dutch designer Robin Stam came up with the idea to create the real-life bridges in 2011, working with a local council to realise the project at a new housing project, reported Dezeen.

The seven bridges opened to the public between 2011 and 2013, and they are all within walking distance of each other in Spijkenisse.

Spijkenisse is easily reached on the Rotterdam metro’s C and D lines.

World.title: 'Out of capacity’: EU warns wildfires are pushing response systems to the limit
World.content:
The European Commission said Europe’s firefighting capacity is struggling to keep pace with increasingly intense wildfires in Spain and France, as blazes continue to overwhelm local resources.

 

"These fires are out of capacity," a Commission official told reporters on Monday, referring to the devastating blazes that have already consumed more than 80,000 hectares in Spain and over 42,000 hectares in France. Both fires remain uncontrolled and have forced more than 320,000 people to leave their homes.

As wildfires continue to rage across Spain and France despite one of the EU's largest-ever emergency responses, Commission officials conceded that the EU is facing staggering blazes that are spreading faster than firefighting efforts can contain. The crisis is also highlighting the growing strain on the EU’s civil protection system and its ability to respond to large-scale disasters.

European Commission for Humanitarian Aid and Crisis Management, Hadja Lahbib, recently acknowledged in the French newspaper Le Monde that the bloc's civil protection mechanism is "under pressure" but insisted that "it is working".

Related Hundreds of thousands evacuated in France and Spain as wildfires rage on

Nevertheless, Brussels is moving to expand its firefighting fleet for future emergencies and enhance cross-border disaster response capabilities. EU officials acknowledged on Monday that climate change is lengthening wildfire seasons and driving increasingly severe fires that differ significantly from those witnessed just a few years ago.

In a recent wildfire in Spain, flames spread at an estimated speed of around six kilometres per hour, far outpacing firefighters on the ground, who were able to advance and contain the blaze at only about 300 metres per hour.

The Commission official argued that responding to the fires was not the only answer, as Europe must invest far more heavily in preventing catastrophic fires rather than relying on increasingly costly emergency interventions.

His remarks acknowledge that Europe’s civil protection model — which relies on member states sharing aircraft, equipment, and personnel during emergencies — is facing increasing pressure as multiple countries are forced to battle major wildfires at the same time.

Planes and helicopters deployed

The Commission has mobilised seven aircraft and four helicopters to France, six aircraft and three ground firefighting teams to Spain, while also supporting Tunisia through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, its main emergency response tool.

Five firefighter planes from Canada were deployed across both countries.

More than 770 firefighters from 14 countries have been pre-positioned across southern Europe for the summer.

"Two helicopters should be deployed shortly from Germany to Spain. Another two additional planes are also expected from Turkey," the Commission said.

However, officials stressed that Brussels could not simply mobilise its entire firefighting fleet, explaining that the aircraft remain owned or operated by member states, many of which are simultaneously dealing with severe domestic wildfires. They also noted that operational constraints mean that not every aircraft is suitable for every type of fire or terrain.

While the EU searches for additional firefighting aircraft and helicopters, more than 100,000 hectares of land are ablaze and thousands of families are being forced to evacuate. At the same time, several Russian firefighting helicopters remain grounded in Spain as a result of EU sanctions introduced in March 2022.

The Commission had not responded to a Euronews request by the time of publication on whether it would consider a temporary exemption to allow the use of this equipment, given the scale and severity of the ongoing fires.

EU's civil protection mechanism being tested

The bloc’s primary emergency response mechanism is facing growing pressure as simultaneous climate-related disasters strike across Europe, with officials warning that the strain on the system is likely to increase in the years ahead.

The Commission said this year's wildfire season began exceptionally early, with the first activation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism coming at the end of April. Officials warned the season could now last until October or even November.

"We started the fire season before last year," the Commission official added. "At the end of May the problem was fires reaching hundreds of hectares. By June they were reaching thousands. Right now, we are counting fires in tens of thousands of hectares."

The Commission is attempting to bolster its long-term capacity by purchasing a permanent European fleet of 12 Canadair aircraft and five helicopters. But deliveries will not be completed until 2030, leaving the bloc dependent on nationally based aircraft for several more summers.

Brussels has also strengthened its Emergency Response Coordination Centre by adding wildfire behaviour analysts capable of modelling how fires are likely to evolve, allowing authorities to position resources before conditions deteriorate.

But officials repeatedly argued that technology and additional aircraft alone cannot solve the problem.

"What we are advocating is an integrated management approach," said a second Commission official, pointing to the need for better forest management, including reducing combustible vegetation in forests and landscapes.

The EU officials also highlighted how climate adaptation is becoming inseparable from civil protection policy. Following successive heatwaves that dried vegetation across southern Europe, Commission officials said fire conditions are now consistently exceeding historical norms and warned that extreme fire danger is forecast to spread towards Greece.

While the Commission stopped short of predicting whether 2026 would eclipse last year's record wildfire season, officials acknowledged that activity is already running above previous trends.
