World.title: 'Nauseating': Boy George faces heated backlash for new pro-Israel song
World.content:
British singer Boy George, frontman of the band Culture Club, has released a song in solidarity with Israel.

 

Titled ‘Od Nirkod (We Will Dance Again)’, the reggae-style song has not been made available on streaming platforms and was instead posted on the artist's X account, along with the caption "Shalom".

The song's title is a phrase closely associated with the 7 October Hamas attack on the Supernova Sukkot Gathering festival, which led to the death of 378 people and Israel to launch its military campaign in Gaza. It is also the title of a 2024 documentary about the attack.

The song features the opening lyrics: "You say genocide / I say war / When you're attacked / That's what the army is for / Does it get ugly? / You bet it does / When I know you want to kill / Every last one of us..." It openly denies that a genocide is currently underway in Gaza – despite reports from Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations proving otherwise.

A recent report by a UN independent commission has found that "Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank." The report cited a conclusion by the commission last year, which stated that “Israel had committed genocide against the Palestinian group in the Gaza Strip, found that the intense scale and systematic nature of the Israeli military operations have continued, resulting in unprecedented death, injury and trauma of Palestinian children.”

Other song lyrics include: "Young girls raped against trees / Murdered brutally / You condemn the Jews / With selective memory / Musicians holding flags / Mouthing like sheep / Propaganda fuelled by the internet / Feels so weak.”

The song has been trashed online and the singer of ‘Karma Chameleon’ is facing backlash over the lyrics.

"Don’t you know over 20.000 children have been slaughtered, ethnically cleansed a population into a concentration camp, destroyed over 80% of the infrastructure, destroyed and ethnically cleansed thousands in the West Bank, shame on you," wrote one X user, while another said: "What a depraved piece of repellant zionist propaganda that's designed to justify the slaughter of over 80,000 Palestinians, inc. over 20,000 kids, and their continuing oppression, dispossession, humiliation and massacre."

Another commented: "Awful music, awful person, and he's sunk to supporting a genocide just to try and be contrary in the hopes it pays off - it won't. You're ruined any good faith anyone might have had in you, and you've only dug a deeper grave for your dead career."

Another echoed this sentiment, posting: "He has sold his soul, so disappointed. His Irish freedom fighting relatives would be horrified."

Check out some of the reactions below:

Many online have also made reference to a 2007 case in which Boy George was sentenced to 15 months in jail for falsely imprisoning a male escort by handcuffing him to a wall and beating him with a metal chain.

Boy George, who was raised in an Irish Catholic household and is not Jewish, has been vocal about his support of Israel.

Earlier this year, he said at a Eurovision event in London: “I have many, many Jewish friends that I’ve had since I was 15 or 16 years old. Are people asking me as a principled human being to turn my back on my Jewish friends? It’s not going to happen, it’s never going to happen.”

Unlike many artists who have called out the genocide and boycotted Israel, Boy George has rejected calls from the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement to perform in Tel Aviv.

World.title: A new Hello Kitty ‘hotel’ in Tokyo allows guests to check-in but not stay
World.content:
As this travel journalist knows, when it comes to Sanrio, the obsession knows no bounds.

 

An unending collection of plushies, stocking up on kawaii stationery, decking your room with Hello Kitty bedding, and the list goes on from there.

If you don’t already have enough merch, there’s only one thing left to do: board a flight to Japan’s capital city and visit a Sanrio-themed “hotel” experience. We say hotel, but it’s not a place where you can stay the night…

Tokyo’s Shinjuku-ku ward is currently hosting Sanrio fan favourites as part of the "Hotel Floria Tokyo - Sanrio Characters Exhibition" at the Tokyu Kabukicho Tower – less than a 10-minute walk away from a number of train stations.

Here, visitors can “check in” and tour themed rooms of beloved characters from the world of Sanrio – from Cinnamoroll and My Melody to, of course, Hello Kitty herself.

This comes after a successful run in Seoul, Korea, where the exhibit first made its debut as the brainchild of digital design and art company D’strict.

“Set in a hotel filled with the characters’ dreams, each room and installation allows visitors to discover their distinctive personalities and charm,” a Hotel Floria Tokyo spokesperson told Euronews Travel.

Running in Tokyo until May 2027 across 11 themed rooms, general entry starts at ¥2,400 (€12.87) during weekdays, with “check-in” prices slightly higher over the weekends and holidays.

Guests are handed their very own character-designed “Luc-key” entry pass at reception. But there’s a catch: much like a Sanrio blind box, guests don’t get to know or choose which character they get, instead, the reveal is entirely at random.

After passing the lobby, guests can wander through rooms and pay a visit to Sanrio favourites before a trip to the exhibit’s garden, pond, art gallery and indoor beach experience. Fun for all ages, the hotel-inspired exhibition also has a dedicated “Photo Zone”.

“Beyond taking photographs, guests can walk through, explore and experience these worlds for themselves,” Hotel Floria Tokyo said. “This creates the feeling of becoming part of the story, as an immersive experience that can be enjoyed by children and adults alike.

“Adults can reconnect with fond childhood memories and a sense of nostalgia, while children can enjoy discovering them for the first time.”

The ‘hotel’s’ top pick

If time is not on your side and there are only enough minutes to visit one exhibition area, Hotel Floria Tokyo recommends making a beeline for the Beach Zone.

There, pink hues ripple as part of an ocean sunset display on a floor-to-ceiling screen while real sand crunches beneath guests’ feet. In this daydream, Hello Kitty (in statue form) is standing beside her electric pink surfboard, while her canine friend Pochacco plays in the sand nearby.

“Visitors do more than simply watch images on a screen,” the organisers said. “As they walk across real sand, the visuals, sound and sensation beneath their feet naturally come together as one seamless experience.

“Rather than merely viewing the dreamlike scenery imagined by the Sanrio characters, visitors can walk through it and experience it with all their senses. This is what makes the Beach Zone so special.”

World.title: One year on, is the Turnberry deal already at risk?
World.content:
It's a bittersweet birthday for the EU-US trade deal. One year after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and US President Donald Trump struck the landmark agreement in Turnberry, Scotland, transatlantic trade relations are being jeopardised by fresh threats from the US.

 

Last week's €890 million fine imposed by the Commission on US tech giant Google sent the Trump administration into a fury. Posting on Truth Social, the president said the US will launch investigations into unfair trade practices, signalling that his administration is prepared to retaliatewhenthe EU enforces its digital rules against US firms.

However, Trump may have to anticipate consequences himself. After months of negotiations to implement the Turnberry agreement – which imposes 15 percent US tariffs on EU goods and removes EU duties on US industrial products – the Europeans introduced safeguards allowing them to reimpose tariffs on US goods under specific circumstances.

Euronews takes a closer look at how serious the US threat is and what the chances are of the deal being suspended.

What happened after the EU fined Google?

Once the EU announced it was fining Google because of its dominance in the EU's digital markets, Washington fired two warning shots.

On Thursday night, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the EU's fine created “uncertainty” for the Turnberry deal, jeopardising the EU-US dialogue on the EU's digital rules.

The following day, the US threat became more serious with Trump's post on Truth Social, in which he wrote: “The United States of America is not a ‘PIGGYBANK’ for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!”

He added that his administration would launch a Section 301 investigation under the US Trade Act of 1974, which allows the federal government to counter unfair trade practices by foreign countries.

“The European Union will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct, which I have consistently warned them about,” he said. “Stay tuned!”

How serious are Trump's threats?

Since the Turnberry agreement was struck, Europeans have grown used to receiving threats from Trump on social media. More often than not, they no longer react.

In December 2025, Washington threatened a list of EU tech companies, including Accenture, Siemens and Spotify, with restrictions or fees if the EU continued regulating US Big Tech through its digital rules.

The Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Digital Markets Act (DMA) – two landmark pieces of EU digital legislation – have been repeatedly criticised by the Trump administration since its return to power as non-tariff barriers targeting mainly US firms.

“Let's see what time will bring,” German Socialist MEP Bernd Lange, the European Parliament's trade chief, told Euronews. He added that discussions with the US about EU digital regulations are underway, but said he could not know for sure whether it would lead to "concrete” results.

Nonetheless, Lange believes that if Trump's threats turn out to be serious, the US could impose restrictions on EU digital services.

What can the EU do if Trump follows through?

On 19 May, after hours of negotiations, the EU's member states and the European Parliament struck a deal to remove EU tariffs on US goods as of 1 July.

However, in an effort to ensure stability for EU businesses, lawmakers pushed to include safeguards to shield the agreement from future threats.

The Commission can now suspend the deal if the US does not respect the 15 percent ceiling or if it “undermines access of Union economic operators to the United States’ market, discriminates against or targets Union economic operators aiming to operate, or already operating, in the United States”.

The regulation removing EU duties adds that it can also be suspended if the US “disrupts the trade and investment relationship between the Union and the United States.”

Croatian conservative MEP Željana Zovko told Euronews that the “responsibility” for suspending the deal “has rightly been entrusted to the Commission.”

“I am confident it will act at the right time and on the basis of facts,” she added.

Who in the EU would want to suspend the deal?

Over recent weeks, the Commission has appeared to take the view that regardless of whether the US imposes new tariffs, it was prepared to accept them as long as they respected the 15 percent ceiling.

That is what happened on Friday, when a new US tariff regime replaced the one imposed after a February ruling by the US Supreme Court. The EU executive was satisfied to see the new US tariffs set at 10 percent, even though they were imposed over alleged failures to ban imports made with forced labour – an accusation the EU rejects, saying it has strict rules in place to keep such products out of its market.

But what might happen if EU services were targeted?

Lange said there was an agreement with the Commission that if it had to suspend the deal, it would take Parliament's views into account.

“So if we are pushing for the suspension, then I guess they will do it as well,” he said, adding that there would be sufficient political will in Parliament for such a move.

“We have much more self-confidence than a year ago.”

World.title: This European airline is offering free ‘teddy trackers’ for families travelling this summer
World.content:
The difference between packing for an adult and a child isn’t all that much. You both need weather-appropriate clothing, shoes, toiletries, and, of course, your unmentionables.

 

There is one essential that kids need that (most) adults don’t: Their teddy.

Whether your little one’s beloved stuffed toy comes in a traditional bear shape or in the form of some other animal, it’s imperative that they come with you on your adventures – and make it back safely – or you may face some serious tantrums.

Luckily for you, easyJet has unveiled a new initiative to make sure cuddly toys make it there and back again, and if they are lost, you can easily be reunited with them.

That’s because the airline has partnered with Life360 to offer customers free tile trackers that can be attached to their kids’ companions.

Families will be able to collect their teddy trackers at easyJet bag drop from 31 July at London Gatwick, Manchester, Edinburgh and Belfast airports while stocks last. Simply attach the tracker to the toy, download the app and connect it to your device with Bluetooth, and away you go.

“For many children, a favourite teddy or comfort toy is an important part of the journey and losing it can be upsetting at what should be an exciting time,” Stuart Wright, customer director at easyJet holidays, said.

“That's why we've launched Teddy Trackers, giving families extra peace of mind while they're away. Creating brilliant holiday experiences is at the heart of what we do, and we're delighted to be offering another simple way to make family holidays as smooth and stress-free as possible.”

While it may seem silly to some, a poll of more than 1,000 parents of children aged under 10 has revealed that 55% of parents would change their plans while away to retrieve a missing companion.

In case you were wondering, the most common companion in 2026 is a stuffed bunny (26%), followed by teddy bears (25%), then action figures or dolls (15%), according to the easyJet survey. The top names reported are Bunny, Teddy, Fluffy and Billy.

World.title: Israel's move to recognise Armenian genocide stalls under regional pressure
World.content:
The Israeli parliament's decision to postpone a vote on recognising the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey is being seen as a triumph for regional diplomacy, as Azerbaijan in particular seeks to avert a further escalation in tensions between its close allies.

Advertising

The Israeli government gave no official reason for postponing the vote to formally recognise the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey during World War I, which would have ratified a motion approved by the cabinet last month.

Ankara strongly denies the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Armenians constitute genocide.

While the motion's architect, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, called recognition a “moral duty”, critics say the move took aim at Turkey amidst rising tensions.

Based in Tbilisi, Israeli defence and security expert Eugene Kogan claims Israel badly miscalculated. “Foreign Minister Sa'ar could have waited and not just dropped a bomb that led to different repercussions coming from different sides,” he said.

Armenia, which is seeking to normalise ties with Turkey, reacted coolly, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan saying he saw no need to comment. Meanwhile, Israel’s close ally Azerbaijan reportedly lobbied Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to drop the motion.

“At the end of the day, it might be either dropped or dismissed, and it will not come again to the new parliament agenda,” predicted Kogan.

The Knesset dissolved on 17 July and won't reconvene until after elections scheduled for 27 October.

Israel's recognition of the Armenian genocide unsettles Turkey and Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan's influence

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that pressure from Azerbaijan tipped the scales, though officials deny it.

Azerbaijan supplies nearly 40 percent of Israel’s oil and is a major customer for Israeli arms. The two countries’ partnership involves frequent Israeli ministerial visits and strong military cooperation, especially crucial for Israel given Azerbaijan’s border with Iran.

Baku also maintains a deep alliance with Ankara, summed up in the phrase “one nation, two states”. As Israeli-Turkish tensions flare over the Gaza conflict and Ankara’s support for Hamas, Azerbaijan is walking a diplomatic tightrope.

Zaur Gasimov, a Caucasus expert at Istanbul’s Turkish-German University, believes Baku viewed the Israeli genocide motion as a direct threat to its difficult balancing act.

“I can imagine that there were negotiations and talks on various levels between political elites of both countries,” he said. “For Israel, Azerbaijan is still of paramount importance. I would even say it's much more significant than it used to be with regard to the situation in and around Iran. So Baku was and is maybe the key intermediary between Israel and the Republic of Turkey.”

In what may be a calculated move to turn up the heat on Israel, Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev welcomed Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa this month. It was the first visit by a Palestinian leader since 2011.

“They [Israel] perceive it with a great sense of caution,” claimed analyst Kogan. “They don't know exactly what came out of this particular meeting between Aliyev and the Palestinian prime minister. And so there is a lot of guessing games right now taking place in both Tel Aviv and Jerusalem about the outcome.”

Such ambiguity over Baku’s intentions could strengthen its diplomatic hand, he suggested: “If Aliyev is involved in this Palestinian issue directly and no longer indirectly, it makes the situation very different for the Israelis.”

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Syrian precedent

Baku is already leveraging its strong relationships with both Israel and Turkey to cool tempers.

“We have organised meetings between Turkey and Israel in Baku, specifically at the very beginning of the change of the Assad regime in Syria, where both parties had their own legitimate concerns,” said Hikmet Hajiyev, chief foreign policy adviser to the Azerbaijani president.

Syria is viewed as a potential flashpoint, with Israel and Turkey having a military presence. One tangible outcome of Azeri-brokered talks was the establishment last year of a military hotline in Syria, providing a rare glimmer of hope as tensions continue to mount.

“It's not unavoidable that Israel and Turkey will reach confrontation. I think we can stop this process,” argued Gallia Lindenstrauss, a specialist in Turkish foreign policy at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies.

“They have a hotline between the Israeli Air Force and the Turkish Air Force, making sure that we will not have a collision in the skies of Syria, because we know both air forces are operating there. And the hotline has managed to keep the situation quiet. If I'm trying to find some anchor of reassurance that Turkish-Israeli relations can be controlled, it's Syria.”

As Israel approaches elections, a temporary lull in Turkish-Israeli tensions is anticipated. Still, since the main opposition shares the government’s concerns over Turkey, relations are set to remain fraught.

World.title: Indian youth score a win over Modi with humor and grit
World.content:
Driven by social media satire, the Gen-Z-led "Cockroach" protest movement spurned by grievances over an exam scandal caused a shake-up in India's government. DW spoke with a few protesters in New Delhi.

Walking from Jantar Mantar to Connaught Place in central New Delhi on Saturday evening provided an unusual sight for the prime corridor of power in the world's largest democracy.

Satirical posters mocking India's legislative, executive and judiciary were plastered on the walls, and the pavement was sprayed with sometimes "vulgar" graffiti mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

These were all remnants of thousands of young "Cockroach" movement protesters who had flooded the streets hours earlier after India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

Celebrating Pradhan's resignation, which had been a core protest demand, some protesters where heard telling security officials "see you at the next protest," coming only days after several people were injured in clashes with baton-wielding police who fired tear gas into crowds.

Protesters dispersed on Saturday evening in central New Delhi Image: ANI/ANI News/IMAGO

Instagram was also full of images from cities across India with young people dancing in front of police officials to the line "Everybody knows that I'm a good girl, officer " from Lana Del Ray's song "Playing Dangerous."

Others held posters reading: "Cuff me, daddy" and some were seen climbing atop police barricades.

India's Gen Z rattles government into change

The movement, known as the Cockroach Janta Party movement (CJP), came after an Indian minister publicly referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is also a play on Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Since a scandal broke in May involving a highly competitive university entrance exam, the Gen Z protests have spread across India, challenging the political establishment with Instagram reels, viral trends, sarcastic jingles and posters.

"In our generation humor has become the defense mechanism from pain, frustration and helplessness. This entire protest is driven by humor, driven by Instagram and social media," Karan Azad, a 24-year-old law student, told DW at the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.

Another protester held a sign addressed to Modi reading in transliterated Hindi: "Buddy, you can't even make tea," alluding to Modi's boyhood days as a tea seller.

A protesters holds a sign reading "Buddy, you can't even make tea" mocking PM Modi Image: Dharvi Vaid/DW

"I had to do my part. I am the youth. If we don't stand up for ourselves no one else will, we have to fight this battle ourselves," she told DW without giving her name.

A protesters named Tushar, also 24, was holding up a print out of Modi depicted as a fairy with words that read "I am fairy, don't touch me."

He said he wasn't "afraid of a backlash" from the authorities, but rather "would have had FOMO (fear of missing out)" had he not joined the protest.

Ridhima, a 17-year-old school student, said: "If not us then who? Those who are not here, it just speaks to their cowardice and I am talking about people who are sitting on their chairs in positions of power."

What drove the Cockroach movement?

Content creator Arun Singh, known by his social media handle "TheJhumroo," said that meme culture kept the satire and humor fresh throughout the protests."

"It's the meme culture which fuelled this kind of emotion. As millennials, we developed the language of memes as we adapted to the internet culture, but this younger generation was born with memes being their language. This is how they communicate," he told DW.

Singh said that the young protesters are best described as "fearless."

"They don't fear anyone, they don't worry about how they would be perceived and that's what happens when you're absolutely young. That is what is driving their grit," he said.

A sign in broken English describing the stress Indian students face Image: Dharvi Vaid/DW

Mumbai-based comedian Aditi Mittal observes that the fearlessness of the Gen Z protesters comes from them living in a "hyper visible world".

"All of them have 500 followers at a minimum. If something goes up on their stories, it's not going to go vastly ignored," she told DW.

Mittal also thinks that India's Gen Z inherited the "perfect protest."

"The generation prior to ours wanted better infrastructure. We millennials aspired to have a more equal world, ours was a time distinct with, for example, the mistreatment of Muslims. We grew up in that and were constantly gaslit into… it's not that bad, it's not happening. We were also overly forbearing," she told DW.

"Gen Z inherited the perfect protest. Education goes beyond religion and secularism, It can resonate, especially for a country like ours where education has been the tool of escape from social class or a financial situation," Mittal said.

Mittal also points out differences between today and the 2019 citizenship law (CAA) protests, one of the last big protests that had challenged the Modi government, and was centered on discrimination against Muslims.

"The anti-CAA protests constantly demanded the perfection of the protesters. Be nice to them [authorities] even as they beat you or hold a gun to you, that was the language spoken to us. But these younger kids don't stand around and wait. They are not tripping over themselves to be perfect," she said.

Getting attention with political humor

Satire is not new to India's politics. For example, caricatures were used as a means to channel anti-colonial anger in Bengal. Political cartoonists like Abu Abraham and R K Laxman challenged censorship brought on by former Primei Minister and Congress leader Indira Gandhi's imposition of a state of emergency that suspended civil liberties between 1975 to 1977.

"Satire is a great way of putting your word across. It's like eating a healthy food, but cooked in an interesting way, which is munchable. Humor has better penetration when it comes to content. It gets more eyeballs," content creator Singh told DW.

Academic and writer Ananya Vajpeyi said that this sense of humor built sympathy with the students and kept the mood light and non-threatening.

"These were young boys and girls who looked tiny, not strong, not threatening, not even articulate sometimes, who had drawn or written something funny on a piece of paper. The violent crackdown backfired immediately because these were not two equal forces facing each other," she told DW.

'The whole city is on fire, and the judiciary is having fun,' reads this sign in New Delhi Image: Dharvi Vaid/DW

India's Gen-Z rattles 'brand Modi'

Modi is seen as an image-conscious politician and his 12 years in India's seat of power have been defined by a carefully crafted image that relies heavily on perception management and public relations.

Many of the protesters directly mocked Modi, challenging his brand.

"The whole atmosphere has been so stifled since the anti-CAA protest was shut down. People have been punished for expressing any kind of criticism or dissent, And here you have thousands of students from every corner of the country, just like cockroaches crawling out of the woodwork and making life hell for the Modi establishment," Vajpeyi told DW.

Vajpeyi says the ire against Modi has likely caused "embarrassment" for the prime minister.

"What these kids are saying is like a punch in the stomach for Modi, if he is able to see all this. It's possible that he's being kept from it by those around him but the opposition sees it. The rest of the country who is on social media sees it," she said.

World.title: Ghana's community service bill: A fix for the prison crisis?
World.content:
The community service bill offers community service as an alternative to prison sentences, particularly for minor offenses. It's meant to decongest Ghana's prisons and prevent overcrowding once it's signed into law.

Ghana's parliament recently passed the Community Service Bill , 2026. The piece of legislation is designed to introduce community service as an alternative to custodial sentences for minor offenses. The bill also seeks to ease pressure on the country's overcrowded prisons and reshape how justice is administered for minor crimes.

The legislation establishes a National Community Service Secretariat and provides a legal framework for courts to impose community service in Ghana instead of imprisonment for specified offenses.

According to the government, the move will reduce the financial strain of maintaining prison facilities, which have long suffered from inadequate budgets, high medical costs and chronic congestion .

Ghana's parliament has passed the community service bill and now it only awaits President Mahama's signature to become law Image: Misper Apawu/AP Photo/picture alliance

"If you check the current prison population, overcrowding is over 37%. We have a current population of over 13,000 prisoners. Today the cost of maintaining them, feeding them alone, requires 10 million cedis (€752,000, $859,000) a quarter," Ghana's Interior Minister, Muntaka Mubarak, who tabled the bill in parliament , told the house during a debate.

Which offenses are covered under the community service bill?

Under the bill, community service applies to offenses punishable by not more than three years' imprisonment, with or without a fine. Courts may also impose community service for offenses that carry fines alone or fines combined with imprisonment.

This means petty crimes such as false publication or traffic offenses could now attract noncustodial penalties.

Legal practitioner Christian Malm Hesse described the bill as "a step in the right direction," noting its potential to reduce prison overcrowding. He told DW that the bill provides a structured alternative for misdemeanor offenses that previously defaulted to custodial sentences.

However, some Ghanaians believe that its effectiveness will depend on proper categorization of offenses and public education.

According to DW correspondent Eric Mawuena Egbeta, many Ghanaians still need clarity on which offenses qualify. "An offense which is higher than a misdemeanor would mean that you will not get a community sentence… a lot more persons would need education on it," Egbeta said.

For legal practitioners like Hesse, one key safeguard in the bill is the requirement for a social inquiry report, which helps judges assess an offender's background, circumstances, and suitability for community service. Hesse said such measures ensure that sentencing decisions are informed and consistent, reducing the risk of arbitrary application.

Africa's shift toward noncustodial sentencing

Ghana's new passage aligns with a growing trend across Africa, where countries such as Nigeria, Kenya, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda have adopted similar noncustodial sentencing legislation.

International bodies, including the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, have long encouraged alternatives to establish, citing benefits such as reduced recidivism (where a person returns to criminal behavior and is sent back to jail after finishing a past sentence), lower state expenditure, and improved community reintegration.

Surviving Kenya's Prison System To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Ghana, the bill represents the culmination of a decade-long policy process initiated in 2014 by the Ministry of the Interior with support from UNICEF. The resulting framework aims to modernize justice administration and align national laws with global best practices on restorative justice.

Experts say the bill could be a game-changer for the continent, offering a model for balancing accountability with rehabilitation. By redirecting minor offenders toward community labor, skills development, and civic responsibility, Ghana joins a broader African effort to rethink punishment beyond incarceration.

What do Ghanaians think about the bill?

Christabel Success, a Ghanaian journalist, said the law is "most appropriate for minor offenses," but stressed the need for fairness in its application. "The method of application is what will determine whether it is a good bill or not," she told DW.

"It will help us with our capacity building, nation building, and ridding our communities and our environment of waste," Nurah Suglo, an Accra-based resident, told DW. "We'd have cleaner cities, cleaner regions, and make good use of our labor instead of overcrowding our prisons. People with minor offenses get to also do something that will contribute to the nation as a whole," Success added.

Educating prisoners in Nigeria To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Egbeta, however, noted that crimes classified as second-degree felonies, such as stealing after breaking into a home, remain outside the bill's scope, which may disappoint those hoping for broader reforms. Although Parliament has passed the Community Service Bill, it cannot take effect until President John Dramani Mahama gives his assent.

Despite hailing its passage, Hesse explained that another crucial step for the bill is the creation of a Legislative Instrument (L.I). "What is left is an L.I. When bills like this are passed, it becomes the secondary legislation under which operations become effective," Hesse said.

This article was adapted from an AfricaLink Podcast. You can listen to the podcast here .

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu

World.title: Fujimori takes charge in Peru amid China, US balancing act
World.content:
Peru's new president, Keiko Fujimori, has promised more security and investment. As she takes office, she'll have to find space for the South American nation amid Washington and Beijing's geopolitical rivalry.

When Keiko Fujimori steps into the presidential office on Tuesday, she'll bring back a political movement that hasn't been in power for more than a quarter century.

Fujimorism, a mix of neoliberalism, populism and strict government policies, characterized the 1990-2000 presidency of her father, the late Alberto Fujimori. Keiko Fujimori is stepping in amid a climate of social polarization, with promises to deliver more security, economic recovery and improvements in the health and education sectors.

Fujimori has been clear she wants to align more closely with the US and other conservative governments Image: Martin Mejia/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

But beyond those domestic projects, Fujimori is taking charge at a time of increased strategic importance for Peru. The country has become one of the key battlegrounds in the growing competition between the United States and China for political influence in South America.

Tough on crime

Fujimori has already signaled that security will be the top priority for her government.

On the agenda: more video surveillance, a stronger police presence, tougher punishment for crimes and organized gangs, and command and control centers across the country. Part of the crackdown includes the construction of four mega-prisons, like those in El Salvador.

Eliana Carlin, a political science expert at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru in Lima, is concerned by how Fujimori's plans will affect human rights.

"Behind [these measures] lie strong ideological positions intended to justify making the police and the armed forces solely subject to military jurisdiction," she said.

In addition to a stronger focus on security, Fujimori has said she intends to advance infrastructure projects, attract private investment, build new schools and hospitals and modernize the country with the help of technology and artificial intelligence.

But delivering on these pledges depends largely on whether the government can find the necessary funds. Infrastructure and essential services continue to face significant deficits. Added to that is the surging crime rate and the threat of the strengthening El Nino weather pattern, which could hit Peru with increased drought, extreme heat, flooding and other climate-related disruptions.

How a 'super El Nino' could change global weather To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Strategic player in South America

Foreign policy will also be a major challenge for Fujimori's administration. The opening of the Chancay port and logistics hub has turned Peru into a strategic player in regional trade — and made it a central focus in the geopolitical rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

The estimated $3.5 billion (€3 billion) project is part of China's world-spanning Belt ⁠and Road Initiative. Once fully operational, the port is expected to reduce the shipping time between Peru and China from around 40 to about 23 days, turning Chancay into a new gateway to Asia.

Thanks to the port and other investments, China has become Peru's most important trading partner. Bilateral trade between the two countries exceeded $40 billion in 2024, according to official figures. In second place is the US, with nearly $25 billion in trade.

Michael Shifter, an adjunct professor at Georgetown University in Washington teaching Latin American politics, said there's a lot at stake in Peru.

"Beijing has played a very important role in the Peruvian economy for many years, while at the same time the US is seeking to expand its influence. Nowhere is the competition between Beijing and Washington as evident as in Peru," he told DW.

Why is China's new megaport in Peru facing pushback? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Shifter, the port at Chancay will be important for both Peru and its regional neighbors. "It will reduce transportation costs and facilitate trade with Asia, particularly with China," he said. "The project has enormous potential for the future of the South American economy."

Part of a planned "bioceanic" corridor between Brazil and Peru, the Pacific hub at Chancay will be connected via rail and road projects to the Atlantic Ocean, facilitating the export of products from all over South America to Asia.

Balancing China, US 'will not be easy'

Fujimori has also announced plans to expand her cooperation with the US, particularly in the areas of security and the fight against organized crime. For Shifter, the challenge will be to maintain the delicate balance between Washington and Beijing.

The Chancay port is a part of China's world-spanning Belt ⁠and Road Initiative Image: Angela Ponce/REUTERS

"Keiko wants to align herself with Washington and avoid tensions with the US. At the same time, China has been indispensable to the Peruvian economy for many years, and the port of Chancay enjoys broad support in Peru. Balancing this relationship will not be easy," he said.

To stay on the US president's good side, Peru's participation in the so-called "Shield of the Americas" will also be key. The alliance, initiated by Donald Trump to combat organized crime, has already welcomed the cooperation of, among others, the right-wing governments of Argentina, Chile, Ecuador and El Salvador.

According to Shifter, involvement in "the 'Shield of the Americas' would also serve to demonstrate a closeness to the Trump administration."

New roll for Peru in Latin America

Fujimori's inauguration comes at a time when conservative forces have gained influence in several Latin American countries. For Shifter, however, Peru's case is unique.

"It's tempting to interpret her election victory as yet another shift to the right in Latin America. But Peru is more complex than that. Keiko Fujimori has shaped Peruvian politics for many years, and the country had already been pursuing a rather pragmatic course," he said.

Political scientist Carlin, however, fully expects a foreign policy shift.

"[Fujimori] has already made it clear that she wants to align more closely with the US and other conservative governments. I think we'll see Peru adopt a tougher foreign policy stance, but I don't think that Peru can do without China," she said. "A break with Beijing would not be realistic."

This article was originally written in Spanish.

World.title: How India's Gen-Z protesters shifted the political debate
World.content:
The resignation of India's education minister amounts to a stunning victory for the youth-led "Cockroach" protest movement. The bigger question is if this political momentum turns into a lasting platform for more reform.

On Saturday, student protesters embraced, danced and climbed onto barricades as chants of victory echoed across New Delhi's historic Jantar Mantar protest site.

After weeks of demonstrations, marathon negotiations and repeated government refusals, a movement named the "Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)" succeeded in its demand for Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to step down.

The movement began on social media as a satirical activist campaign sparked by leaks of a question sheet for the highly competitive NEET exam in early May.

Along with Pradhan's resignation, the government also agreed to provide the maximum possible compensation to families of students who died by suicide following the NEET paper leak controversy. Additionally, it promised to withdraw criminal cases against protesters, refrain from pursuing future legal action and continue discussions on the CJP's five-point charter for academic examination reform.

The CJP, in turn, announced it was calling off further protest action "in good faith" while added that it would closely monitor whether the government promises were implemented.

"This is a victory of democracy," CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke told thousands of jubilant supporters.

Police and protesters clashed in the northeastern Bihar state on Saturday Image: Aftab Alam Siddiqui/ANI

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has insisted meeting some of the protest demands reflects responsible governance rather than capitulation.

"Pradhan's resignation is an example of putting students and the nation above political positions," said Home Minister Amit Shah.

However, the resignation of a cabinet minister following public outcry amounts to a rare retreat by Modi's government. Taken together, the concessions mark a remarkable victory for a movement that the government had initially dismissed as little more than a social media campaign.

"Nobody should underestimate student power. Our voice is finally heard. When we stand united, we can achieve many things," Uma Singh, a CJP supporter from the eastern Bihar state who spent days camping in New Delhi, told DW.

Cockroach movement forces a rare BJP retreat

Some 48 hours before Pradhan's resignation, senior Hindu nationalist BJP and government sources had said removing him was not under serious consideration, even as protests continued to grow in Delhi while solidarity demonstrations spread to cities across India.

Earlier concessions, including the removal of 47 National Testing Agency officials, promises of fast-track courts and administrative reshuffles, failed to satisfy protesters.

At the same time, the government faced growing concern that the confrontation would dominate the monsoon session of parliament and hand the opposition a powerful political issue.

Faced with mounting pressure both on the streets and inside parliament, the BJP reversed course.

Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Indian activist Amrita Johri believes the Cockroach movement's victory amounts to a major shift in political debate in India.

"The movement's significance extends well beyond the resignation of one minister. It showed that a loosely organized generation of young Indians could compel political concessions from a government long regarded as resistant to street pressure," Johri told DW.

"It shifted the debate from examination scandals to larger questions about whether India's institutions are still seen as fair, transparent and accountable. Electoral mandates may confer power, but lasting authority depends on public confidence," she added.

Beyond the immediate political settlement, the government's bigger challenge is rebuilding public trust in institutions that millions of young Indians depend on for opportunity.

Political scientist Gilles Verniers from the Paris-based Sciences Po public research university believes the episode has also exposed a weakness in the BJPs political instincts.

"Modi's usual playbook of staying above the fray, making broad promises and shifting responsibility down the chain failed this time," Verniers told DW.

"The minister's resignation is a clear victory for the protesters and a personal setback for a prime minister who stood by him until the end."

"It exposed a ruling party unprepared for a movement that was neither sectoral nor partisan, and a political class unaccustomed to a generation willing to openly challenge authority rather than defer to it," Verniers added.

BJP normally doesn't budge under pressure

In the past, the Modi government has seldom appeared willing to yield to sustained public pressure.

The closest comparison came during widescale farmers' protests, during which an estimated 700 to 750 protesters died before the government repealed three contentious farm laws in 2021.

Even then, legislation was withdrawn without ministerial accountability. This time, however, a cabinet minister has paid a political price.

Before changing course, the BJP had stuck by its Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan Image: Rahul Singh/ANI

The situation has also presented the opposition with evidence that sustained mobilization around issues such as unemployment, education and governance can put the government under pressure.

Senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh called Pradhan's resignation "a victory for a generation tired of struggling in an unfair and corrupt system," arguing that sustained pressure from students had finally forced the prime minister to withdraw his political backing for the education minister.

The BJP, for its part, argues it acted responsibly to restore confidence in the country's education system and protect students' interests.

Can the protest movement move forward?

The youth-led movement's next test is whether it can convert this political momentum into a lasting platform for institutional reform.

Talks with the government will continue over its five-point examination reform charter, and CJP leaders have warned they will return to the streets if promised changes fail to materialize.

For the government, the challenge is equally significant.

The immediate crisis may have passed, but the government has discovered that a decentralized, youth driven movement can rapidly shape the national political conversation.

Whether the CJP becomes a lasting political force or fades after achieving its immediate goals remains uncertain.

What is no longer in doubt is that it forced one of India's most powerful governments into a concession few believed possible only weeks earlier, reminding both politicians and young voters that organized public pressure can still shape Indian politics.

World.title: Germany: Islamist terror attack on Berlin Pride parade triggers political debate
World.content:
Berlin remains in shock following the attack on the "Christopher Street Day" (CSD) parade on Saturday. Hundreds of thousands of people had been celebrating peacefully and advocating for the rights of queer individuals — until, around 10 p.m., an attacker drove his vehicle into the crowd in the Tiergarten Park, right in the heart of the city.

One woman was killed and 29 others were injured, some seriously. Authorities quickly said the incident was a terrorist act committed by an Islamist. The suspect initially managed to flee but was later killed by police.

On Sunday afternoon, during a memorial service at St. Mary's Church (Marienkirche), not far from the Brandenburg Gate, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) said: "We will do everything to protect the freedom of our country and our society — everything!" He called out to the mourners: "Stand together, celebrate, and show the joyful face of our open, free society." Yet, right now, no one feels like celebrating.

Let us not be intimidated by these crimes: Chancellor Merz To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This sentiment was echoed by the opposition. "Hatred must never triumph," said Luigi Pantisano, leader of the socialist Left Party. "Regardless of whether the hatred stems from religious fanaticism or if the attacks and hostility come from elsewhere," he continued.

The suspect was known to police

The suspected perpetrator was a 21-year-old German national, born to a woman of Lebanese origin. He was known to the police as a sympathizer with the Islamist terrorist militia "Islamic State" (IS) in Syria. In the summer of 2025, he attempted to travel to Syria via Turkey and Lebanon to join IS fighters. However, he was detained in Lebanon, brought back to Germany in November 2025, and placed in pre-trial detention.

He stood trial in Berlin on charges of preparing a serious act of violence. Prosecutors sought a prison sentence of two years and ten months. However, the court released the young man, handing down a suspended sentence of one year and ten months. The IS sympathizer had been free since mid-May of this year — a decision the prosecution appealed.

Although the man's phone was wiretapped for a time, he was not subject to comprehensive surveillance.

At liberty despite clear IS sympathies? That must not happen again, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) said on Sunday: "Part of the review process will be determining whether suspended sentences are actually appropriate in such cases," Dobrindt told public broadcaster ZDF. "It is simply a matter of being able to restrict the freedom of movement of such individuals," Dobrindt concluded.

Germany calls deadly Pride attack 'Islamic terror' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The main opposition party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) spoke of a total failure of security policy. "If an Islamist 'threat actor' known to the police was able to commit such an act, there must be a thorough investigation into why he was able to move about freely in the first place," said AfD interior policy spokesperson Martin Hess.

Konstantin von Notz of the environmentalist Green Party called for greater powers for security agencies in dealing with violent Islamists and drew a parallel to previous incidents: "It leaves one utterly stunned that this apparently involves yet another 'person of interest' who was already on the authorities' radar," the Green Party politician said.

Criminal prosecution under scrutiny

"What actually happened after his release from prison? With whom did he maintain contact? Even though he was under surveillance, there was clearly a gap here; that is precisely what we need to examine in minute detail — and rest assured, we will," said Sebastian Fiedler of the center-left Social Democratic Party(SPD) which is currently part of the federal government as junior coalition partner to the conservative CDU/CSU bloc.

"Overall, our criminal laws regarding terrorism are too lenient," terrorism expert Peter Neumann of King's College London told public broadcaster ZDF. He noted that prison sentences in Germany are short by European standards, particularly when compared to those in France and the United Kingdom.

Queer life around Berlin's Nollendorfplatz To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, many experts also point out that it is difficult to maintain comprehensive surveillance on individuals whom German courts have not sentenced to prison. The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, estimates that there are currently around 420 individuals in Germany classified as "Islamist security threats" — a term referring to people whom authorities believe capable of committing a terrorist act. It remains unclear whether the suspected perpetrator Abdul B.* was among them. Security experts estimate, however, that placing all such individuals under round-the-clock surveillance would completely overwhelm the authorities — especially given that the total number of potentially violent Islamists in Germany is estimated to be significantly higher, at around 9,000 people.

Dirk Peglow, chairman of the Association of German Criminal Investigators (BDK), told the Handelsblatt newspaper on Monday: "In the case of an individual posing such a high level of risk, release from custody must not mean the end of state monitoring." However, Peglow also pointed out that if authorities are expected to monitor particularly dangerous individuals over extended periods, state security and surveillance units must be "appropriately equipped in terms of personnel, technology, and organization"— which, at present, they are not.

The court had ordered the young man to attend a total of 26 appointments at a deradicalization center. Abdul B. had already completed two of these; a third counseling session was scheduled for that Monday. There is widespread criticism now of whether such trainings de facto serve their purpose.

This article has been translated from German.

*DW withholds the full names of perpetrators in order not to increase their publicity and the likelihood of copycat killers.

World.title: 'Amnesia' about measles risk and low vaccination rates have helped US infections grow
World.content:
The latest US data show measles cases from January to mid-July 2026 totaled more than all cases in 2025. Experts blame a fall in vaccination and warn that people have forgotten measles can be life-threatening.

Behind the familiar symptoms of fever and spots is an extremely contagious virus that can cause lasting harm or death. That's the reality of measles.

But many people in the US appear to have forgotten the seriousness of a measles infection, with outbreaks mainly in under-vaccinated communities.

In fact, infections have hit a 35-year high as declining vaccination rates have created growing pockets of susceptible people.

Experts warn that the fading memories of the once-common disease have left too many people unaware of its dangers.

The number of measles cases in the United States up to mid-July 2026 surpassed the total number of cases in 2025. By the week of July 13-19, 2026, the number of reported measles cases was 2,321. By comparison, the total number of US measles cases in 2025 was 2,286, according to the US Measles Tracker run by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

What does the rise in measles cases mean?

Johns Hopkins epidemiologist William Moss expects the surge in measles cases to result in the US losing the measles-elimination status it has held since 2000.

"The significance of reaching this milestone is that the US has not been able to stop measles virus transmission or outbreaks as it has in the past," Moss told DW.

Moss said the virus was now spreading "from one susceptible community to another within the US," rather than being limited to infections brought in from abroad.

Measles virus is contagious before spots appear

Measles is the most contagious virus on Earth, spreading far more easily than the common cold. Nine out of 10 non-immune people exposed to the virus will become infected.

Measles spreads through virus-containing droplets released from an infected person's nose, throat and lungs when they breathe, talk or cough. The smallest particles can remain suspended in the air long after the person has left the room.

Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"You just have to be in somebody's airspace within two hours of them being there," said Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia.

Crucially, people can transmit measles before realizing they are infected.

Patients typically become contagious around four days before the characteristic spots or rash appear.

The combination of airborne particles, extreme contagion and transmission before obvious symptoms allows the virus to exploit even relatively small gaps in vaccination.

Measles complications can emerge years later

In the US, about one in five people with measles are hospitalized.

One in 20 infected children develops pneumonia, while around one in 1,000 develops encephalitis, a form of brain inflammation that can cause permanent brain damage.

Between one and three of every 1,000 infected children die from respiratory or neurological complications.

"We had two unvaccinated children — a healthy little six-year-old, a healthy little eight-year-old — die of measles this past year," Offit told DW.

Both died with pneumonia. "It's like dying of suffocation," he said. "It's a terrible way to die."

Among those who survive, the harm can persist long after the fever and spots disappear.

Measles can suppress the immune system for years, erasing some of the protection it had previously developed against other viruses and bacteria.

Another delayed complication is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a rare but fatal degenerative brain disease that can appear up to 10 years after the original infection.

Measles spots spread downward across the body in an easy-to-recognize manner Image: Alejandro Ernesto/dpa/picture alliance

"Children get infected, they get better, they're fine," Offit said. "And then five years later, seven years later, they come in with a deterioration in handwriting skills, deterioration in personality and then they descend into a vegetative state and die."

Has the danger of measles been forgotten?

Vaccination pushed measles out of everyday life in the US. But that success has also weakened public understanding of why vaccination is necessary.

"We've not just largely eliminated measles from our country; we've eliminated the memory of measles," Offit said.

"The most serious complications of measles are relatively rare and only become apparent when there is a large number of cases," said Moss. "Unfortunately, the increasing number of measles cases in the US will once again teach us that this is not always a harmless childhood infection."

Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist who publishes a Substack newsletter called "Your Local Epidemiologist," said falling vaccination rates reflected a "general amnesia about these diseases," falsehoods on social media and a wider loss of trust in institutions.

"The outbreaks remain among under-vaccinated communities," Jetelina said. "There are unvaccinated pockets all around the nation. All it takes is a spark for this disease to spread like wildfire in those pockets."

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: FIFA boss Infantino takes aim at World Cup critics
World.content:
In a strongly worded open statement, FIFA President Gianni Infantino has hit out at those he says were too "consumed by hate and criticism" to enjoy the tournament. Infantino brushed off a number of corruption concerns.

Gianni Infantino is not a man used to apologizing. And even though he said sorry three times on the second slide of a 15-page Instagram post, that remains the case.

"To everyone who missed our beautiful game, the emotions, the celebrations, the laughter, the crying, the deception, and the joy. To all of you who missed watching kids, babies, grandparents, and parents come together for the beautiful game, I say sorry that the matches are now over and sorry that you missed all that joy and togetherness. Sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all," read a missive from the FIFA president posted on FIFA's website, his personal Instagram account, and FIFA's online and social channels. Comments were turned off.

The Swiss executive went on to claim that the World Cup, had brought "no violence, no incidents, 100% safety and security, only joy and happiness!” The exclamation mark was not the only part of the message reminiscent of US President Donald Trump's communication style.

Infantino claims to have 'united' Iran and USA

"While you spread hatred, we worked tirelessly to unite two countries at war. Iran entered the United States without incident or conflict," Infantino wrote.

In fact, Iran were treated differently to any of the other 47 teams at the World Cup. They were forced to stay in Mexico and travel to their games in the US and had further last minute restrictions imposed on them after their matches.

Iran head coach Amir Ghalenoei said his team were the "most oppressed" at the World Cup after the travel chaos came on top of several support staff being denied visas.

Travel bans and visa refusals were a running theme of the tournament. Trump's travel bans denied entry to fans from several participating countries, including Haiti, Senegal, Iran and the Ivory Coast, which faced varying levels of bans or restrictions.

Iran at the 2026 World Cup To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Furthermore Somali referee Omar Artan was denied entry to the US due to unsubstantiated US government claims that he had an "association with suspected members of terror organizations," despite the fact that he held a diplomatic passport and the had been issued the correct visa.

FIFA and UEFA split becoming clearer

But, Infantino said, people should instead be looking at FIFA's successes.

"You mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world. Because football unites the world, and it was demonstrated impressively this summer," he added.

Infantino's relationship with Trump has been another bone of contention for many. After awarding Trump the newly introduced FIFA Peace Prize in December, Trump admitted to phoning Infantino to lobby on behalf of US striker Folarin Balogun, whose red card ban was suspended in a near-unprecedented move at a World Cup.

Could Europe's football union ditch FIFA? To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

"Indeed, "arguable" referees' decisions or "strange" disciplinary rulings such as for instance potentially mistaken red or yellow cards or subsequent decisions not to ban players in certain situations are routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide," Infantino wrote.

However, FIFA's own rules state that red card bans at World Cups cannot be appealed or overturned, which Balogun's, in a World Cup context at least, was.

"It's curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticizing," continued Infantino in what appeared to be a shot at European governing body UEFA, which publicly said FIFA had "crossed a red line" in the Balogun incident. UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin failed to attend the World Cup final, a move widely understood to have been in protest – with FIFA and its biggest continental association at loggerheads.

Trump wants Infantino as UN Secretary-General

Shortly after the final, Trump recommended Infantino for the post of secretary-general of the United Nations, which is up for grabs at the end of this year.

But, despite the thoughts of his "close friend," Infantino looks set to remain at FIFA, where he is expected to be elected unopposed once again next year. In Sunday's message he praised his own organization for delivering despite the further criticism of hydration breaks and FIFA breaking their own rules to extend halftime in the final.

"To the pens and papers, to all the screens, may you find love and peace where the people behind you couldn't.

2026 World Cup, the tournament that changed football forever To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

May you find peace; we at FIFA have found ours and we deliver it, by delivering the most outstanding FIFA World Cup. May football rise above all hate."

It's a message that the Iranian team, Haitian fans and Omar Artan may well have shared, had they been allowed to enjoy the World Cup with the same freedoms as Infantino.

World.title: Última hora de los incendios forestales en España, en directo | Los equipos de extinción trabajan contra reloj en el incendio de Madrid antes de la llegada de otra ola de calor
World.content:
Vista del humo del incendio forestal en Mijares, Ávila, Castilla y León, este lunes. El incendio forestal de Burgohondo, Ávila, ha calcinado 55000 hectáreas, convirtiéndose en el mayor incendio registrado en España.

Los incendios han afectado más de 170.000 hectáreas en España en lo que va del año | El fuego en la sierra oeste de Madrid se encuentra en “una situación endemoniada” y obliga a desalojar el municipio de Valdemaqueda | Pedro Sánchez alerta de que “quedan horas difíciles”

La ministra para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico, Sara Aagesen, ha cifrado este lunes en más de 170.000 las hectáreas que han sido afectadas por los incendios forestales en España en lo que va del año, un número seis veces mayor que las hectáreas afectadas en 2025. El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha visitado este lunes la zona afectada por el incendio de la Vall d’Uixó (Castellón), que lleva más de 7.200 hectáreas afectadas y ha obligado a desalojar a más de 16.000 personas. Ha alertado de que “quedan horas difíciles” en la lucha contra el fuego ante la llegada de una nueva ola de calor y ha pedido extremar la precaución. El incendio que arrasa la Sierra Oeste madrileña y que afecta ya a 25.000 hectáreas en la región sigue activo. 112 Comunidad de Madrid señala que las rachas del viento de hasta 30 kilómetros por hora “complicarán las labores de extinción”, que se están concentrando sobre todo en la zona del embalse de San Juan, en el entorno del municipio de San Martín de Valdeiglesias. Allí es donde las llamas han confluido con las del incendio de Burgohondo (Ávila), que ha quemado ya unas 50.000 hectáreas. La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha explicado que la situación en la región sigue siendo muy complicada, especialmente en el flanco oeste y la zona del pantano de San Juan. “Es una situación endemoniada”, ha dicho.

EL PAÍS ofrece de forma gratuita la última hora de los incendios. Si quieres apoyar nuestro periodismo, suscríbete.

World.title: El incendio de La Vall d’Uixó ya arrasa 7.200 hectáreas y encara horas críticas
World.content:
El incendio que amenaza con devorar el pulmón verde de Castellón avanza sin freno. El fuego, que se originó el sábado por la mañana en un barrio de La Vall d’Uixó, junto a la montaña, sigue ganando terreno y ya ha arrasado 7.200 hectáreas, la mayor parte de ellas en el parque natural de la Sierra de Espadán. Hasta el Puesto de Mando Avanzado de la Vall d’Uixó se ha desplazado este lunes el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, quien, tras reunirse con los responsables del dispositivo, ha advertido de que “quedan horas difíciles y complejas”. La preocupación, ha señalado, aumenta ante la inminente llegada de una nueva ola de calor, que traerá un nuevo ascenso de las temperaturas y complicará aún más el trabajo de los equipos desplegados sobre el terreno. Ante ese escenario, Sánchez ha apelado a la ciudadanía para que extreme la prevención.

El incendio de la Sierra de Espadán es un episodio más de un verano marcado por el fuego. Mientras los equipos de extinción combaten las llamas en varios puntos del país, el presidente del Gobierno ha advertido de la magnitud de una campaña que ya deja cifras inéditas: más de 170.000 hectáreas calcinadas en una decena de grandes incendios, seis veces más que las registradas a estas alturas del año pasado. Un balance que, unido a la nueva ola de calor prevista para los próximos días, anticipa un verano todavía largo para los servicios de emergencia y para las poblaciones que conviven con el avance de las llamas.

Bajo el incesante ir y venir de los helicópteros y con una fina lluvia de cenizas cayendo sobre la Vall d’Uixó, Pedro Sánchez ha aprovechado su visita para volver a defender la necesidad de un pacto de Estado frente a la emergencia climática. El presidente ha anunciado además que el Consejo de Ministros aprobará este martes “un real decreto ley de zona gravemente afectada por una emergencia de Protección Civil”.

La Brigada de Refuerzo de Incendios Forestales de Daroca (Aragón) que intervienen en la extinción del incendio forestal de la Vall d'Uixó. Carme Ripollés

Junto a Sánchez ha comparecido el presidente de la Generalitat, Juan Francisco Pérez Llorca, que ha endurecido el tono al referirse al origen del incendio. Si finalmente se confirma que detrás de las llamas hubo una acción intencionada, ha dicho, espera que “recaiga todo el peso de la ley” sobre el responsable. Incluso ha planteado abrir un debate para endurecer las penas frente a lo que ha calificado como “atentados medioambientales” que dejan una huella “muy difícil de reparar”.

El origen de las llamas sigue siendo el gran interrogante de un incendio que ya ha arrasado miles de hectáreas, aunque las primeras pesquisas apuntan a una posible intencionalidad. La aparición de varios focos consecutivos el sábado por la mañana en La Vall d’Uixó ha llevado a los investigadores a centrar sus esfuerzos en esa hipótesis. El Servicio de Protección de la Naturaleza (Seprona) de la Guardia Civil mantiene abiertas todas las líneas de investigación, aunque advierte de que el proceso será complejo y llevará tiempo. En la misma línea, la delegada del Gobierno en la Comunidad Valenciana, Pilar Bernabé, ha confirmado que los agentes ya han tomado declaración a varias personas para tratar de esclarecer el origen del fuego.

Más información Última hora de los incendios forestales, en directo

Mientras la investigación avanza, sobre el terreno la prioridad sigue siendo la de frenar un incendio que continúa fuera de control. “Ni está controlado, ni estabilizado”, ha afirmado con rotundidad el director de Extinción de los Bomberos, Fernando Pérez, este lunes tras la reunión del Cecopi. Al responsable del operativo le preocupan especialmente las próximas horas, que ha calificado como “muy difíciles”, ya que desde el mediodía las condiciones meteorológicas se han complicado con rachas de viento de hasta 30 kilómetros por hora. El objetivo de los bomberos es contener el avance de las llamas hasta la noche, cuando el aumento de la humedad pueda ofrecer un respiro. Aun así, dan por hecho que el incendio no quedará controlado este lunes y continúa obligando a mantener evacuadas a 16.000 personas.

Vista general de una zona afectada por el incendio forestal en la Vall d'Uixo (Castellón), este lunes. Eva Manez (REUTERS)

Más de 400 efectivos terrestres y 25 medios aéreos concentran ahora sus esfuerzos en tres frentes especialmente sensibles: Eslida, la urbanización Montserrat, en Betxí, y el paraje del Montí, en Onda. Allí se libra la batalla más intensa para contener el avance de las llamas. “Es un mal sueño del que vamos a salir”, ha asegurado la alcaldesa de la Vall d’Uixó, Tania Baños, quien ha subrayado la “absoluta necesidad” de que todas las administraciones actúen de forma coordinada para hacer frente a la emergencia. Baños ha querido mirar más allá de la emergencia y ha puesto el foco en la recuperación de la Sierra de Espadán cuando las llamas se extingan. “Es nuestra manera de relacionarnos con el territorio. Cuando termina un mal día de trabajo o cuando nos reunimos con la familia y los amigos, acudimos a nuestras montañas”, ha dicho la alcaldesa, reivindicando el profundo vínculo de los vecinos de la sierra.

World.title: La CNMC multa a RTVE con 300.000 euros por emitir publicidad sin identificar y fuera del horario permitido
World.content:
La Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC), con potestad sancionadora sobre la actividad audiovisual en España, ha multado con 307.300,80 euros a RTVE por emitir publicidad sin identificar y fuera del horario permitido. La resolución dictada por la Sala de Supervisión regulatoria a principios de julio y difundida este lunes sanciona dos emisiones matinales de los programas MasterChef y MasterChef Celebrity por anunciar vino en ese tramo y realizar promociones comerciales sin identificar como publicidad. El escrito explica que el importe inicial de las dos multas por contravenir la Ley General de Comunicación Audiovisual (LGCA) ascendía a 512.168 euros, si bien la corporación de medios públicos españoles ha solventado el pago tras la aplicación reducida de un 40%.

Los hechos se remontan a 2024 e implicaron a sendas emisiones matinales el 5 de mayo y el 10 de noviembre del programa en cuestión que emite La1 de Televisión Española. En septiembre del año siguiente se acordó la incoación de expediente sancionador, “al entender que se había podido infringir lo dispuesto en los artículos 123 y 136 de la LGCA”. En sus alegaciones, RTVE argumentó que aquellas emisiones no eran las “primarias de tales programas, ya que ambos están específicamente destinados para la programación nocturna”. Asimismo, la corporación consideró que “las menciones del vino MasterChef se hacen en un contexto gastronómico del más alto nivel”. Y añadió que “el mensaje de consumo moderado del vino está implícito en la propia forma y en el contexto de presentación del vino” dentro del programa. RTVE también afirmó que “dada la extensa tradición de la presentación de elementos o productos derivados del programa, como el vino, el restaurante, los libros de cocina o el videojuego MasterChef, los telespectadores ya identifican claramente todas estas menciones publicitarias”.

“Un verdejito rico, qué mínimo”

El acta de visionado del 5 de mayo de 2024 entre las 10.49 y las 13.54 horas menciona un momento en el que la copresentadora de entonces, Samantha Vallejo-Nájera —hoy fuera del programa—, proponía “un brindis” con “un Rioja Crianza, vino MasterChef”. Entre otros mensajes autopromocionales, el copresentador Pepe Rodríguez anuncia en otro momento la “biblia saludable de MasterChef”. El tercer copresentador Jordi Cruz interviene más adelante: “Si quieres vivir la experiencia MasterChef, ahora puedes hacerlo con MasterChef, el videojuego oficial”. Respecto al acta de visionado del 10 de noviembre de 2024, entre las 10.42 y las 13.54 horas, un pasaje hacia el mediodía recrea la conversación de Jordi Cruz con el cantante Pitingo: “No puede ser que estés aquí comiéndote unos buenos percebes y no tengas tu copita, ahí, esos percebes buenos de MasterChef hay que comerlos con un vino de MasterChef, un verdejito rico, qué mínimo, eh, así lo degustas como Dios manda”. En otro pasaje, Vallejo-Nájera propone “un brindis con el vino blanco de MasterChef”.

Escenas donde se promocionan productos de 'MasterChef' durante la emisión del programa, incluidas en la resolución de la CNMC que multa con 300.000 euros a RTVE.

La resolución recuerda que el artículo 123 de la LGCA prohíbe los anuncios de bebidas alcohólicas que no incluyan un mensaje de consumo moderado y de bajo riesgo, así como la promoción de las que tienen un “nivel igual o inferior a veinte grados, excepto cuando sea emitida entre las 20.30 horas y las 5.00 horas y fuera de ese horario cuando dichas comunicaciones comerciales audiovisuales formen parte indivisible de la adquisición de derechos y de la producción de la señal a difundir”. Por otra parte, el artículo 136 de la misma ley exige que “la comunicación comercial audiovisual cuyas características de emisión puedan confundir al espectador sobre su carácter publicitario incluirá una sobreimpresión permanente y legible con la indicación ‘publicidad”.

La Sala Regulatoria de la CNMC considera acreditada la vulneración de ambos artículos por pasajes como los mencionados, y cita en su resolución que RTVE “ha reconocido expresamente su responsabilidad de los hechos probados”. Las dos multas impuestas sumaban 512.168 euros, desgajados en una sanción de 243.334 euros y otra de 268.834 euros por las vulneraciones de los artículos 123 y 136 de la LGCA, respectivamente. El reconocimiento de la responsabilidad por parte de la corporación supuso la terminación del procedimiento, así como una reducción del 20% de la sanción añadido a otro 20% por el pago voluntario que ascendió a los 307.300,80 euros definitivos.
