(Photo source: Fernbach Antal|Dreamstime.com)

World.title: Romanian worker dies after being struck by beam at Barcelona’s Camp Nou stadium
World.content:
A Romanian worker died after being struck in the head by a beam while carrying out painting work on a platform at the construction site of Barcelona's famed stadium Camp Nou.

Rescue crews confirmed the death of the 54-year-old man. His death was the first fatality registered at Camp Nou, Barcelona's legendary stadium, which has been undergoing modernization works since 2023. An investigation has been opened after the death.

"FC Barcelona deeply regrets the death of the worker who lost his life yesterday in the workplace accident that occurred during the renovation works at Spotify Camp Nou. The Club wishes to express its deepest condolences and extend its heartfelt support to his family, friends, and colleagues. FC Barcelona President Joan Laporta wishes to personally convey his condolences to the family and places himself at their disposal on behalf of the entire Club," the Catalan club said in a statement posted on X.

The Camp Nou construction site is staffed mainly by Romanian and Albanian workers, according to sources cited by TVRInfo.

Set to be fully renovated by 2028, the stadium already hosts matches by Barcelona’s world-famous football team. Once complete, the stadium will be able to accommodate more than 100,000 spectators in the stands.

World.title: What’s Driving the Real-Estate Price Surges in Eastern and South-East Europe?
World.content:
Rapidly rising real estate prices to the east and south of the Trieste-Szczecin line made existing dwelling owners happy - but potential buyers, especially younger people, less so.

According to Eurostat, in the first quarter of 2026, property prices in Bulgaria, Slovakia, and Croatia recorded price growth of 14 per cent over the first quarter of 2025. In a longer perspective of 3 and 10 years, the fortunes of individual countries have changed.

Generally, the total appreciation of housing real estate has been rapid, with Hungary in 10 years heading the list, followed by Bulgaria, Czechia, and Croatia.

However, Eurostat does not provide comparable data for countries southeast of Croatia, but Bosnia, Serbia, Montenegro, and others have followed similar paths. According to the Agency for Statistics of Bosnia, housing real estate prices increased by 20.4 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the first quarter of 2025. Nussubpekova recently reported a double-digit growth rate for Serbia.

World.title: North Macedonia Mourns Much-Loved Actor Goce Todorovski
World.content:
Goce Todorovski. Photo: Drama Theatre.

Actor Goce Todorovski has died aged 75, his family and the Drama Theatre in Skopje, where he spent most of his career, confirmed on Monday. The cause of death was not immediately announced.

Born in the western town of Kichevo in 1951, Todorovski graduated from the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Skopje before joining the Drama Theatre in 1978. He went on to perform in more than 50 theatre productions, while also building a prolific career in television, radio and cinema.

His gift for comedy made him one of the country’s most enduring and popular actors.

For many Macedonians, Todorovski will be remembered above all for his appearances in the cult television series Macedonian Folk Tales (Makedonski Narodni Prikazni), whose humorous adaptations of traditional folklore became a fixture of family viewing for decades.

He was also a familiar face to generations of children through the educational television series “Scruffy Alphabet” (Bushava Azbuka), while radio audiences knew him from the long-running satirical comedy programme Hihiriku.

His film career included memorable roles in several classics of Macedonian and former Yugoslav cinema, including Happy New ’49 (Srekna Nova ’49), Weekend of the Dead (Vikend na Mrtovci), Trieste Via Skopje (Trst via Skopje), The Red Horse (Crveniot Konj), and many others.

Beyond his screen work, Todorovski was one of the leading comic actors of the Macedonian stage, collaborating with many of the country’s best-known theatre directors and helping shape the repertoire of the Drama Theatre for nearly five decades.

“Goce Todorovski never sought the audience’s affection. He won it from the moment he stepped onto the stage,” the Drama Theatre wrote in its farewell.

“His performances possessed a rare immediacy: a precise acting rhythm that seemed entirely effortless, expressive facial gestures, a distinctive stage presence, and the roguish charm with which he could effortlessly bridge the gap between the stage and the audience,” it said.

Todorovski’s performances earned numerous awards, including the state “23 October” prize for culture and the lifetime achievement award at the Vojdan Chernodrinski Theatre Festival in 2025, as well as the Presidential Order of Merit in 2023.

News of his death prompted an outpouring of tributes from fellow actors, public figures and audiences, many recalling the humour, warmth and distinctive characters that made Todorovski one of the defining faces of North Macedonia’s acting scene.

Actress Maja Andonovska Ilijevski wrote that Macedonian theatre had lost “a great man and a great actor”. Recalling their time filming the cult TV series Macedonian Folk Tales, she said Todorovski had been not only an acting legend but also a wonderful colleague, whose humour and warmth made those days unforgettable.

Andonovska said the countless characters Todorovski brought to life will remain part of the country’s collective memory, adding that “some people never truly leave – they live on through their roles, the memories of their colleagues and the love of their audience”.

Photographer Goran Anastasovski described Todorovski as “the man who made us laugh for decades” and “a giant on stage”, adding that his legacy of bringing smiles to various generations will endure.

World.title: The Digital Front of Albania’s ‘Flamingo Revolution’
World.content:
On May 30, protests broke out in Albania in response to a luxury development project in the Vjosa-Narta protected area, linked to investments backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and a network of powerful local business interests and individuals with a history of legal troubles.

What began as an environmental protest grew into a movement known as the ‘Flamingo Revolution’, a reference to one of the many species of birds that inhabit the protected coastal area.

Alongside demands for environmental protection and the preservation of biodiversity, the movement has evolved into an expression of collective frustration with the status quo, calling for accountability, transparency, and political change.

Rejecting affiliation with the political forces that have dominated Albania’s political landscape for more than three decades, protesters have presented the movement as an independent civic initiative. For more than 50 days straight, they have called for the resignation of a prime minister and government they see as corrupt.

World.title: North Macedonia’s Judiciary ‘Nearing Collapse’, Rights Monitor Warns
World.content:
For Ivana Petkovska, the European Commission's latest rule-of-law report this month highlighted very familiar themes for North Macedonia – political pressure on the courts, insufficient funding and the limited impact of legal reforms.

The programme coordinator at the the All for Fair Trials Coalition, a leading judicial monitoring organisation in North Macedonia, said the report reinforces what watchdogs like hers have been saying for years.

“It is not the first time that international reports have concluded that the judiciary is facing political pressure from the executive or legislative branches,” Petkovska says.

As well as political interference, funding and staffing shortages are rendering the justice system dysfunctional, with the public ultimately paying the price through delayed verdicts and growing legal costs, she argues.

World.title: Child Maintenance Systems Failing Single Mothers in the Balkans and Beyond
World.content:
“According to the French census of 2020, 76 per cent of children under 18 live mostly with their mother, 12 per cent live alternately with each of their parents [shared physical custody], 12 per cent live mostly with their father,” said Emilie Biland, a professor of sociology at Sciences Po in Paris.

The burden of raising children, which falls mainly on the mother after a divorce, contributes to a fall in her standard of living, Biland told BIRN.

“In the year following a separation, half of the mothers who have physical custody of their child(ren) experience a decline in their standard of living of at least 20 per cent,” she said in a written reply. On average, children also experience a decline in living standards of 15 per cent in the year following the separation or divorce of their parents.

In France, child maintenance orders are not automatic. Parents have to claim them.

“Claiming for child support is an administrative burden for mothers,” said Biland. “Some of them may abandon their claim, either because they find the process too time-consuming and uncertain, or because it risks poisoning relations with the father.”

Because of this, France has one of the lowest rates of child maintenance payments in the EU, according to Biland’s research.

“To avoid non-take up, procedures to get child support should be lightened,” she told BIRN. “For example, it could be calculated as soon as a parent comes to the family benefit office to declare he or she does not live with the other parent.”

Tax rules for child support, as well as rules regarding social benefits, should be reformed, Biland said.

“So far, French parents receiving child support amounts have to pay income tax on them [they can lose some social benefits too], while parents paying for child support will pay fewer amounts of tax income.”

In France, the family support allowance, or ASF, provides financial assistance when one or both parents are not contributing to the cost of a child’s upbringing or when court-ordered child maintenance payments are too low.

In 2023, a quarter of children in single-parent families received the allowance, said Biland, adding that “1.4 million children are beneficiaries of ASF, which is more than the number of children who get child support payments overall”.

“It should be kept in mind that only single parents can receive it: mothers who move in with a new partner are no longer eligible for ASF payments,” Biland added. “Child support payments [from the second parent] do not stop when the parent is repartnering, of course.”

A French mother of two said she sees the state fund as her only hope of child support.

“The father should also have contributed by paying child support, but he didn’t,” the mother said in answers to the BIRN questionnaire. “You have to go through the court, and irresponsible fathers avoid it. We, mothers, are the ones who are penalised. Only the state provides help.”

Yet even a court order is not always enough to ensure that a parent comply with their obligations.

“At the hearing, the Family Court Judge ordered the child support to be paid retroactively, but the other parent still has not paid the retroactive amount, even after two years,” said another French mother, who said she waited a full year between filing her application and appearing before the judge.

World.title: Serbian Flag on Cocaine Haul from Ecuador is a Clue – Not Proof
World.content:
On July 21, the Italian authorities seized 650 packages with more than 770 kilograms of cocaine at the port of Vado Ligure. The drugs were hidden among pallets of bananas in a refrigerated container from Ecuador.

Concealing cocaine in commercial shipments of fresh fruit, particularly bananas from Ecuador, is a well-known method used by criminal actors, including groups from the Balkans.

The Vado Ligure seizure, therefore, fits a broader pattern of maritime cocaine trafficking into Europe.

In Serbia, however, it wasn’t the size of the seizure or its route that attracted most attention but the Serbian flag displayed on some of the packages.

Although the comments posted under the media reports offer only a snapshot of public opinion, they reveal two recurring reactions.

World.title: Law and Justice Suffers Split Ahead of Poland’s 2027 Election
World.content:
Following a months-long power struggle, more than 30 MPs – including former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki – are set to be expelled from the Law and Justice party, in the biggest rupture seen on the Polish right in many years.

Law and Justice, or PiS, is Poland’s largest opposition party and one of the country’s two dominant political forces, alongside the governing Civic Coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. The split could sharply reduce PiS’s chances of returning to power in next year’s parliamentary election.

On early Friday afternoon, PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski announced that “around 30-something” of the party’s 186 MPs had effectively chosen to leave after refusing to sign declarations of loyalty. The documents required them to state that they did not belong to any political associations operating within the party – an obvious reference to Development Plus (Rozwoj Plus), an organisation created by Morawiecki, until now one of PiS’s deputy leaders.

“Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” Kaczynski said. “And so they made the decision they did.”

Kaczynski has been PiS’s undisputed leader and chief power broker for more than two decades, selecting loyal candidates for prime minister who largely continued to defer to him once in office. Morawiecki was initially one of them, serving as prime minister between 2017 and 2023.

But in recent years, Morawiecki – an economist, former banker and comparatively moderate conservative – has grown increasingly impatient with Kaczynski’s dominance. He has pushed for changes to both the party’s internal structure and its political program, arguing that PiS was failing to speak convincingly to younger voters and entrepreneurs.

Friday’s rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open conflict.

“Until the very last moment, we fought for the unity of the Law and Justice camp,” Morawiecki said at a press conference. “We could not accept being forced to sign a loyalty pledge.”

He accused the party leadership of using ultimatums and political blackmail to discard a strategy that had been agreed only recently.

Morawiecki did not formally announce the creation of a new party. He did, however, declare the beginning of “a new chapter in Poland’s political history”, promise a major nationwide tour and announce that his camp would soon present a new political program.

He said his political circle now included 40 MPs (which stands at odds with Kaczynski’s estimate), one senator and three members of the European Parliament, describing it as a “very strong representation”. Its offer, he said, would reach beyond PiS’s traditional base and target young people, entrepreneurs, local-government officials and even some voters currently supporting the governing coalition.

Morawiecki presented his project as a modern, patriotic and pro-state conservative force, capable of responding to social and economic change without falling back on outdated ideas.

The electoral consequences could be enormous. An Opinia24 poll conducted before the split tested precisely such a scenario. With PiS united, the party would receive 23 per cent of the vote, behind Civic Coalition on 31.6 per cent. When respondents were offered a separate Morawiecki-led Rozwoj Plus list, support for PiS fell to 17.7 per cent, while Morawiecki’s group received 6.2 per cent. Civic Coalition remained clearly ahead on 30.9 per cent.

Tusk responded with a single cutting line: “They are fighting so hard for party unity that there won’t be one stone left standing.”

Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski was blunter: “Kaczynski went all in and lost.”

World.title: Croatia Braces for Another Heatwave as Temperatures Could Reach 40°C
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – Following a brief but very welcome period of cooler, fresher and somewhat unstable weather, Croatia is set to face another heatwave with temperatures likely to reach 40 degrees.

After a brief spell of unsettled and sometimes stormy weather, Croatia is preparing for another intense heatwave, with temperatures expected to climb steadily throughout the week and potentially reach 40°C in some inland areas. Index reports that meteorologists are claiming that the hottest conditions are likely to arrive during the second half of the week.

above 35 degrees by the end of the week

Weather conditions are expected to stabilise on Tuesday and onwards. Daytime temperatures will rise each day, with much of the country seeing highs above 35°C by the end of the week. Forecasters say isolated locations could even record temperatures of around 40°C if current forecasts hold.

The Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service (DHMZ) has already issued an initial yellow heat warning for Thursday, cautioning that the heat could pose a risk to human health. Meteorologists warn that higher-level warnings may be introduced if temperatures continue to increase as expected.

The upcoming heatwave follows an unusual period of unstable weather that brought thunderstorms, strong winds and a series of strange meteotsunamis along parts of the Adriatic coast. Once the current weather system moves away, a strengthening area of high pressure is expected to bring prolonged sunshine and very little rainfall.

records were broken in june

Forecasters also pointed to this summer’s exceptional conditions. During June, fourteen of Croatia’s 35 main meteorological stations recorded new monthly temperature records, while Split reached an all-time record of 40°C at the Marjan weather station. Staggeringly, even sea temperatures climbed to around 30°C in some areas, highlighting the intensity of this year’s hot summer season.

Authorities are advising residents and visitors to stay hydrated, avoid prolonged exposure to the sun during the hottest part of the day and keep a close eye on vulnerable groups, including the elderly, young children and those with existing health conditions, as Croatia prepares for another spell of extreme summer heat.

World.title: Sea Floods Stari Grad on Hvar for the Third Time in Just 10 Days
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – The sea has created floods in Stari Grad on the island of Hvar for the third time in just 10 days due to repeated meteotsunamis.

Index reports that visitors and residents of Stari Grad on the island of Hvar have once again found themselves dealing with flooded streets after the sea overflowed onto the town’s waterfront, marking the third such event in just ten days. The repeated flooding has drawn attention to increasingly unusual sea level fluctuations affecting parts of Croatia’s coastline and islands.

Videos shared by residents showed seawater spilling over the promenade and into the historic centre, covering streets and public spaces before gradually receding. Although the flooding caused disruption, there were no reports of serious injuries or major structural damage.

According to meteorologists, the flooding was not caused by rainfall but by a combination of low atmospheric pressure, strong southerly winds and elevated sea levels. These conditions created what is known as a storm surge, pushing large volumes of seawater onto the shoreline and into low-lying coastal areas.

The phenomenon has affected Stari Grad several times over the past two weeks, with each event occurring under similar weather conditions. Locals say the repeated flooding has become a growing concern, particularly for businesses and residents along the waterfront who have had to repeatedly clear seawater from their properties.

Experts note that enclosed bays and historic harbour towns such as Stari Grad are especially vulnerable to this type of coastal flooding. When strong winds coincide with low air pressure, sea levels can temporarily rise enough to overwhelm quays, promenades and streets built just above normal sea level.

As weather conditions improved, the seawater gradually retreated and life returned to normal. However, the latest flooding serves as another reminder of how quickly changing weather patterns can impact Croatia’s coastal communities, with residents hoping calmer conditions will prevent another repeat in the coming days.

World.title: Sveti Ivan Beach: The Hidden Paradise That Requires a 50-Minute Hike
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – The entire island of Cres is stunning, but Sveti Ivan beach takes it a step further. If we’re being honest, it takes it many steps further, as a 50-minute hike is needed to reach this hidden paradise. Trust us, it’s so worth it.

Hidden beneath the ancient hilltop village of Lubenice on the island of Cres lies one of Croatia’s most spectacular beaches, Sveti Ivan beach. Putni kofer reveals that it is best known for its white pebbles, crystal-clear waters and particularly dramatic surroundings. It is very often considered one of the most beautiful beaches on the Croatian coast (and that’s a challenging title to receive in itself).

The beach sits in a secluded bay beneath the historic settlement of Lubenice, which is perched high on a cliff overlooking the Adriatic. Surrounded by steep rocks and untouched nature, Sveti Ivan offers the kind of peaceful atmosphere that is becoming increasingly rare on the Croatian coast.

Part of what keeps this beach so special is also what makes it difficult to reach. Visitors who choose to walk from Lubenice must follow a steep trail that takes around 50 minutes downhill, and the return journey can be even more challenging, especially during the intense summer heat. Proper footwear and enough water are essential, and we’d go as far as to discourage anyone doing this during the height of summer.

Because of the demanding access, even during the height of summer Sveti Ivan usually avoids the large crowds found at many other Croatian beaches. Those who make the journey are rewarded with incredible views, peaceful surroundings and some of the clearest waters on the Adriatic.

The beach can also be reached by sea, either with a private boat, organised excursion or water taxi. Nearby is another natural attraction, Plava Grota, a sea cave where sunlight creates beautiful blue reflections inside the cave.

Above the beach sits Lubenice, one of the oldest settlements on the Croatian islands. Located on a 378-metre-high cliff, the village has a history stretching back more than 4,000 years, with archaeological remains from the Bronze and Iron Ages found in the surrounding area.

Once one of Cres’ most important settlements, Lubenice is now home to only two permanent residents. However, during the summer months, visitors arrive to explore its ancient stone streets, admire the views and discover one of Croatia’s most breathtaking beaches down below.

World.title: Should Croatia Charge Tourists Who Need Emergency Help After Excessive Drinking?
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – Should Croatia be charging tourists who take it too far and require emergency medical help after excessive drinking or even illicit drug use?

Every single summer, Split in particular faces the same old problem, and that is tourists being found unconscious on city streets after heavy nights of drinking, with emergency services called to help them. The issue has sparked a debate over whether people who put themselves in danger through excessive alcohol consumption should contribute to the cost of medical interventions.

over 50 calls because of alcohol in june alone

During June alone, the Split-Dalmatia County Emergency Medical Service recorded more than 50 calls related to alcohol intoxication. Lukrecija Zderic reveals for Index that medical teams treated 44 people, while eight people were no longer at the location when emergency crews arrived. Among those who received help were also two minors.

Many of these cases involve young foreign tourists visiting Split during the summer season. Locals say it has become common to find intoxicated visitors lying on streets in the early morning hours after nights out and organised pub crawl tours.

The question now being raised is whether tourists who end up needing emergency medical assistance because of extreme alcohol consumption should help cover the cost. Some European countries already charge part of the expense in similar situations, but Croatia currently does not have such a system.

an abuse of already thin resources

Croatia’s emergency services are required to help anyone whose health is at risk, regardless of how the situation happened. However, every intervention requires medical staff, vehicles and resources.

The Croatian Health Insurance Fund explained that emergency medical teams are funded through contracted healthcare costs. A single emergency team consisting of a doctor, nurse and driver represents a significant annual expense for the healthcare system.

For foreign visitors, the final bill depends on their insurance situation. Tourists from EU countries, the European Economic Area and Switzerland with valid European Health Insurance Cards have their costs covered through international healthcare agreements. Visitors from countries without such agreements may have to pay themselves unless they have travel insurance.

irresponsible behaviour should face consequences

However, if a tourist leaves Croatia without paying a medical bill, the unpaid cost can ultimately fall on Croatian public funds. This means taxpayers may end up covering expenses that were never recovered.The debate comes as Split continues to balance the benefits of being one of Croatia’s most popular tourist destinations with the challenges that come from large numbers of visitors, particularly during the peak summer months.

As tourism grows, Croatia faces an ongoing question: should irresponsible behaviour surrounding alcohol and drug use that requires emergency medical intervention come with a financial consequence?

World.title: Search Underway After Skipper Falls Overboard Near Šolta
World.content:
July the 26th, 2026 – A frantic search is currently underway after a skipper fell overboard into the sea not far from Šolta, marking the second serious maritime incident near the island in a short time.

Index reports that a major search and rescue operation is currently underway in the waters off the island of Šolta after a skipper fell overboard from a charter catamaran and disappeared within minutes amid extremely poor weather conditions. The incident was reported at around 09:10, triggering an immediate response from Croatia’s maritime rescue services.

According to the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure, the missing man is an Austrian skipper. At the time of the accident, the sea was being battered by strong winds and rough conditions, making the search particularly difficult.

A large-scale rescue effort was launched involving two rescue boats from the Milna Harbour Master’s Office, one rescue boat from Hvar, three vessels from the Split Maritime and Airport Police, a Pilatus aircraft, and later a helicopter to assist with the aerial search. Authorities also issued a PAN-PAN urgency message via Split Radio, asking all vessels in the area to keep watch for the missing skipper.

The remaining six passengers, all of whom are Austrian nationals, were located unharmed aboard the catamaran. A replacement skipper was transferred to the vessel so it could safely continue to its next destination, where the passengers would disembark.

As of the latest update, the search remains ongoing, with emergency services continuing to comb the waters around Šolta in the hope of finding the missing skipper. Authorities have not released further details while the operation continues.

World.title: Croatian Firefighting Pilots Battle Massive Wildfires in France
World.content:
July the 26th, 2026 – Croatian firefighting pilots are battling massive wildfires in France, which have caused unimaginable destruction in the southwest of the country.

Index reports that Croatian military firefighters are playing a key role in the fight against devastating wildfires sweeping southwestern France, where huge blazes continue to threaten communities near Bordeaux.

Members of the 855th Firefighting Squadron of the Croatian Air Force have been deployed to France as part of an international firefighting effort. They are currently operating in the Biscarrosse area, where large wildfires remain active and conditions continue to challenge emergency crews.

The Croatian crews arrived in France on the 24th of July. On their first day they were assigned to fires near Salernes, before being redeployed to the Bordeaux region as the situation worsened. During their first two days of operations, the crews completed 72 flights, logged a total of 13.5 flying hours, and dropped 402 tonnes of water on the enormous flames.

According to the Croatian Ministry of Defence, the mission remains highly demanding due to the scale of the fires and rapidly changing conditions on the ground. Major Tomislav Vranjić said the situation is still extremely complex, with Croatian pilots making every effort to support French firefighters in bringing the blazes under control.

The deployment comes as France battles one of its largest wildfire outbreaks in decades. The fires in the Gironde region have burned tens of thousands of hectares, forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people and prompted international assistance from across Europe.

Croatia’s Canadair crews are among Europe’s most experienced aerial firefighters, regularly assisting other countries through the European Union’s civil protection cooperation mechanisms. Their latest mission once again highlights Croatia’s expertise in tackling large-scale wildfires beyond its own borders.

World.title: Analysis of 1.6 Million Reviews Reveals What Tourists Think of Croatia
World.content:
July the 26th, 2026 – An analysis of a staggering 1.6 million reviews reveals precisely what tourists really think of Croatia in comparison to its competition.

Croatia has triumphantly emerged as the highest-rated major Mediterranean destination based on an analysis of more than 1.6 million online guest reviews, but the data also highlights several areas where the country is falling behind its competitors. This study, as reported by Ivan Ivankovic for Index, examined 1,622,218 reviews written by travellers themselves, offering a broad picture of how visitors perceive Croatia compared with other leading Mediterranean destinations.

greece is still leaving a stronger impression…

The overall results are encouraging. Croatia achieved an average rating of 8.91, narrowly edging out nearby Greece and comfortably outperforming Spain, neighbouring Italy and Turkey in overall guest satisfaction. However, when travellers who had visited both Croatia and Greece were asked which destination they preferred, 11 out of 12 nationalities chose Greece, suggesting that while visitors rate Croatia highly, Greece leaves a stronger overall impression.

One of Croatia’s biggest strengths is its location. Visitors consistently praise the country’s remarkable coastline, islands and natural beauty, while also giving high marks for cleanliness. The analysis found that Croatia is also viewed as one of the fairest destinations in the Mediterranean, with comparatively few complaints about scams, hidden charges or tourist traps.

croatia has the highest number of reviews calling it “too expensive”

The biggest criticism, however, is price. Croatia recorded the highest number of reviews mentioning that it is too expensive, with complaints focusing mainly on restaurants, drinks and other spending outside accommodation rather than hotel prices themselves. Among everyday purchases, tourists most often criticised the cost of bottled water, while cocktail prices were also seen as relatively high. Coffee prices, on the other hand, attracted fewer complaints.

The research also identified several recurring frustrations. Guests most frequently complained about parking, air conditioning, Wi-Fi, noise, cleanliness in some locations and showers or water facilities. Croatia also performed poorly when it came to cashless payments, with many visitors noting that some businesses still accept only cash, which represents a growing inconvenience for international travellers.

croatia performs better outside of the main summer season

Another notable finding is that Croatia receives better reviews during the pre-season and post-season than at the height of summer. This suggests that overcrowding and peak-season prices continue to affect the visitor experience during the busiest months.

The analysis paints a nuanced picture of Croatian tourism as a whole. Visitors continue to love the country’s scenery, safety and overall quality, making it one of the Mediterranean’s top-rated destinations. However, if Croatia wants to remain competitive against rivals such as Greece, the findings suggest it will need to address concerns over pricing, infrastructure and service during the busiest part of the tourist season.

World.title: The Green Cave: One of the Vis Archipelago’s Most Magical Wonders
World.content:
July the 26th, 2026 – The Green Cave is one of the beautiful Vis archipelago’s most incredible natural wonders, and instead of being limited to viewing it by boat, you can swim inside it.

Just off the southern coast of the far-flung island of Vis, the tiny, uninhabited islet of Ravnik is home to one of Croatia’s most spectacular natural attractions, the remarkable Green Cave (Zelena špilja). Putni kofer reveals that unlike very many sea caves in Croatia and indeed elsewhere that can only be admired from a boat, this one offers visitors the rare opportunity to swim inside and experience its unique beauty up close and personal.

This unusual cave gets its name from the remarkable emerald-green glow that fills the interior. Sunlight enters through a circular opening in the cave’s ceiling and reflects off the seabed, which is covered with various types of green algae. Around midday, when the sun is at its highest, the effect is at its most dramatic, bathing the water in an almost unreal green light. Unlike the famous Blue Cave on nearby Biševo, the Green Cave has two large entrances, allowing smaller boats to sail directly inside. Visitors can also jump into the crystal-clear sea and swim beneath the beam of sunlight that shines through the roof, creating one of the Adriatic’s most memorable swimming experiences.

The cave has been protected as a geomorphological natural monument since 1967, while the islet of Ravnik itself is a protected significant landscape. Over the years, the cave has inspired countless visitors, including Emperor Franz Joseph I, who is said to have visited during his tour of the Adriatic back during the 19th century and who was left thoroughly enchanted by it. During World War II, local stories suggest that its spacious interior even provided secretive shelter for small military vessels.

Most visitors reach the Green Cave as part of a boat excursion departing from Vis, Komiža or Hvar, often combined with stops at the Blue Cave, Stiniva Cove and other highlights of the Vis archipelago. Entry is managed under a concession system, with visitors paying a small admission fee before entering or swimming inside the cave.

Although the Blue Cave often attracts the bigger crowds and is definitely much better known globally, many travellers consider the Green Cave an equally unforgettable experience. Its combination of emerald light, clear Adriatic waters and the chance to swim inside a protected natural monument makes it one of the hidden gems of Croatia’s coastline.

World.title: Conservationist highlights Estonia's most beautiful bogs
World.content:
Estonia's bogs are among the country's most valuable ecosystems, offering striking landscapes while storing and filtering water, Climate Ministry adviser Hanno Zingel said.

Speaking on International Bog Day on Sunday, Zingel, an adviser at the ministry's Biodiversity Protection Department, highlighted Laukasoo Bog in Lahemaa National Park and Järva County's Kakerdaja Bog as Estonia's two most beautiful.

"They are truly picturesque places," he said, adding that while the colors, openness and landscape may seem similar at first, every aspect between the two is also unique. "There's so much there to take in all at once."

A raba, or raised bog, is a mature stage of a soo, or bog, Zingel explained, noting that the raised bog has developed its own, independent balance as an ecosystem.

He noted that bogs and wetlands have declined significantly both in Estonia and around the world, with only about one-fifth of their former extent possibly remaining.

"Estonia has been paying special attention to protecting bogs since 1938," Zingel said, adding that those efforts have only expanded over time.

Bog ecosystems play a key role in protecting water resources by filtering water, releasing it during droughts and absorbing excess water during floods.

Part of Laukasoo Bog undergoing restoration. Source: Marko Kohv

"A bog is a special ecosystem that is essential for humanity, because it stores clean water and also purifies it," the adviser said. "It's a self-regulating system."

'We know how to bring bogs back'

He stressed that while bog water is clean and sterile, and can safely be used to rinse your hands and face, it isn't generally suitable as a source of drinking water as it lacks essential salts due to its acidity.

"Bog water may fool your thirst, but it certainly isn't a long-term solution," Zingel said.

Today, peat is gaining popularity in the beauty industry, where it is valued for its mineral content and use in skincare products.

Estonia's bogs also attract visitors from around the world, which Zingel credits in part to the country's nearly century of conservation efforts and growing experience with restoring damaged wetlands.

"Today we know how to bring bogs back," he said, adding that Estonia's restoration efforts are now among the world's leading examples of how to revive and strengthen ecosystems.

World.title: Household loans in Estonia exceed €16 billion as borrowing picks up
World.content:
The volume of loans and leases held by Estonian households surpassed €16 billion this June. Compared with the same period a year earlier, the increase is 8.6 percent, Bank of Estonia said. Corporate loan and lease volumes have grown at a similarly brisk pace.

"Bank loan growth in Estonia was more than twice as fast as the euro‑area average," noted Bank of Estonia economist Taavi Raudsaar. "The housing loan portfolio is still growing the fastest, with the loan balance increasing by nearly 10 percent."

Former Bank of Estonia president Madis Müller said in an interview that it is not surprising that loan growth in Estonia is faster than the euro‑area average — this has been the case for some time.

"Our loan volumes have grown steadily throughout the past year," Müller noted. He added that this is a sign the Estonian economy is quietly gathering strength.

"If both companies and individuals are willing to take on new obligations and invest, it means they believe in their future ability to service those loans and in the growth of their incomes," he said.

When the economy improves, it usually brings slightly faster overall price increases. However, inflation has continued to slow, and the Bank of Estonia expects it to reach around 3.4 percent this year.

Annual growth of the loan portfolio. Source: Bank of Estonia

Export‑oriented companies in Estonia have begun to perform better, and domestic‑market companies also have a more positive outlook this year as people's purchasing power and incomes have increased.

"For an average wage earner, net salary is more than 10 percent higher this year than a year ago," Müller said. "This certainly enables people to consume more goods and services, and this is one of the drivers of Estonia's economic growth this year."

Looking at how well mortgage borrowers and companies are managing their loan payments, the share of clients in difficulty is very small. Only 0.2 percent of the entire mortgage portfolio is more than 60 days overdue. Overall, Estonian borrowers are handling their payments very well.

Müller noted that loan volumes are also rising partly because housing prices are increasing. However, real estate prices have not risen by 10 percent annually, so the growth in loan volumes also reflects broader optimism.

World.title: Ministry does not support bill allowing allied citizens in Estonia's defense
World.content:
The Ministry of Defense does not support a bill in its current form that would expand the options for citizens of other allied countries to participate in Estonia's national defense, but has proposed an alternative Defense League membership.

Last month, Estonian lawmakers proposed changes that would allow citizens of other NATO member states who belong to the Defense League to take on voluntary military service obligations and serve in wartime posts that require a military rank.

The legislation, backed by 53 members of the Riigikogu in June, was meant to strengthen the readiness of both the Defense League and the armed forces by giving foreign members a clear legal pathway to participate in Estonia's defense.

The amendments would not have imposed conscription on NATO citizens. Instead, it proposed an opt‑in system for those over 18 who have taken the military oath.

The changes would also have established a legal basis for appointing NATO citizens to wartime positions, which would improve planning for training, command structures and equipment distribution.

However, after reviewing the document, the Ministry of Defense said it did not support the plan.

Lack of clarity

"It is important to emphasise that the Ministry of Defense fully supports the idea of involving citizens of allied countries in Estonia's national defense. However, we cannot support the proposed solution, which requires considerably more thorough consideration and further development of the bill," said Roland Murof, deputy director of the Ministry of Defense's strategic communications department.

The ministry said the distinction between different categories of Defense League membership must not be blurred.

"The main difference between an active member and a supporting member is that a supporting member does not participate actively in military training and is not assigned a wartime position. Therefore, situations where the substantive distinction between Defense League membership categories disappears and members with different statuses, levels of training and health requirements begin carrying out the same tasks must be avoided," the ministry said.

Additionally, Murof said: "We cannot assign wartime duties to Defense League supporting members who lack the necessary training and do not meet the established health requirements. That is dangerous both for the individual and for the fulfilment of the task."

Secondly, the ministry believes that the obligations, guarantees and responsibilities of those who would be involved are unclear.

'Active member status'

Thirdly, the ministry argues the state must have a clear legal right and the ability to carry out thorough background checks on foreign nationals entering Estonia's national defence in order to mitigate security risks.

"To address these concerns, the Ministry of Defense proposes creating a separate active member status in the Defense League for foreign nationals. This would ensure that people contributing to national defence meet clear health, training and reliability requirements and have undergone security screening," Murof said.

The ministry also drew attention to the need to mitigate potential security risks. For example, a solution is needed for situations where a citizen of a NATO member state volunteers for service in Estonia during peacetime but poses a security threat.

"The Ministry of the Interior has also pointed out that the person concerned may not have any previous criminal convictions, but may be linked to extremist or terrorist organisations, organised crime, be ideologically radicalised or suspected of offences against the state. Given that the person is a foreign national, Estonian authorities may have only limited information about their background," the ministry said.

World.title: Estonian government rejects plan to restrict officials' private sector moves
World.content:
The Estonian government has rejected a proposal to impose a cooling-off period before senior public officials can take jobs in industries they previously oversaw.

A bill of amendments to the Anti-Corruption Act, introduced in June by the Riigikogu's Anti-Corruption Select Committee, followed concerns raised in the Estonian Internal Security Service's (ISS) annual yearbook over the so-called "revolving door" between civil service and the private sector.

The ISS argued that officials overseeing procurements worth hundreds of millions of euros — particularly in defense and energy — should face a waiting or "cooling-off" period before joining companies in the same sector.

"This would help prevent conflicts of interest in which information, networks or influence acquired in a previous role affects decisions in a subsequent position," the yearbook read.

The select committee's proposed changes would require the state to identify positions with elevated conflict-of-interest risks and allow officials in those roles to be barred from taking related private-sector jobs for up to one year.

In feedback submitted on behalf of the government, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200), standing in for Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) during her vacation, said the government cabinet found no evidence the problem in question exists in Estonia on the scale suggested by the bill.

MP Anastassia Kovalenko-Kõlvart (Center) Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

"Neither the bill nor its explanatory memo demonstrates a problem that would require the solution as proposed," Tsahkna wrote.

He also argued the proposal lacks precision, would increase bureaucracy and could disproportionately restrict officials whose contact with a private company may have only been formal in nature.

'He may not have understood what he was signing'

Center Party MP and Anti-Corruption Select Committee chair Anastassia Kovalenko-Kõlvart, one of the leading lawmakers behind the bill, called the government's position startling, saying the ISS and other security agencies have repeatedly warned the committee of the risks of the "revolving door" effect.

She said Tsahkna "may simply not have understood what he was signing," suggesting the issue should maybe await Pakosta's return. The feedback was nevertheless submitted on behalf of the entire government.

The bill is expected to return to the Riigikogu's Constitutional Committee during the fall session, where Kovalenko-Kõlvart said she remains open to proposed changes and hopes MPs will assess the proposal on its merits rather than along coalition lines.

World.title: Gallery: Vanemuine's 16th summer concert took place in Tartu

The Vanemuine Symphony Orchestra's summer concert took place in Kassitoome Valley in Tartu on Sunday, drawing thousands of spectators.

For the first time, the concert program also featured a ballet performance, with Jevgeni Grib and Ketlin Oja.

World.title: Estonia to see partial solar eclipse on August 12
World.content:
On August 12, a partial solar eclipse will be visible from Estonia just before sunset, but viewers will need a clear western horizon to catch the event. At its maximum, the moon will block more than 80 percent of the sun's surface, said University of Tartu astronomer Tõnis Eenmäe. The sun will not disappear completely from view, but the light will take on an unusual pale, silvery hue. "People will definitely notice that the light is different somehow, and animals will likely sense it the same way," he said, recalling a total eclipse he once witnessed in Turkey that prompted nearby sheep to gather around their shepherd as darkness approached. A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes between Earth and the sun, partially to fully blocking its light. In Tallinn, the August 12 eclipse will begin at 8:02 p.m., peak at 8:53 p.m. and end at 9:19 p.m. as the sun sets. At maximum eclipse, the sun will appear as a thin crescent just above the horizon. Because of the low angle, trees, buildings and other obstacles could easily block the view. Eenmäe recommends choosing an open spot facing west, such as a coastline, lakeshore or field. How to watch safely Even near sunset, viewers should not look directly at the sun without proper protection. Eenmäe recommends certified eclipse glasses or solar filters.

Other items can also be used to view the eclipse directly or indirectly, such as welding glasses or helmets with a sufficient shade number or an unprinted silver CD, or a simple pinhole projector made from cardboard.

Regular sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes without solar filters should not be used to view the sun; doing so can cause permanent eye damage.

Totality visible elsewhere in Europe

While Estonia will see only a partial eclipse, the path of totality will cross parts of Europe, including Iceland and Spain, casting regions into darkness while briefly revealing the sun's outer atmosphere, or corona.

Solar eclipses have helped researchers make discoveries such as helium, and despite advances in space-based monitoring, ground-based observations remain valuable as well.

"I'm positive there are plenty of observations that can provide useful information if made during a solar eclipse," Eenmäe added.

Observers can use NASA's eclipse resources or the free Stellarium software to plan their viewing.

For those watching in Estonia, the key essentials are a clear horizon and proper eye protection.

World.title: Tartuff to show 21 films and shorts at extended film festival
World.content:
The 21st iteration of the Tartu-based film festival, Tartuff, will show a total of 13 feature films and 8 short films from Europe, Asia, the Americas, and Australia this year.

Taking place from August 8–15, the festival has extended its run by two days this year.

A total of 14 films will be shown on the large outdoor screen at Raekoja plats, while documentaries and children's films will be screened at Tartu Elektriteater.

This year's festival features acclaimed international films, classics, documentaries and, for the first time, a curated selection of short films exploring love and human relationships.

The festival opens with Thai drama Gohan directed by Chayanop Boonprakob, Nattawut Poonpiriya, and Atta Hemwadee. Inspired by stray dogs and modern-day loneliness, the film follows Gohan, a rescued dog whose journey through three different homes changes the lives of everyone he meets.

The closing night will feature Baz Luhrmann's musical classic Moulin Rouge!, celebrating the film's 25th anniversary.

Tartuff is the largest open-air film festival in the Baltics, attracting 12,000 visitors last year.

World.title: Social minister urges hospital ER to raise tick‑removal fee to €90
World.content:
The North Estonia Medical Centre (PERH) set the fee for tick removal at €50, but Social Minister Karmen Joller says they could charge €90 — the same price as the procedure costs at a veterinary clinic.

A regulation that took effect on April 1 in hospital emergency departments allows staff to direct patients with simpler health issues to a family doctor or pharmacist. For example, PERH's ER now sends people back if they come in only to have a tick removed — or they must pay for the service, Postimees reports.

"Since April 1, tick removal is a paid service if the tick is located on a part of the body where the person can remove it themselves. The fee is €50, based on the hospital's price list for paid services," explained PERH Emergency Medicine Centre head Dr. Marit Märk.

Last summer, 200 people came to PERH requesting tick removal. Before a patient is sent to a triage nurse, they are informed at registration that the service is paid.

"I recommend that the regional hospital review its price list, because I know that removing a tick at a veterinary clinic costs €90," Joller said in her podcast. "Thinking of my dog Pontu — before we managed to apply tick medication, we removed them five at a time. The vet clinic could have made a good profit off Pontu, but we removed the ticks ourselves."

In local pharmacies, special tick removal hooks are available, costing a few euros, to remove ticks either independently or with help from someone close.

Source: Postimees

World.title: Saudi Arabia says Iran-backed militias launch drones from Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Saudi Arabia’s Defense Ministry claimed on Saturday that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed multiple drones fired from Iraqi territory, targeting sites in the Kingdom’s Eastern Province and the capital, Riyadh.

Major General Turki al-Maliki, a spokeswoman for the Defense Ministry, claimed the drones were fired by Iran-backed militias operating from Iraq and branded the strikes as “terrorist attempts.”

He added that Saudi Arabia is entitled to reply “at the appropriate time and place.”

There was no immediate response from the Iraqi government or any armed organization claiming credit for the strike.

The event occurs as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi prepares to visit Saudi Arabia in the coming days for discussions with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

The two sides are set to discuss economic cooperation, investment, and regional security.

Baghdad has pushed to boost ties with Riyadh recently as part of a larger campaign to improve relations with Gulf Arab governments, attract Saudi investment, and increase economic and energy cooperation.

The alleged drone launches highlight the Iraqi government’s ongoing problem in exercising control over armed forces linked with Iran, whose activities have sometimes affected Baghdad’s foreign policy and relations with regional allies.

Saudi Arabia has regularly accused Iran-backed organizations of carrying out cross-border assaults against the kingdom, while Iraq has committed to preventing its territory from being used to launch attacks on neighboring countries.

World.title: Iraq seeks to increase oil exports through Turkey’s Ceyhan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – An Iraqi government source stated on Saturday that a delegation from the Oil Ministry recently traveled to Turkey to discuss a mutually agreeable process for exporting Iraqi oil through Turkish ports.

The Iraqi officials held discussions with Turkish energy officials, including Turkey’s Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources, according to local news outlet Shafaq News.

The discussions focused on renewing the operating agreement for the pipeline, ensuring a steady oil flow from Kirkuk and Iraqi Kurdistan and negotiating terms to enhance export capacity through the port of Ceyhan.

The push for an oil flow increase is prompted by the region’s unstable security situation, which has directly affected the volume of Iraqi oil shipments to global markets, resulting in lower financial profits.

The discussions focused on specific aspects of the export process, such as pipeline protection and procedures for boosting export capacity.

The step takes place ahead of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s upcoming visit to Turkey, which may lead to the finalization of various bilateral agreements, including those related to oil. The development comes at a time when Iraq is seeking alternative and secure avenues to market its oil internationally.

Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair stated recently that Iraq is speeding up plans to build an oil pipeline to Mediterranean ports in Turkey and Syria, as the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz continues to restrict shipments.

The government-controlled North Oil Company (NOC) declared on July 18 that it had met the requirements needed to start exporting crude oil via the vital pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.

World.title: General Electric to add 10,000 megawatts to Iraq’s grid in 2027
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s recent agreement with General Electric (GE) involves securing 10,000 megawatts of cross-border electricity imports from neighboring countries by 2027, according to member of Parliament’s Electricity and Energy Committee, Riyadh Adai.

Adai’s remarks followed the committee’s meeting with the Iraqi electricity minister on Saturday, according to local news outlet Shafaq News.

Under the new deal, the US energy company will be able to get 10,000 megawatts via electricity interconnections with countries in the region.

The agreement signed during the recent visit of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to the United States also includes the expansion of domestic combined-cycle power plants, as well as the upgrade of national transmission networks.

Earlier in July, Iraqi Electricity Minister Ali Saadi Wahib said that the government prioritizes the electricity interconnection project with Saudi Arabia as part of its efforts to diversify energy sources.

In an interview with Asharq News in Washington, Wahib stated that Iraq’s electricity grid now has a shortage ranging between 35,000 and 40,000 megawatts.

Baghdad is actively working to diversify its electricity sources through various regional interconnection projects. According to Wahib, Iraq has a 600-megawatt interconnection project with Turkey and an approximately 500-megawatt project with Jordan. Additionally, there is a 600-megawatt interconnection project with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) grid that is still in progress.

The electrical interconnection project with Saudi Arabia, projected to have a capacity of 1,000 to 2,000 megawatts, has not yet entered the execution phase. However, it has become a priority for the Iraqi government, according to Wahib.

Iraq experiences significant summer energy shortages, with peak demand exceeding 60,000 megawatts and limited local power generation capacity.

Electricity interconnection with neighboring countries will lessen dependency on centralized power providers while stabilizing local grid performance.

World.title: Iraqi PM to visit Saudi Arabia this week following Turkey’s trip
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is scheduled to fly to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for an official visit, following a diplomatic stop in the Turkish capital, Ankara, on Tuesday.

The trip is part of a larger regional diplomatic tour aiming to maintain regional balance and strengthen Iraq’s business connections.

The prime minister recently conducted high-level diplomatic visits to the United States on July 13 and Iran on July 23.

Several memoranda of understanding covering a wide range of economic and development sectors are expected to be signed during Al-Zaidi’s trip to Saudi Arabia.

The agreements are expected to increase Saudi investments in Iraq and strengthen economic cooperation in different sectors.

Al-Zaidi will have high-level bilateral discussions with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and other top Saudi officials.

The discussions will largely focus on security cooperation, counterterrorism, and minimizing the economic shocks resulting from ongoing regional crises.

Al-Zaidi’s trip to Saudi Arabia will prioritize growing economic relationships, strengthening security collaboration, and maintaining regional neutrality.

World.title: Oil prices sink as US-Iran pause fuels fresh Hormuz hopes
World.content:
Hong Kong – Oil prices tumbled on Monday as a pause in tit-for-tat strikes between the United States and Iran boosted hopes for a return to their ceasefire and negotiations on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

The United States held fire at the weekend after 13 days of attacks on sites in the Islamic republic, and Donald Trump’s UN envoy said the US president was “giving talks some space”.

Tehran said in turn it would stop its retaliatory attacks on regional neighbours, handing Gulf shipping and the oil industry a respite.

The two resumed hostilities this month, breaking a fragile truce, after Iran attacked ships passing through Omani waters in the Strait of Hormuz, sparking a pattern of escalation.

That derailed diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran, but the conflict then expanded beyond the vital energy corridor when Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen hit Saudi vessels in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a crucial passage into the Red Sea.

Crude prices soared on the flare-up, with Brent breaking back above $100 a barrel last week for the first time since May. News that shipping continued in the Red Sea helped investors pare the gains on Friday.

However, Trump’s decision to hold off on more strikes and Iran’s claims on Sunday that it had made progress in talks with Oman on management of the Strait of Hormuz provided some much-needed relief.

The discussions focused on “common principles and operational mechanisms” for ensuring the safe passage of shipping through the strait while respecting the sovereign rights of the two states, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said.

A report also said mediator Pakistan was looking at resuming US-Iran peace talks, following a push initiated by China.

Both main oil contracts sank on Monday, with Brent shedding more than seven percent at one point to briefly drop back below $90.

“It looks as if developments in the Middle East have moved in a positive direction over the weekend, adding some credibility to the notion that oil above $100 a barrel seems to induce de-escalatory behaviour from both sides,” wrote National Australia Bank’s Sally Auld.

– Inflation fears ease –

The positive developments eased worries about a reignition of inflation and a fresh round of interest rate hikes, in turn helping equity markets higher.

However, concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom and questions over the eye-watering sums pumped into the sector continue to dog traders, as tech firms bear the brunt of selling.

Seoul, which has led the rout in recent weeks, rose one percent with chip giants SK hynix and Samsung enjoying some much-needed buying interest.

Tokyo rose, though tech firms Advantest and Kioxia suffered more hefty selling pressure.

Hong Kong, Sydney, Shanghai, Wellington, Singapore, Mumbai and Manila were also up.

London, Paris and Frankfurt rose at the open.

Taipei and Bangkok fell, while Jakarta was also in retreat following the surprise resignation of Indonesian central bank boss Perry Warjiyo citing personal reasons.

Traders will be keenly awaiting the release of earnings from SK hynix, Samsung and Japan’s Kioxia this week, while US titans Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Amazon are also due, with focus on their outlooks and spending plans.

Tim Waterer of KCM Trade said: “Traders remain somewhat nervy about the scale of the capex being committed, given lingering concerns over how long the return-on-investment phase may take to fully materialise.”

Also in view this week is the Federal Reserve’s policy decision in light of the latest US-Iran flare-up and recent data indicating inflation easing.

Bets on a hike have risen over the past week, though analysts expect officials to stand pat on Wednesday.

However, Jenny Zeng at Allianz Global Investors warned: “While the (policy board) is likely to remain on hold in July, we continue to expect 50 basis points of tightening by year-end.”

In company news, China’s leading memory chipmaker CXMT jumped 530 percent on its market debut in Shanghai to take it past megabank ICBC as the mainland’s most valuable company, before later paring the gains to end up 465 percent.

The breathtaking surge came after the Anhui-based company had raised $9.8 billion in a blockbuster initial public offering, Bloomberg News reported, making it China’s biggest mainland tech share sale.

World.title: France, Spain race to contain ‘monster’ fires ahead of new heatwave
World.content:
Bordeaux – Shelters in France and Spain on Monday overflowed with exhausted locals and holidaymakers forced to flee blazes so massive some were forming their own mini weather systems, as authorities warned a new heatwave was set to descend on parts of the region.

The fires tearing through forests in southwest France, around the prized wine-making region of Bordeaux, and in central Spain around the capital Madrid have been some of the worst in decades and have hit at the height of the summer holiday season.

More than 325,000 people have fled their homes in the face of the blazes feeding on forests left super-dry by successive heatwaves and lack of rain since May.

“Everyone had to get out of the village quickly — it was a critical situation and people were scared,” Olga Congacha, 50, told AFP on a highway in the Madrid region, where police had closed off access to her home, Robledo de Chavela.

“My husband and I left with all that we could grab — our important documents and some clothes.”

France’s fire has caused a “pyrocumulonimbus” — a giant fire cloud that can create its own winds and packs lightning and sometimes tornadoes that can cause more blazes, according to France’s national firefighters federation, who said the phenomenon had never before been seen in the country.

“It’s a David-versus-Goliath scenario… at some point, we’ll find a weak spot and strike there,” said federation spokesman Eric Brocardi.

Thousands of firefighters, backed by specialised water-bombing aircraft have been battling the blazes and the clouds of toxic smoke.

French President Emmanuel Macron will hold a crisis cabinet meeting to discuss the emergency on Monday, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez will visit a fire-hit area in Valencia, in the east of the country where firefighters are battling a new blaze.

Spain’s civil protection chief Virginia Barcones on Sunday said the country was battling a “monster” in the fire around Avila.

“We are dealing with a perimeter of 280 kilometres encompassing 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres),” Barcones told state broadcaster TVE.

– ‘Extremely intense’ –

Scientists say climate change is making such extreme weather events more frequent and intense.

In France, the prefect of the southwestern Gironde region, where the country’s fires are concentrated, urged tourists to stay away and seek “other destinations”.

“The wind is changing so much, it’s really the fire calling the shots,” a firefighter said.

The fire has ravaged 42,000 hectares in Gironde — an area seven times the size of Manhattan — since Wednesday.

Around 220,000 people have been evacuated in the region, with 45 campsites forced to shut, ruining the holiday plans of around 40,000 people. Another 30,000 people have been forced to flee fires in other regions in France.

The Gironde local authority said early Monday that the fire had remained “broadly stable” overnight.

Garden hose in hand, Georges Clivaz sprayed water along a road leading to his property in Saint-Jean-d’Illac in Gironde as the blaze burned a few kilometres away.

“We’re doing this to slow down the fire’s advance; we want to save our homes,” he told AFP.

Although the village was evacuated on Friday, Clivaz said he and his family were trying to hold out.

“But the firefighters are telling us that in two or three hours the fire will be here.”

– New heatwave –

Weather forecasters warn another heatwave could hit France from Tuesday, with temperatures reaching 40C in some areas.

Around 75,000 residents have been evacuated from the Madrid region, Avila, Toledo and from the eastern region of Castellon in Valencia.

On Monday authorities said the fire “was not yet under control” but in a sign of progress said they would reopen a campsite where 4,500 people had been evacuated and also allow elderly residents back home in another area, if the conditions permit.

Officials said winds were pushing wildfires near Madrid to the south, away from the capital for now, but forcing more evacuations of villages in their path.

The fire near Valencia in Spain killed one person on Saturday, the only civilian death reported so far in the blazes. In France, two firefighters died near Bordeaux on Tuesday.

World.title: Iraqi oil exports continue as Red Sea and Hormuz shipping slows
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Shipping activity through two of the world’s most critical maritime chokepoints has slowed sharply following renewed security concerns in the Middle East, according to new data from maritime analytics firm Kpler.

The latest figures show vessel traffic through both the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to its lowest levels in months, as shipping companies remain cautious despite changing regional dynamics.

According to Kpler, traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait slowed significantly after Houthi forces launched attacks on Saudi Aramco oil facilities in Jizan and Yanbu.

The attacks have added fresh uncertainty to Red Sea shipping routes, prompting many operators to reassess transit schedules and security risks. The Red Sea remains one of the world’s busiest energy corridors, making any disruption closely watched by global oil markets.

Shipping activity through the Strait of Hormuz also remained subdued, even after direct military strikes between the United States and Iran came to a halt.

Kpler data shows vessel movements stayed limited over the weekend, reflecting continued caution among shipping companies despite the easing of immediate hostilities. Security concerns continue to influence routing decisions, insurance costs, and freight rates across the Gulf.

Despite the ongoing maritime disruptions, Iraq’s oil exports continue to move through the Strait of Hormuz. According to Kpler, two Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) carrying Iraqi and Emirati crude successfully transited the strategic waterway on Friday as part of outbound shipments from the Gulf.

The movements indicate that Iraqi crude exports are continuing, although regional security risks remain elevated.

Several additional oil tankers departed the Red Sea carrying Saudi, Emirati, and Russian crude destined for China. Another tanker loaded with Saudi crude also departed for Pakistan, highlighting that regional energy exports continue despite heightened security concerns.

However, markets remain focused on whether prolonged disruptions could tighten global energy supplies and push shipping costs even higher.

The combined slowdown in Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz underscores the growing impact geopolitical tensions are having on global trade. Both waterways are vital for international energy supplies, and prolonged instability could reshape shipping patterns, increase transportation costs, and place additional pressure on global oil markets.

For Iraq, maintaining uninterrupted crude exports through Hormuz remains critical, as oil revenues continue to account for the vast majority of government income.

World.title: Iraq weather forecast: Temperatures to rise again, with southern provinces to hit 47°C
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Temperatures are set to climb across Iraq once again this week, with the Iraqi Meteorological Authority forecasting another spell of intense summer heat beginning on Tuesday.

According to the latest forecast, most parts of the country will experience clear skies, while northern provinces are expected to see occasional cloud cover. The renewed rise in temperatures comes after a brief period of relatively milder conditions, with southern Iraq once again expected to record the highest readings.

The Meteorological Authority said Tuesday and Wednesday will be mostly sunny nationwide, with some clouds over northern Iraq. Temperatures are expected to increase slightly compared to previous days across all regions.

Maximum temperatures for Tuesday

Duhok, Sulaymaniyah: 42°C

Erbil, Anbar: 43°C

Baghdad, Kirkuk, Karbala, Nineveh, Salahaddin, Diyala: 44°C

Wasit, Najaf, Babil, Diwaniyah, Muthanna: 45°C

Basra, Dhi Qar, Maysan: 47°C

Southern provinces will remain the hottest areas in the country, with temperatures approaching the upper 40s.

The weather is expected to remain clear across most of Iraq through Thursday and Friday. Northern areas will continue to experience intermittent cloud cover, while the central region is forecast to see a slight increase in temperatures on Thursday.

By Friday, temperatures are expected to remain largely unchanged across the country, maintaining the hot summer conditions.

The latest forecast indicates that Iraq will continue to experience typical peak-summer weather, with daytime temperatures remaining well above 40°C in most provinces.

Authorities generally advise residents to avoid prolonged outdoor activities during peak afternoon hours, stay hydrated, and take precautions against heat-related illnesses as temperatures remain exceptionally high.

World.title: Bihar's dairy push: New plant in Nalanda to boost farmer incomes, create jobs
World.content:
Bihar laid the foundation stone for a modern 20 metric tonne per day curd and lassi processing plant in Nalanda, on Monday. This marks a significant step in the state's ambition to emerge as a stronger player in India's fast-growing dairy industry.

Chief minister Samrat Choudhary laid the foundation for the facility at the Biharsharif Dairy Project, which is expected to substantially enhance the production capacity of COMFED's flagship brand Sudha. The expansion aims to meet rising demand for value-added dairy products while preparing the brand to compete in global markets as India strengthens its position as the world's largest milk producer.

The new facility is expected to encourage further investments in dairy processing, reinforce Bihar's efforts to build a robust dairy value chain, and deliver higher returns to farmers.

It also positions the state to capitalise on India's growing competitive advantage in the global dairy sector.

The expansion is closely aligned with Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of 'Sahkar Se Samriddhi' (Prosperity through Cooperation) and the objectives of White Revolution 2.0, launched by Union home and cooperation minister Amit Shah. As India seeks to strengthen its dairy cooperative movement and enhance the global footprint of Indian dairy products, Sudha is steadily evolving from a trusted regional brand into a nationally respected and globally competitive dairy brand.





Towards this objective, COMFED is expanding village-level dairy cooperative societies, increasing milk procurement, and promoting greater participation of women in the dairy economy.

Addressing the gathering, chief minister Choudhary commended COMFED and Bihar's dairy cooperatives for their contribution to the state's rural economy and expressed confidence that Sudha would evolve into a globally competitive dairy brand.

"Sudha represents much more than a dairy brand. It is the backbone of the livelihoods, self-reliance and aspirations of millions of dairy farmers across Bihar," he said.

Through its extensive cooperative network, Sudha has ensured that producers receive fair remuneration while strengthening the rural economy and creating sustainable livelihood opportunities.

COMFED outlines expansion roadmap

Shirsat Kapil Ashok, Managing Director of COMFED, highlighted the federation's achievements during the first 100 days of the present government, including the formation of more than 2,500 new dairy cooperative societies across Bihar.

This has resulted in an increase of over 300,000 litres of milk procurement per day compared to the previous year.

Outlining the roadmap for the next 100 days, Ashok said COMFED would expand initiatives such as Sudha Sakhi and the Prime Minister's Veterinary Medicine Centres, while implementing key livestock breed improvement projects. These include a proposed Semen Station in Lakhisarai and an AITI Centre in Munger, aimed at improving cattle genetics and productivity.

The chief minister distributed deep freezers to 300 retailers to strengthen Sudha's frozen products distribution network and flagged off a specially designed vehicle for transporting sick and infirm livestock.

World.title: 'Modi govt fears truth and non-violence': Rahul Gandhi on Ken-Betwa protest crackdown
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress leader

on Monday said the Modi government fears "both truth and non-violent resistance", days after police

tribal protests against the Ken-Betwa river linking project in BJP-ruled Madhya Pradesh.

"The tribal brothers and sisters of Madhya Pradesh had sat on a water satyagraha and hunger strike because their land was taken away for the Ken-Betwa project, but they received neither fair compensation nor dignified rehabilitation," the Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition wrote on X.

Rahul Gandhi X post

Calling tribals the country's "original owners", Rahul Gandhi asserted that the first right over water, forests and land "belongs to them alone."

"And their 'satyagraha' is because that very right is being snatched from them today. In their unique way, their demand is simply this: provide a proper means of livelihoodâor else life is no different from a funeral pyre. But even this is unacceptable to the BJP government. Instead of listening to them, their peaceful protest is being crushed with police force," the Raebareli MP added.

The former Congress chief expressed solidarity with the protesting tribal communities and asserted that his party would ensure justice, including fair compensation and proper rehabilitation for them.





Rahul Gandhi also shared a video clip highlighting the protests in Madhya Pradesh.

On July 19, police in Madhya Pradesh's Chhatarpur district removed protesters from the site, bringing their 15-day agitation to an end.

The Rs 44,605-crore Ken-Betwa Link Project is India's first river-linking project under the National Perspective Plan. It aims to irrigate 1.062 million hectares of land, provide drinking water to around 6.2 million people, and generate hydropower in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region spanning Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: NEET fast-track court's first hearing stalls as CBI skips proceedings
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The first hearing before Delhi's newly designated fast-track court for the NEET paper leak case ended without any substantive proceedings on Monday after no lawyer appeared on behalf of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), prompting the court to adjourn the matter.

The case came up before Special Judge Anu Grover Baliga, who recently assumed charge of the special court set up to exclusively hear offences related to paper leaks and other unfair means in public examinations.

The court was scheduled to hear the bail applications of two accused, Dinesh Biwal and Vikas Biwal. However, with no prosecutor representing the investigating agency present until 10.45 am, the judge recorded the absence in the order, news agency PTI reported.

Counsel for the accused requested that the matter be deferred, informing the court that he had to appear in another case before the Rohini district courts and could not wait further. Accepting the request, the judge adjourned the hearing to August 3.
