He said there was a growing perception that Europe’s larger states were seeking to reshape the EU’s system of governance, warning that such changes would threaten both the continent’s political balance and the bloc’s enlargement process, as well as the principles on which the European Union was founded.

Papuashvili was commenting on remarks by Germany’s foreign minister, who said several countries had joined Berlin’s initiative to abolish unanimity in EU decision-making.

According to Papuashvili, if such a reform were implemented, the European Union could evolve from a union of equal member states into one dominated largely by its biggest countries.

“EU membership is not an end in itself. That is true neither for current member states nor for candidate countries. Brexit was the clearest proof of that,” the parliament speaker wrote.

According to Papuashvili, the main purpose of joining the European Union is to expand a country’s opportunities, better protect its national interests and increase its influence over international decision-making. He argued that the principle of consensus is one of the key guarantees of that influence for smaller states, as it allows them to block decisions they consider harmful and defend their national interests.

“If the principle of consensus is abolished and decision-making comes to depend entirely on the will of larger states or a stable majority, smaller countries will lose this fundamental lever,” he wrote.

In his view, EU membership would then cease to represent the voluntary delegation of part of a country’s sovereignty in pursuit of shared economic and political goals, and could instead become a process that significantly reduces the influence of smaller states.

Papuashvili argued that a country which can no longer prevent decisions it considers harmful gradually loses both its political freedom and its ability to make sovereign decisions.

He said such a model could benefit larger states, whose economic and political weight already gives them considerable influence, but would represent a “catastrophic change” for smaller countries.

“That is why the question will become increasingly relevant: what’s the point of membership if you’re stripped of its main advantage and leverage from the very beginning?”

Papuashvili argued that the EU’s value lies precisely in allowing member states to defend their interests, influence decisions and block measures they consider undesirable.

He said the debate over changing the unanimity rule could also result in a slowdown of the EU’s future enlargement.

“Candidate countries are being offered not equal membership in the existing union, but a pre-designed system in which they will assume all the obligations of membership while their rights and influence are curtailed.”

According to Papuashvili, the key question for Georgia should not only be when it joins the European Union, but also what kind of European Union it joins and what rights new members will have.

“Membership that deprives a country of its sovereign rights and offers no mechanisms to defend them is not integration – it is the abolition of sovereignty.”

Papuashvili concluded his statement with an apparent reference to Greek mythology: “It seems that even Jupiter’s abduction of Europa is forgiven.”

Papuashvili questions value of EU membership

World.title: EU sanctions Inter RAO, Russian company controlling energy assets in Georgia
World.content:
The European Union has imposed sanctions on Russian state-owned energy company Inter RAO, which indirectly owns Georgia’s Telasi, Telmico, Khrami HPP I and Khrami HPP II through its subsidiaries.

The decision could affect Inter RAO’s assets in Georgia as well as ongoing corporate transactions.

Telasi and Telmico both operate in Georgia’s electricity sector, but they perform different roles. Khrami HPP I and Khrami HPP II (the Khrami hydropower cascade) form one of Georgia’s largest hydropower complexes. Located on the Khrami River in the Kvemo Kartli region, the two plants generate electricity and are an important part of Georgia’s power system, contributing significantly to the country’s domestic electricity production. Telasi is the electricity distribution network operator for Tbilisi. The company owns and manages the capital’s power distribution infrastructure—including power lines, substations and other grid assets—and is responsible for delivering electricity to consumers. Telmico is an electricity supply company. It purchases electricity on the wholesale market and supplies it to residential and commercial customers in Tbilisi. The company issues electricity bills and signs supply contracts with consumers.

Inter RAO was added to the EU sanctions list on 23 July as part of the bloc’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia.

According to the Council of the European Union, the Russian government-controlled company is one of the country’s largest energy groups and plays a significant role in the Russian economy.

According to the Council, the Russian Federation benefits financially from Inter RAO through both the taxes paid by the company and the dividends received by its owners. For that reason, the EU considers the company to be providing financial support to the Russian authorities, which Brussels holds responsible for the aggression against Ukraine and the annexation of Crimea.

According to the company’s ownership structure, Inter RAO is the indirect owner of 100% of the shares in the Netherlands-registered Silk Road Holdings B.V. The company directly owns a 75.108% stake in Telasi and a 75.471% stake in Telmico.

Inter RAO also indirectly owns the Netherlands-registered Gardabani Holdings B.V., which has full ownership of Khrami HPP I and Khrami HPP II.

At the same time, Silk Road Holdings has launched a tender offer to acquire the remaining 24.892% stake in Telasi. The offer closes on 31 July, applications will be reviewed until 7 August, and the transaction is scheduled to be completed on 21 August.

What impact could the sanctions have?

The inclusion of Inter RAO on the EU sanctions list could also affect the operations of the companies it indirectly controls in Georgia. Under EU sanctions, banks and companies based in the bloc may be prohibited from carrying out financial transactions, providing economic resources or delivering certain services to legal entities that are directly or indirectly controlled by a sanctioned company.

The restrictions could also limit Inter RAO’s ability to exercise its shareholder rights through its Netherlands-registered subsidiaries. This could affect voting rights, the appointment of directors, the approval and receipt of dividends, the acquisition or disposal of shareholdings, and other key corporate decisions.

Particular attention is also being paid to the planned acquisition of the remaining stake in Telasi. Because the tender offer is being made by the Netherlands-registered Silk Road Holdings, the transaction may require approval from the relevant Dutch regulatory authority, increasing the risk of delays or even suspension of the deal.

At the same time, the EU has not listed Telasi, Telmico or the Khrami hydropower plants as separate sanctioned entities. However, under EU sanctions rules, asset-freezing measures generally extend to companies that are directly or indirectly owned or majority-controlled by a sanctioned individual or entity.

Inter RAO sanctioned by the EU

World.title: $94.3m in violations: What Azerbaijan’s mid-year audit reveals
World.content:
Report by the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan

In the first half of 2026, the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan identified financial violations and shortcomings worth a total of 160.3 million manats ($94.3m) following state financial oversight activities.

The figures were published in the chamber’s report on its activities for the first six months of the year and were also reported by several media outlets.

The chamber said it had ordered the recovery of 35 million manats ($20.5m) linked to the identified violations. Materials concerning violations worth 14.8 million manats ($8.71m) were referred to law enforcement agencies. The remaining 110.5 million manats ($65m) were classified as “other violations.”

During the reporting period, the chamber carried out 33 oversight activities, including 20 compliance audits, two financial audits, eight performance audits and three analytical reviews.

The audits covered the sectors of education, capital investment, public administration, water supply and irrigation, agriculture, and social protection. Twenty-one of the audited entities were inspected for the first time.

Comparison with previous years

These figures are significantly higher than those reported for the same period in previous years. In the first half of 2024, the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan identified financial violations worth 91 million manats ($53.5m). In the first half of 2025, the figure was estimated at around 65–70 million manats ($38–42m). For the whole of 2025, the chamber reported violations totaling 1.554 billion manats ($915m).

The 160.3 million manats ($94.3m) recorded in the first six months of 2026 is higher than the figures for the corresponding periods of both 2024 and 2025. This may reflect an increase in the number of audits or an expansion in the scope of inspections. At the same time, the data suggests that the scale of detected violations has not decreased.

The public classification of the identified violations remains limited. Reports from previous years, particularly for 2025, showed that the largest share involved breaches of budget legislation, accounting for around 50%, while violations of public procurement rules made up about 24%.

The data for the first half of 2026 does not provide a category-by-category breakdown of the violations. It only identifies the sectors covered by the audits, including capital investment, education and social protection. Previous reports indicate that audits in the construction and public procurement sectors have repeatedly uncovered violations such as inflated project costs, breaches of contract terms and improper documentation.

The role of the Accounts Chamber and the impact of its reports

The Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan is the country’s highest external public financial oversight body. Its reports are submitted to the Milli Majlis and, in principle, can influence the budget process. In practice, however, a significant share of the identified violations is classified as “other violations.”

Of the total 160.3 million manats ($94.3m) in identified violations, the chamber ordered the recovery of funds in only 35 million manats ($20.5m), or about 22% of the total. Materials relating to violations worth 14.8 million manats ($8.71m), around 9%, were referred to law enforcement agencies. The fate of the remaining amount has not been disclosed, and it remains unclear what action, if any, was taken by the relevant institutions or whether any officials were held accountable.

The issue appears to be systemic. Reports from previous years reveal a similar pattern: while violations involving substantial sums have been identified, the amount of recovered funds and the scale of legal action have remained limited. The same types of irregularities continue to be recorded year after year in public procurement, construction projects and the management of public funds, including incomplete documentation, inefficient spending and breaches of contract terms.

The chamber has also repeatedly pointed to weaknesses in internal audit mechanisms. However, the limited public discussion of its reports and the lack of detailed disclosure reduce the practical impact of state financial oversight.

Against the backdrop of Karabakh reconstruction and major government programmes

In recent years, funds allocated for the reconstruction of territories retaken from Armenian control have accounted for a significant share of Azerbaijan’s state budget spending. Billions of manats have been earmarked for capital investment under the Great Return programme and other large-scale government initiatives.

Notably, some of the violations identified in the first half of 2026 were linked to capital investment projects. However, the report does not specify which projects were involved, the sums affected or the nature of the violations.

This makes questions of transparency and the efficient use of public funds even more pressing. The risks of misuse or inefficient spending are particularly significant in large infrastructure and social projects, as these investments are directly tied to the return of displaced residents, the restoration of living conditions and the long-term development of the region.

The absence of a separate, detailed assessment of these programmes in the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan report—or the lack of public disclosure of such information—makes it difficult to objectively assess the risks involved.

Why do the violations recur year after year?

The repeated discovery of financial violations involving large sums may be explained by several factors.

First, insufficient oversight and weak internal audit mechanisms.

Second, a lack of transparency in public procurement and construction projects.

Third, limited accountability. A significant share of the identified violations does not result in disciplinary or legal action against individual officials or the institutions involved.

Based on publicly available information, it is not possible to clearly distinguish between corruption, poor management and procedural violations. However, the scale of the violations and their repeated occurrence suggest that the problem is systemic rather than isolated.

In this context, the limited public scrutiny of the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan’s reports is also significant. As a rule, the full reports, the names of specific projects, the list of audited institutions and detailed information about the identified violations are not made public. This limits opportunities for independent analysis and public oversight.

What does this mean for the public?

The 160.3 million manats ($94.3m) in identified violations involve public funds financed through taxpayers’ money and other state revenues. If part of these funds was spent in breach of financial rules, it means that the money could otherwise have been used for education, healthcare, social protection or infrastructure projects. The recovery of 35 million manats ($20.5m) represents a positive step, but the lack of clarity over the remaining amount raises further questions.

The findings underscore the need for greater transparency, stronger independent audit mechanisms and broader public scrutiny of audit reports.

Key questions remain unanswered: which institutions and projects were responsible for the violations; what became of the 110.5 million manats ($65m) classified as “other violations”; what concrete outcomes resulted from referring cases to law enforcement agencies; and what systemic measures, if any, will be introduced to prevent similar problems from recurring in the same sectors.

Report by the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan

World.title: From Avlabari to parliament: new route for pro-European marches in Tbilisi. Video blog “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Another activist in Georgia convicted over insulting Facebook post: doctor Giorgi Akhobadze
World.content:
Georgia: activist Giorgi Akhobadze sentenced over FB post

On July 24, another person in Georgia was sentenced to administrative detention over a Facebook post containing profanity. Giorgi Akhobadze, a doctor and active participant in the country’s pro-European protests, was sentenced to 25 days in detention.

Giorgi Akhobadze

The ruling was issued by Tbilisi City Court. Giorgi Akhobadze did not attend the hearing.

He was represented by his lawyer, Mikheil Zakareishvili.

A few hours after the ruling, Akhobadze was arrested during a special police operation at his home.

Administrative proceedings against Giorgi Akhobadze were initiated following a complaint by the Interior Ministry’s recently established Department for Monitoring Hate Speech.

Akhobadze was sentenced over a Facebook post in which he used profanity to insult police officers who had testified against him in an earlier criminal case.

In December 2024, Akhobadze was returning home from a pro-European protest (which has continued in Georgia for nearly two years) when he was detained by police. He was searched and charged with purchasing and possessing drugs.

Akhobadze and his lawyers maintained that the drugs had been planted on him during the arrest. After an eight-month trial, he was acquitted and released from the courtroom in August 2025.

The Facebook post that led to his current administrative sentence referred specifically to the police officers whom Akhobadze accuses of planting the drugs.

“I stand by every word of that post,” Akhobadze told TV Pirveli after learning of the court’s decision, repeating the profane insult directed at the police officers.

“I’ll spend 25 days in a cell, get some rest, and if they think I’ll come out thinking differently, they’re very much mistaken,” Akhobadze said before his arrest.

On fines and detention for offensive social media posts

Giorgi Akhobadze is the second person to receive a jail sentence over comments posted on social media.

A few days earlier, on July 22, Tbilisi City Court sentenced well-known journalist and Formula TV host Vakho Sanaia to 14 days of administrative detention.

Sanaia had published a Facebook post containing profane and insulting language directed at senior officials of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Administrative cases over opinions expressed in public are being initiated on the basis of reports filed by the Interior Ministry’s new Department for Monitoring Hate Speech, which began operating on June 1.

The department’s mandate is to monitor and proactively identify statements that violate human dignity, are insulting, or incite hatred, where they may constitute an administrative offence.

According to the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, between June 1 and July 2 the department identified 170 alleged administrative offences and referred 150 cases to court.

Courts have already ruled on 33 of those cases: 31 people were fined and two received verbal warnings. Most of those fined are activists taking part in the mass protests demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration.

News in Georgia

World.title: Netanyahu accuses New York's Mamdani of making Jews feel 'unsafe'
World.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he will still attend the United Nations General Assembly in September despite claiming the "rhetoric" of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is making Jews feel "unsafe" in the city.

Mr Mamdani has backed away from earlier comments suggesting he would seek Mr Netanyahu's arrest when the Israeli leader visited New York under an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant alleging war crimes.

Mr Mamdani, who became New York City's first Muslim mayor last year, later acknowledged he had no legal authority to enforce the ICC warrant.

Mr Netanyahu is a close ally of US President Donald Trump and a key partner in the ongoing US-Israeli military campaign against Iran.

Zohran Mamdani became New York's first Muslim mayor last November. (Reuters: Jeenah Moon)

The Israeli leader told Fox News on Sunday he was "not concerned" about the prospect of legal action if he travelled to New York.

But he blasted Mr Mamdani for his words that he says is dividing America's most famous city.

"He's fomenting hate. He's supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers — Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone," Mr Netanyahu told host Maria Bartiromo.

"But he's trying to turn one group against the other. I speak to Jewish Americans, and they're afraid right now.

"Mamdani celebrated the October 7th massacre, the worst massacre against Jews since the Holocaust.

"He's supporting the Hamas murderers who raped our women, then beheaded them, burned babies alive, slaughtered our men, took innocent people, hostages, 251 men, women, children, babies."

Mr Mamdani has repeatedly condemned the October 7th attacks during his campaign to become mayor.

A supporter of Palestinian rights, the mayor said earlier this month that his administration had been exploring options to arrest the Israeli prime minister over alleged war crimes in Gaza.

“I believe that prime minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” Mr Mamdani said in a speech. “He’s a war criminal who has been charged by the international criminal court, and what you will find is that is an opinion that is held by many, purely because of what his actions have wrought over these past many years.”

The Israeli prime minister's comments to Fox News about the mayor were slammed by progressive groups on social media.

Mr Netanyahu linked his concerns to two stabbing attacks in Manhattan last week, claiming they reflected growing fears among Jewish New Yorkers.

Police allege a suspect stabbed a Jewish man and an Asian man just blocks apart while shouting "Allahu akbar".

While both victims survived, the suspect has been charged with hate crimes in relation to the attacks.

Lindsey Graham dies suddenly at 71 US senator Lindsey Graham, a key Republican who went from a vocal critic of Donald Trump to one of his most loyal allies, has died at age 71.

Mr Netanyahu is due to arrive in the US this week on a separate visit, with New York not part of the itinerary.

He will meet Mr Trump at the White House on Tuesday before attending the funeral of former US senator Lindsey Graham.

Mr Graham, a staunch supporter of Israel who called for the US to escalate the war against Iran, died on July 11 at the age of 71 after a heart problem at his at his Washington DC home.

"Lindsey Graham was one of the greatest friends the State of Israel has ever known. And I am certain that in this matter," Mr Netanyahu said in a later interview translated from Hebrew as he prepared to board his flight to the US.

ABC/wires

World.title: Boycotts and withdrawn funding 'part and parcel' of working in arts today
World.content:
Singaporean curator Low Kee Hong has been appointed artistic director of the 2028 Biennale of Sydney, after this year's edition was troubled by controversy.

Kee Hong is the first leader of the biennale to hail from south-east Asia since it began in 1973, and follows 2026 artistic director, Emirati curator Hoor Al Qasimi.

A new artwork considers the legacy of the Cronulla riots Artist Abdul Abdullah says the Cronulla riots were a "moment of revelation" for many Australians as he unveils a new work for Sydney Biennale.

"I'm really looking forward to the next couple of years of trying to articulate an exhibition that makes sense for now," Kee Hong says.

For Kee Hong, this means grappling with "very challenging times", where conversations and ideas are flattened by social media and a lack of nuanced engagement with difficult subjects.

"It's about leaning into how artists are reflecting this moment in time and protecting space for deep listening," he says.

" Now more than ever, it's super important that we listen to each other. "

Kee Hong comes to the Sydney role with extensive credentials.

Kee Hong is excited to draw upon his background in both visual arts and performance to create the next edition of the biennale. (Pictured: Behrouz Boochani, Hoda Afshar and Vernon Ah Kee's biennale work CODE BLACK/Riot.) (Supplied: Biennale of Sydney)

He is currently creative director of Manchester arts organisation Factory International, which runs the biennial Manchester International Festival.

Previously, he worked in Hong Kong, at the West Kowloon District Authority, and in Singapore, as artistic director of Singapore Arts Festival and founding director of the Singapore Biennale.

A troubled event

This year's Biennale of Sydney, which closed last month, was subjected to community, commercial and political pressures and accusations of anti-Semitism, which began when vocally pro-Palestine curator Al Qasimi was appointed in 2024.

Hoor Al Qasimi, the artistic director of the 2026 biennale, took the event to Penrith Regional Gallery for the first time. (Supplied: Biennale of Sydney/Daniel Boud)

Donors were reported to have withdrawn, while the contract for an ambassador for the biennale's philanthropic program, who was also vocally pro-Palestine, was terminated due to "operational constraints" following complaints to the biennale board.

Amid further complaints artists on the program were anti-Semitic, Al Qasimi conducted a walk-through of the biennale with NSW Jewish Board of Deputies President David Ossip ahead of the exhibition opening in March.

Mr Ossip told the Australian Financial Review he intended to "call out" any perceived lack of "balance".

Then, on stage on opening night, American DJ Zubeyda Muzeyyen, who performs as DJ Haram, urged attendees to "oppose the Zio-Australian-Epstein empire".

Her comments were condemned by NSW Arts Minister John Graham, and resulted in accounting firm PwC dropping its sponsorship of the biennale.

Her statements also led to a review by the biennale and a NSW Police investigation into whether she breached racial hate laws. Police found there was "insufficient evidence to commence proceedings".

53hr drive to showcase Pilbara art in Sydney From the Pilbara to Penrith, an Indigenous WA community has taken its prized cultural and artistic possessions across the country for the Biennale of Sydney.

While Kee Hong would not be drawn on the specifics of the 2026 Biennale of Sydney out of respect for Al Qasimi, he describes the challenge for curators of navigating a charged political climate as a "global question".

"Working and living in Manchester, we are also subject to a lot of very similar conversations that we have observed around the world, in particular America and parts of Europe," he says.

"People pulling out, cancellations, the withdrawal of funding; it's all part and parcel of working within an art institution in this day and age."

For Kee Hong, what's important is "protecting spaces for nuanced conversation", often created by artists and contemporary art.

"We live in a world that doesn't really give space for that," he says.

" It's a very quick-fire draw: Do you agree or not? If you're not for me, you're against me. That is such a difficult landscape to navigate. "

Kee Hong, who lived in Hong Kong during the 2014 pro-democracy protests, sees the biennale and other arts organisations and arts festivals as exactly to place to have difficult conversations.

"I still very much believe in the power of communities coming together to celebrate each other, regardless of ideology," he says.

Listen to 2026 biennale artist Cannupa Hanska Luger on ABC Radio National's Critics Corner Cannupa Hanksa Luger is interested in ideas of Indigenous futurism, using that speculative fiction to speak back to the present moment. His work for the Biennale of Sydney includes a series of ceramic whistles shaped into the likeness of dingoes.

"Social gathering is quite powerful, to assemble in ways which are unexpected, bringing together different parts of the community that don't naturally sit with each other."

As an example, he points to Factory International's series titled Artists in Times of Upheaval, which has featured artists including Chinese artist and activist Ai Weiwei and Ukrainian playwright Tetiana Kytsenko.

"We invite artists who still live and work in the context of extreme conflict," he says. "It's not one perspective.

"For us, it's an important space to insist that you hear more and you engage more than just didactic, throwaway ideological lines."

Making connections

Kee Hong is a long-time attendee of the Biennale of Sydney, and plans to spend time in the city in October and after he delivers Manchester International Festival in July 2027.

Kee Hong recalls French artist Pierre Huyghe's 2008 biennale work, where he transformed the Opera House concert hall into the Amazon rainforest for 24 hours. (ABC News)

That's when he plans to engage with artists and communities both in Sydney and across Australia, including by going on Country to learn about plant life and nature in Australia from Indigenous communities.

"[I want] to sit with Indigenous Elders so I can understand the world view and cosmologies around medicine, around food, around bringing communities together," he says.

When he visits Sydney, he also plans to collaborate with the city's arts institutions, so that works created for the biennale have a "sustained impact".

"I work a lot via collaborations," he says. "Even for a particular commission, we think about multiple partners co-investing in making a work, so we'll start to think about the future life of the projects post the Biennale of Sydney."

Kee Hong stresses the biennale is more than just a three-month exhibition.

"What happens before and after is quite critical," he says.

"[The biennale is] not an international spaceship that lands and it happens and then goes away," Kee Hong says. (Pictured: Ema Shin and her 2026 work Hearts of Absent Women (Tree of Family).) (Supplied: Biennale of Sydney/Daniel Boud)

"We can think about projects that exist in terms of thousands of years or tens of thousands of years; the framework Indigenous communities have been operating in for the longest time.

"It's a way to approach your relationship with land, sky, sea, earth and time very differently.

" This, for me, is the magic sauce Australia and the Pacific can offer to the world. "

The Biennale of Sydney begins on March 21, 2028.

World.title: Australia's first new oil refinery in decades touted for WA
World.content:
Australia could build its first new oil refinery in decades, with the federal government set to investigate constructing a large-scale facility in Western Australia as part of its energy security response.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and WA Premier Roger Cook will announce a $4 million pre-feasibility study on Tuesday, the ABC understands.

The new refinery was proposed and would be built by Perth-headquartered Perdaman, a multinational organisation known for its fertiliser production operations.

An oil refinery in Geelong is one of only two remaining in Australia. (AFP: William West)

There are just two oil refineries remaining in Australia, located in Brisbane and Geelong.

In 2021, BP closed its oil refinery in Kwinana, south of Perth, which was the country's largest.

The ABC understands the pre-feasibility study for the new refinery is part of a $15 billion package from the federal government to secure the nation's fuel security and energy sovereignty.

Refining crisis The loss of Melbourne's Altona refinery, on top of the looming Kwinana closure in Perth, raise fresh concerns about the nation's ability to maintain fuel supplies in a crisis, writes Gareth Hutchens.

Just over two decades ago, Australia had eight oil refineries. Many then closed after being deemed economically unviable.

Mr Cook appointed a Fuel Supply State Controller in March to respond to fuel supply issues in WA amid the Middle East war.

In April, the WA government said it would invoke emergency powers, forcing fuel companies to share supply chain information.

The government said the move would ensure it could allocate fuel where it was needed most, which included regional WA.

'Doing everything we can'

In a statement, Mr Albanese said the federal government was working to ensure it could meet future challenges, beyond conflict overseas.

"The longer war in the Middle East goes on, the greater the impact on Australia will be," he said, adding his government would "do everything we can to shield Australia from the worst effects".

Last week, the Commonwealth government confirmed the country had 42 days' worth of petrol, 38 days' worth of diesel, and 32 days' worth of jet fuel.

Mr Cook said he supported Perdaman's efforts to rebuild the state's capacity to produce and distribute its own fuel.

The continued war in the Middle East has been threatening Australia's fuel security since February. (ABC Pilbara: Michelle Stanley)

"This includes diesel to support the regional communities which drive WA's economy and which have been most at risk amid this conflict," he said.

Federal Climate Change and Energy Minister Bowen said the government would work with all states and territories to build a "more sovereign and secure energy system".

Earlier this month, WA's Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson told the ABC she thought WA was in a strong position to undertake the feasibility study.

"We're a large jurisdiction, heavily reliant on fuel for our industry and our economic success," she said.

"We need to make sure that we have that refining capacity."

World.title: Not satire: The Utopia-style regulations holding Australia back from building homes
World.content:
A local council tells a property developer they need more trees for their new building, but the local fire authority says they need to minimise canopy to avoid a fire risk.

A compact Sydney apartment wins design awards for its 'clever' and 'thoughtful' design, but falls afoul of the state's design guide because its floor space is too small.

A family knocks down their home to build a prefabricated model in its place, only to discover council rules require the new home to be smaller.

Each story sounds fit for an episode of Utopia, but the real examples are symptoms of a rotten system of overlapping and contradictory regulations that make it too hard to build new and affordable homes, according to a new study by the Productivity Commission.

Tasked by Treasurer Jim Chalmers to study what governments can do to unlock more new homes, the taxpayer-funded research outfit called for a top-down rethink of regulations, replacing a restrictive system with a permissive "build mindset".

The commission's interim report did not make formal recommendations, but flagged its support for calls from the Grattan Institute and pro-housing groups to allow at least three storeys to be built on most residential land.

It also advocated the softening or total removal of rules that dictate minimum floor space, window or balcony size, car parking requirements, and subjective factors like 'neighbourhood character', while also reviewing heritage controls.

"Regulation is important, but too much or poorly designed regulation can stop new homes being built, make projects slower and more expensive, and reduce the types of housing available to us," Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood said.

"The rules should allow us to build enough housing in the right places, while still protecting the things Australians value."

Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood said poorly-designed regulations were standing in the way of new housing. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

PC: Cut red tape to get closer to national homes target

Federal, state and territory governments have jointly agreed to target 1.2 million new homes between mid-2024 and mid-2029, on the basis that this will make housing more affordable for owners and renters. The target is just over 200,000 homes behind track.

The commission's interim report came down in favour of this aspiration, finding a "strong causal link" from building more housing to lower house prices and cheaper rents, citing successful examples from Auckland and elsewhere.

But it warned efforts to make housing affordable would not be successful without a comprehensive review of the "thicket" of existing regulations or rules.

The surprising city where new housing is easiest to approve Four years on from a national pledge to unlock more housing, only one capital city allows townhouses or three-storey developments on most of its residential land.

While the report identified "upzoning" — rezoning residential land to permit higher density — as the highest priority for state and local governments, it found the benefits would be limited if other rules did not change.

For example, recent reforms to allow townhouses or mid-rise apartments in designated areas had unlocked zoning capacity for 650,000 new homes in Sydney and 980,000 in Melbourne, but less than half of this was commercially feasible given other restrictions.

Other restrictions fingered in the report include height limits, 'setbacks' (the size of the gap that must be left between the edge of a parcel of land and the building), and 'floor-space ratios' which limit the total floor space that can be built on a lot.

The overlap between these rules could mean that, for example, a four-storey building is technically allowed on a parcel of land but is architecturally impossible because of a large setback or a short height restriction.

The report argued that other restrictions on aesthetics or amenities, such as mandates on windows, balconies, detailing, storage capacity, or parking space should be pared back, focusing only on essential requirements like ventilation or insulation.

One cited example was a Darlinghurst apartment designed by Brad Swartz, which won an architectural award in 2015 for making clever use of a small space with sliding doors, flaps and hatches, but which was incompatible with the NSW apartment style guide.

A Darlinghurst apartment designed by Brad Swartz and photographed by Katherine Lu won best apartment at the Houses Awards in 2015 for its effective use of a small space. (Supplied: Houses Awards/Katherine Lu)

Another identified culprit was heritage listing, which the commission suggested should apply building by building or to small areas rather than to whole swathes of suburbs, and should be justified in each case by a cost-benefit study, not imposed subjectively.

Developers made to jump through hoops

The report also identified unnecessary burdens and duplication in the development process, saying these were costing would-be developers thousands of dollars, creating uncertainty, and making many new homes unfeasible.

The commission identified a cost of between $3,900 and $22,000 for development approval, and another $3,700 to $18,000 for building approval, adding to the cost of delivering homes and penalising smaller-scale developers.

Much of this money represents required spending on consultants to prepare documentation for various stages of the approval process. It does not include the extra costs of holding the land if approval timeframes blow out.

Councils to get federal funds for roads, pipes and wires in housing push Treasurer Jim Chalmers will reveal details of the $2 billion fund in Tuesday's federal budget, declaring the cash injection will add an extra 65,000 homes over a decade.

The commission also identified the fact that developers have to deal with multiple levels of government and with different rules in different council areas.

For example, Queensland's Noosa Shire Council has 95 of its own variations to the standard Queensland Development Code, while the nearby Sunshine Coast Council has 51, many of them deemed "subjective or unquantifiable".

In New South Wales, the commission found some developments needed referrals to 22 different government agencies before they could proceed, which could lead to confusing contradictions as well as additional delays.

In one example, a developer had to seek an exemption from the local council's landscaping rules after the council deemed it needed more trees but the local fire authority warned that canopy would pose a fire risk.

"[Another] developer told us that preparing reports and waiting for approvals had added more than three years to the timeline of a 1,600-lot development in Melbourne's growth corridor," Ms Wood said.

Enabling infrastructure

While most of these regulations are for state and local governments, the commission also recommended further measures to plan and co-ordinate the infrastructure that can "enable" new housing, such as pipes and access roads.

The federal government has committed to fund some of this infrastructure in tandem with state and territory governments, but the commission also recommended councils scope out the infrastructure needs of their areas in advance to speed up the process.

All levels of government are under pressure to achieve the flagging national housing target, but official figures from the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council show some are faring better than others.

The Northern Territory, Tasmania and New South Wales are the furthest behind, while Victoria, Western Australia and the ACT are the closest to hitting their targets on schedule.

Share of homes target built Estimated completion Victoria 23% September 2029 Aus Capital Territory 23% September 2029 Western Australia 22% September 2029 South Australia 19% September 2030 Queensland 17% September 2030 New South Wales 15% June 2031 Tasmania 12% September 2033 Northern Territory 5% After 2034 (not specified)

The federal government has also faced calls to take stronger co-ordinating action to improve the target, and has committed to review the National Construction Code, the main national regulatory framework for building design.

The Coalition has vowed to radically shorten the code, but the Productivity Commission said it had heard from developers that getting approval to build was not as difficult as approval to develop.

The commission has sought input from those with experience of the housing regulatory system ahead of its final report, which is due in March of next year.

World.title: Bill Oddie, member of The Goodies comedy series, dead at 85
World.content:
British actor, comedian and broadcaster Bill Oddie, best known to Australian audiences as a member of the 1970s comedy trio The Goodies, has died aged 85.

His agent, David Foster, confirmed his death to the BBC, without revealing the cause.

The Goodies was a surreal British comedy series starring Oddie, Tim Brooke-Taylor and Graeme Garden, blending slapstick, satire, music and visual gags.

It ran for nine seasons between 1970 and 1982, with 76 episodes, screening in Australia on the ABC.

Loading YouTube content

"It is with deep sadness that I announce the passing of Bill Oddie, the country's best-loved birder," Mr Foster said in a statement.

"Bill was a multi-talented entertainer — a wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist.

" Yet it was never fame that he valued. Instead, he encouraged us to respect and protect the environment. "

After The Goodies, Oddie became one of Britain's best-known wildlife broadcasters and conservationists through BBC series including Birding with Bill Oddie and Springwatch.

His death means that Scottish-born Graeme Garden — at 83, the youngest of The Goodies cast — is the one surviving member from TV show's main cast.

Tim Brooke-Taylor died in April 2020, aged 79, after contracting COVID-19 during the early stages of the pandemic.

The bearded Oddie was arguably the wildest member of The Goodies' cast, known for his unpredictable antics and outspoken views.

Loading YouTube content

He wore bright T-shirts, while his cast members were often attired in dress shirts, jackets and ties.

He also wrote The Goodies hit song The Funky Gibbon which reached number four on the UK charts in 1975.

"It was an honour and a privilege to represent him for so many years. I will miss him terribly," Mr Foster said.

The Goodies ran between 1970 and 1982 over 76 episodes. (BBC)

Born in Rochdale in northern England, Oddie grew up in Birmingham before attending Cambridge University where he dabbled in comedy.

In the 1960s, he made a name for himself as a writer, working alongside John Cleese, Michael Palin and Terry Jones, of Monty Python fame.

It was as a writer that he met his future Goodies co-stars Brooke-Taylor and Garden.

Apart from Australia and the UK, The Goodies enjoyed popularity in New Zealand, Canada, South Africa and, to a lesser extent, in the United States.

Oddie is survived by his wife, Laura, and daughters, Bonnie, Kate and Rosie.

World.title: Aussie Rohan Browning clips 'unfair' 100m surprise sprung on sprinters
World.content:
Just a day or two before the start of the athletics program at the Commonwealth Games, the public was made aware that the top eight 100 metre sprinters in the rankings would be given a free ticket into the semifinals in a break from tradition.

It left the rest of the field, including Australians Rohan Browning and Eddie Nketia, to duke it out in a mass time trial across 11 heats.

It was a significant change to the usual system where everybody runs the heats and the top two in each race are automatic qualifiers, with the remaining runners trying to get through on times.

Both Australians finished second in their heats, but Browning could not enjoy the moment after going through in 10.24 seconds in heat seven with four more to come.

Browning said the new rules were as much of a surprise to him as they were for the rest of us.

Glasgow 2026 day four live The athletics program starts on day four of the Commonwealth Games, marking the first of three days that feature swimming as well as track and field.

"It's an unheard of progression, it's extremely weird. It's really hard to know, I have no idea what times have been run, I have no idea where I sit in the placings," he said, asking reporters to clue him in on where he sat in the standings.

"It's gusty out there, so when they just make up these rules about eight guys get to go through and the rest of us goes through on a time trial rather than first or second across the line, the reality is some heats will have better conditions than others, so I don't know what's going on."

Browning made the cut in 16th as the second slowest qualifier and compatriot Eddie Nketia was fourth fastest overall with his 10.07

Browning, who was a controversial inclusion in the team ahead of Josh Azzopardi, said he always turns up prepared to run three rounds but the other folks, including countryman Lachie Kennedy, do not have to.

Eddie Nketia looked powerful as he finished second in his heat. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

"It's not fair, clearly it's not fair," he said.

"It's clearly been engineered to try to achieve a desired outcome. Whatever's motivated that decision, I don't know what it is or if it's reasonable or not, but clearly it's not fair. I think everyone would agree on that."

Nketia said it was out of his control so he was not going to worry too much about it, and Browning acknowledged the best response is probably to just run fast.

Aussie sprinter feels 'robbed' Josh Azzopardi opens up after missing out on selection as a 100 metres runner in Australia's athletics team for the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

"At the end of the day this sport is meritocracy at its finest; if you're quick enough you go through, so I suppose you could say those guys have earned their place," he said.

"In all likelihood they were probably the guys paying the best odds to make the final regardless, but you just don't know. Some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape. I don't even know when they took the performances from."

National record holder Torrie Lewis is experiencing both sides of the coin in the women's events, running the heats in the 100m but granted the automatic progression in the 200m.

"Having a day off in the middle is perfect, so I'm really happy with that," he said after winning her heat in 11.15 seconds to finish as the second-fastest qualifier.

"It would've been better if it was first [past the post], just to eliminate the wind because it's so gusty going around, but what can you do? Just be the fastest no matter what."

World.title: Sally McManus and Michele O'Neil resign from top ACTU jobs
World.content:
The powerful heads of the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), Sally McManus and Michele O'Neil, have announced their resignations to ''make way for a new generation''.

Ms McManus has been the peak body's secretary since 2017 and Ms O'Neil its president since 2018.

Ms McManus will finish in the role at the end of August and Ms O'Neil will depart before the end of the year, in order to ''assist with the leadership transition''.

Michele O'Neil will step down by the end of the year. (ABC News: Tom Hancock)

Their replacements are yet to be decided on, according to a statement from the ACTU.

''The ACTU's union affiliates will decide on the next leadership team, initially with the ACTU Executive filling the casual vacancies and then through an election at next year's Congress, which will coincide with the ACTU's 100th Anniversary," the statement said.

Ms McManus said it was "the right time" for new leaders "to take our movement forward".

''I am proud of our movement's achievements, and it has been an honour to serve the union movement and working people as the secretary of the ACTU for nearly a decade,'' she said.

The Transport Workers' Union was among the first to thank the outgoing leaders, noting their work fighting for the COVID-era JobKeeper scheme and pushing Labor to establish a Fair Work Court, which it announced plans for at the party conference last week.

In 2024 Ms McManus denied she knew about the alleged infiltration of criminals into the Victorian branch of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CMFEU).

She also oversaw the ACTU's suspension divisions of the CFMEU while it cleaned up its act.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also thanked the pair for their "tireless advocacy" for workers, but also for their support to him personally.

"It is fitting that Sally and Michele announce they're stepping down from their respective positions at a time when there have been significant wage increases in critical and long-undervalued sectors, the gender pay gap is at a record low and union membership is growing for the first time in decades" he said in a statement.

"Personally, I will miss the friendship and support these two giants of the labour movement have offered me over many years, but especially since I became Labor Leader in 2019 and then Prime Minister is 2022."

World.title: SA's first industrial manslaughter charges laid against Adelaide company
World.content:
An Adelaide manufacturer has been charged with South Australia's first case of industrial manslaughter two years after the death of a 28-year-old worker, a workplace safety watchdog says.

Lachlan Carslake died after he was allegedly "struck in the head by a metal object" while operating a milling machine at the Nylastex's Edwardstown plant on July 24, 2024, according to court documents.

The Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) filed charges in Adelaide Magistrates Court against Nylastex Tooling Pty Ltd, Nylastex Holdings Pty Ltd and the directors last week.

The charges followed what SafeWork SA described as an "extensive" investigation.

Court documents alleged the companies used a number of milling machines, each fitted with an interlock guarding switch designed to prevent the machine operating at a hazardous speed with the guard open.

According to the documents, this switch was allegedly "in a disabled state" on the machine Mr Carslake was operating on July 24, 2024.

SafeWork SA says the case is the first time the state has filed industrial manslaughter charges. (YouTube: SafeWork SA)

The documents also alleged Mr Carslake "died as a result of" being hit by a metal object ejected from the machine while the switch was disabled and a moveable guard was opened.

SafeWork SA said two days prior to Mr Carslake's death, an external technician engaged by Nylastex Tooling Pty Ltd had allegedly advised the company of "safety concerns" regarding the guarding switch.

SafeWork SA said the companies and its two directors had allegedly "breached" their health and safety duty "by engaging in conduct with gross negligence that caused the death of the worker or were reckless as to the risk of death or serious injury".

A project manager of the company has also been charged for allegedly engaging in gross negligence or reckless conduct under the Work Health and Safety Act 2012.

They were all expected to appear in court in August.

Industrial manslaughter became a criminal offence in South Australia on July 1, 2024, and carries a maximum penalty of 20 years imprisonment while the maximum fine for a corporate is $18 million.

The company has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Hardy wins Australia’s first men’s floor medal in 16 years
World.content:
Australia’s James Hardy has finished on the podium in the men’s floor final, with a score of 13.433 good enough for bronze at Glasgow International Arena today.

The last time Australia won a Commonwealth Games medal in the men’s floor routine was back at Delhi in 2010 when Thomas Pichler won gold.

James Hardy celebrates after his routine in the men’s floor exercise final. Getty Images

England’s Luke Whitehouse won gold with a phenomenal routine that scored him 14.566, ahead of Canada’s Rene Cournoyer on 13.966.

Local favourite Reuben Ward, who won gold in the individual all-around final yesterday, fell flat on his face on the final tumble of his routine, which left with a 12.900 (he was ok) and down in sixth.

That’s Hardy’s second bronze medal of these Games after he also won team bronze three days ago.

We will have to wait a couple of hours to hear from him, as he prepares to compete in the rings final later today.

World.title: Inflation spike: Oil prices could derail economy, Treasury warns
World.content:
Treasury has warned the Australian economy could be hit by an inflation spike and slower growth through the second half of the year as America’s war against Iran, Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, and Ukraine’s assault on Russian oil refineries upend the global petroleum market. Amid forecasts from the chief economist of the nation’s biggest bank that the “clock was ticking” on oil spiking towards $US150 a barrel, Treasury is increasingly worried of a price crunch as nations run down their oil reserves, and supplies out of the Middle East and Russia dry up. Ships like these remain anchored outside the Strait of Hormuz with the war between the US and Iran escalating over the past fortnight. Getty Images Brent crude eased to $US85 on Monday after hitting $US100 a barrel late last week on concerns the renewal of hostilities between the United States and Iran will leave oil refiners struggling to get adequate supplies in coming months. Retail prices have now climbed to their highest level since early June. Over the past week, the national average price for unleaded rose by 9.5¢ to 182.3¢ a litre. Retail prices lifted by 8.9¢ in Sydney to 178.7¢ a litre, while they jumped by 10.1¢ in Melbourne to 181.7¢ a litre.



In formal advice to Treasurer Jim Chalmers, his department – which in the May budget released worst-case modelling of what would occur if oil prices reached $US200 a barrel – warned a series of factors meant the cost of oil was likely to stay elevated, hurting the domestic economy. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At the start of the war in March, members of the International Energy Authority committed to release 400 million barrels of their strategic reserves. About 290 million barrels of that reserve has been drawn down, leaving little to boost global supplies. The move by Houthi rebels to target oil movements through the Red Sea has added to global price pressures. Although oil can still be moved out of Saudi Arabia through the Suez Canal, it adds time and cost to shipping expenses. A new and unexpected development has been the success of Ukraine in using drones to attack Russian oil refineries. A strike last week on a Siberian refinery, almost 2000 kilometres from Ukraine, and a separate facility in the Caspian Sea caused extensive damage.



The attacks have not only forced Russia, one of the world’s largest oil producers, to impose restrictions on domestic use. Exports of diesel have now been banned, depleting global supply. Treasury warned that “upside risks to oil prices” would build if the current state of affairs did not change. Loading Chalmers said the increase in global prices caused by the ongoing turmoil in the Middle East could have a detrimental impact on the global and domestic economy. “The recent escalation of tensions in the Middle East poses a substantial threat to global inflation. There is still so much uncertainty about this war and its ongoing costs and consequences,” he said.



“Like the rest of the world, we are monitoring day-to-day developments very closely because so much hinges on a proper ceasefire and the permanent reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. “From an economic point of view, a proper and permanent end to the war can’t come soon enough.” Commonwealth Bank chief economist Luke Yeaman said markets believed just a few weeks ago there was a good chance of a global over-supply of oil that would bring prices down to between $US60 and $US70 a barrel. Commonwealth Bank chief economist Luke Yeaman says the clock is ticking on oil prices moving towards $US150 a barrel. Alex Ellinghausen But he said the fresh hostilities, on top of the Houthi attacks, the war in Russia and the rundown in global reserves meant there was a real chance oil could hit up to $US150 a barrel within eight to 10 weeks.



“The clock is ticking,” he told this masthead. Yeaman said a surge in oil prices would force up domestic inflation, which by itself would likely prompt an increase in official interest rates by the Reserve Bank. But the bank could then find itself cutting rates to deal with a slowing economy. Related Article Analysis

Trade Donald Trump’s trade war is costing the world a fortune – and the cost is going up “You could see a stagflation impulse, with higher inflation in the short term, but then growth comes down below potential,” he said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will on Tuesday announce $4 million in federal funding for a pre-feasibility study into an oil refinery plant in Western Australia to be built by energy and fertiliser firm Perdaman. The nation has just two refineries – in Queensland and Victoria – with no new ones established since the 1960s.



“The longer war in the Middle East goes on, the greater the impact on Australia will be, and my government will continue to do everything we can to shield Australia from the worst effects – and set us up for the future,” he said. While petrol prices are poised to climb, the electricity market is providing some reason for optimism as renewable energy and batteries decouple Australia’s power prices from the volatile global energy market. Coal-fired power fell to its lowest point on record in the second quarter of the year, and gas hit a 20-year low, as renewable energy generation and in particular battery output grew, according to the latest report by the Australian Energy Market Regulator. As a result, the past quarter’s wholesale price, which is the cost for retailers to buy electricity, was down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year. A big shift in the electricity market during past year is the rise of batteries, including grid-scale and household installations, which has boomed under the Albanese government’s rebate scheme.

World.title: ‘Plainly unfair’: Rohan Browning slams 100m qualifying rules at Commonwealth Games
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games ‘Plainly unfair’: Rohan Browning slams 100m qualifying rules at Commonwealth Games Michael Gleeson July 27, 2026 — 11:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Sprint champion Rohan Browning slammed the 100m qualifying at the Commonwealth Games as “plainly unfair” and manufactured to get certain runners into the finals. Runners with the eight fastest times in the first half of this calendar year have automatically been placed in the semi-finals without having to run heats. Only the 17 fastest times in the heats will advance to the semi-finals in Glasgow. Ordinarily, the first two finishers in each heat, and then two or three of the next fastest runners across all heats, would advance. Unhappy: Gun sprinter Rohan Browning has expressed his displeasure with the new finals format. Getty Images “It’s an unheard-of progression. It’s extremely weird,” said Browning, an Olympic and world championships semi-finalist.



“I mean, it’s gusty out there. So when they just make up these rules about eight guys get to go through and the rest of the field goes through like on the time trial rather than, you know, first or second across the line, the reality is some heats will get better conditions than others. So I don’t know what’s going on. Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Hardy wins Australia’s first men’s floor medal in 16 years “I think when you turn up to a championships, you’re prepared to run three rounds, and the reality is you’ve got to run hard for all of them. So, you know, I felt like I was running hard out there, even if it also felt a little awkward.” Browning qualified for the semi-finals, placing second in his heat with a time of 10.24s. “Of course, it’s not fair. Clearly, it’s not fair,” Browning said of the fact eight athletes had automatically advanced to the semi-finals without running a heat.



“Like it’s clearly been engineered to try to achieve a desired outcome. Whatever’s motivated that decision, I don’t know what it is or if it’s reasonable or not. But clearly, it’s not fair. I think everyone would agree on that. “You would expect to [advance after automatically finishing second] but it’s possible that people might get a slow heat and nobody might go through from that heat. “Look, at the end of the day, this sport is meritocracy at its finest. If you’re quick enough, you go through. “So I suppose you could say those guys have earned their place through the season. In all likelihood, they’re probably the guys who are going to make the final, regardless. But you just don’t know … some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape. ” Further to Browning’s point, for the final heat of the morning, there was a big +3.9m/s tailwind which would make any time illegal, as far as records go. But there was no adjustment for the wind in any of the heats.

World.title: Three storeys everywhere: The radical plan to drive down house prices
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Three storeys everywhere: The radical plan to drive down house prices Shane Wright July 27, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The nation’s sprawling suburbs of single-storey homes would be transformed under a plan from the Productivity Commission to make the property market affordable, with three-storey developments allowed everywhere and high-rise apartment blocks built near train, tram and bus stations. Declaring state and local government planning regulations a key reason for Australia having some of the most expensive homes in the world, the commission also wants the minimum size of home lots to be reduced while allowing more European-style mixed commercial and residential developments. Single-block homes would be replaced by three-storey townhouses under a plan to reduce the cost of housing across Australia. Getty Images Commission chair Danielle Wood said regulation was the handbrake on new homes, with the time needed to save for a deposit climbing by almost 30 per cent over the past 20 years. “When people can’t live near work or family the economy and the community suffers. We cannot solve our housing affordability problem unless we build more homes where people want to live,” she said.



The commission has been charged by Treasurer Jim Chalmers to examine the nation’s building approval process, land use, access to infrastructure and construction methods. Related Article Opinion

Property prices A generations-long belief about house prices has just been shattered Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent The government, which in the budget committed $2 billion towards states and councils for housing-related infrastructure, is more than 100,000 properties behind its own target of building 1.25 million homes between mid-2024 and mid-2029. Despite a slowdown in the nation’s property market since February, house prices are still at record levels of unaffordability. Median house prices in some cities are still climbing, with Perth up 87 per cent since 2020 and in Brisbane up by 92 per cent. In its interim report, the commission said state and territory governments should allow three-storey developments on all residential land, with exceptions only for environmental factors, particular hazards or heritage listings where benefits of protection outweighed the costs.



State and council planning schemes would allow four- to nine-storey and high-rise apartments in high-demand areas with existing transport infrastructure, or where it could be quickly upgraded. Minimum lot sizes on new developments should be cut, especially in designated high-demand areas. Commercial zones that effectively prohibit residential development should also be overhauled to enable mixed-use areas. Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood says the country has to build more homes where people want to live. Eamon Gallagher Commissioner Alison Roberts said there were far too many regulations that had driven up the cost of building or reduced supply. “Regulation is essential – particularly where it ensures buildings are safe and built to a high standard. But too often, other rules are making it illegal or unviable to build the kinds of homes people need in the places they want to live,” she said.



“The kind of rules that stop you adding a granny flat in your garden or replacing a single home with townhouses are at the core of our housing challenge.” The commission said the surge in the cost of housing had led to an almost 18-percentage-point drop in the number of people between 25 and 34 with their own home between 1981 and 2021. Australian mortgage debt is among the highest per person in the developed world. In a bid to reduce construction costs, the commission recommends car parking requirements be reduced or axed completely, especially in areas where there is evidence that off-street parking is not being used or there are high levels of public transport. Loading Broad heritage listings would be replaced by more specific protections that had gone through a cost-benefit analysis. Instead of blanket heritage protections, specific buildings or small areas would attract heritage listings, with more options to delist buildings.



A constant complaint from the housing sector is the imposition of developer contributions for new projects. The Urban Development Institute of Australia estimates developer fees can make up to 20 per cent of the cost of bringing a new lot to market. Related Article Analysis

Property market Saying there’s an upside to falling house prices is sacrilege. But Labor needs to admit it The commission found developer contributions should be used where there is a “close nexus” to the proposed development and local infrastructure needs. Estimates of developer fees should be made before the release or rezoning of land, with proponents given the option to make the payments over a period of time or later in the development process. Under the commission’s proposals, current restrictions in areas such as minimum dwelling and balcony sizes and storage requirements for apartments would be axed. Current dwelling and bedroom size requirements differ between states and territories.



The commission said “state, territory and local governments should avoid regulating observable characteristics that do not negatively affect the wider community”. Restrictions on housing types would also be ditched. Another area targeted by the commission is the time many authorities take to approve new housing. Wood said in one case, a developer spent an extra three years on reports and waiting for approvals for a 1600-lot development on Melbourne’s urban fringe. The commission’s final report is due by March next year. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.content:
“ABC TV 24 News recently ran a story about Qantas adding an additional “20 litre” fuel tank to make the AU-Europe trip in one hop,” notes David Southwell of Pymble. “Not one, but two of the seemingly oblivious presenters read this same story. Ron Burgundy moments, or does Qantas have the most fuel-efficient jet ever? I guess one of the crew has to fill the jerry can with Avgas on the way to work.”

Jo Rainbow’s West Berkshire experience (C8) continues: “In Oxford we drove past Toot Hill Butts. I wonder if it is an effluent area.”

“My first movie (C8) was a charity screening of Jedda in 1959,” recalls Andrew Cohen of Glebe. “There was a garden party afterwards. I was traumatised, terrified, and I recall several stark images that I can’t exclude even now as to how fearful I found them. I recall that director Charles Chauvel sat me on his knee, trying to console me. I wasn’t sobbing but describing at high volume what was scary. I was four and haven’t seen it again.”

George Zivkovic of Northmead perceives that “Roy Masters, in his column, suggested allowing one attacking kick, or forward pass to an offside receiver, per set of six tackles will perhaps achieve ‘global domination’ for rugby league”. Sorry, Roy, but that’s already been happening in the games I’ve been watching this season, along with attackers in front of kickers, dubious play-the-balls and Clayton’s scrums.”

Shout-out to the Manly Observer, an independent publication bucking the trend by adding a print edition along with a real-time digital presence and, as Allan Gibson of Cherrybrook points out, is a dab hand at alliteration, with the headline, “Baby-faced booze bandits busted by bystander”. We give it a B+.

World.title: ‘Really devastated’: Saints coach Lyon reveals King’s anguish after another injury blow
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Max King suffered a season-ending hamstring strain on Sunday.

Brisbane’s Ty Gallop will face a serious misconduct charge.

St Kilda’s Darcy Wilson has re-committed on a new two-year deal. St Kilda coach Ross Lyon maintains the club is committed to keeping Max King at Moorabbin, revealing the injury-prone forward was “really devastated” and asked if the club had had enough of him. The 26-year-old has been put in cotton wool for the rest season but St Kilda stresses the 84-gamer is “incredibly important” to the Saints and they’re determined to get him back playing senior footy. King will not play again until at least next year after it was confirmed on Monday he suffered a season-ending left hamstring strain in his return AFL game against North Melbourne on Sunday. Lyon spoke about the extent of King’s frustration and disappointment, with the Saint seeking assurances that they would still back him as an AFL player.



Max King during his comeback game. Getty Images Tied to the Saints until the end of 2032 after signing a six-year contract extension two years ago, King faces a huge challenge to overcome his injury woes. “His concern was he’d let the club and a lot of his team down,” Lyon said on Fox Footy. “And shame is too strong a word, but [he was] probably embarrassed. “Like [he was] saying, ‘Have you guys had enough of me?’ And I said, ‘Hang on here. We’re in.’”



King’s season-ending left hamstring strain is a devastating blow for the Saints and King, who had not played at AFL level for 757 days before his latest setback, and has now suffered hamstring injuries twice this year. Lyon is adamant the Saints did everything in their power to ensure King was fit enough to return to senior football. Loading “Every parameter … was really strong. I mean he got to half-time [on Sunday] healthy. Anyone who thinks it’s fatigue [is off the mark],” he said. “There’s nothing on the parameters [we look at] or the demand of the game that caused this.”



Lyon had already defended the club’s decision to play King in the senior side and bypass the VFL this time, but the star forward will now have played just once in three seasons after a torturous run that includes injuries to both knees and calf issues. Max King gets a kick away against the Kangaroos. AFL Photos King left Sunday’s 31-point win over North Melbourne midway through the third quarter and did not return. He started each term on the bench and played in six-minute stints, but managed just one kick and one handball while playing at different times on Charlie Comben and Aidan Corr. Saints football boss Lenny Hayes said the club would “wrap our arms” around King.



“It’s an incredibly disappointing outcome for Max, who has done everything possible throughout his rehabilitation to put himself in the best position to return,” said Hayes. “He’s an incredibly important part of our football club. We’ll continue to wrap our arms around him and provide all the support he needs as he works through this latest setback. “Our focus now turns to ensuring Max undertakes a full pre-season to allow him to get back and play consistent senior football in 2027.” King signed a six-year contract extension in October 2024 that ties him to the Saints until the end of the 2032 season. His horror injury run started about three months before he inked that deal, when he sustained a season-ending posterior cruciate ligament tear in his left knee in a two-point loss to Port Adelaide.



King also hurt his right knee in a pre-season game mere months later that ultimately required three separate surgeries and wiped out his 2025 season. After a delayed start to the past off-season, a new calf problem sidelined him again. King made it back from that setback, only to suffer a hamstring strain in his second VFL game in May. The 26-year-old went into an extended rehabilitation period after that, including spending time on the Gold Coast with his twin, Suns focal point Ben, who is expected to sign as a restricted free agent with Hawthorn. Lyon said St Kilda’s high-performance team was satisfied that King had proven he was ready with a significant volume of running, including at high speeds and game-like intensity.



“We stand by our decision to play him,” Lyon said on Sunday. There are still six seasons left on King’s deal, and he will be desperate to repay the Saints’ faith in him to avoid becoming the poster child for how long-term contracts can go wrong. King won’t play again until the 2027 season. AFL Photos The No.4 pick from the 2018 AFL draft displayed his immense potential in a career-best 52-goal season in 2022. St Kilda are clinging to a wildcard berth with a month to go in the home-and-away season, with matches to come against Sydney, Carlton, Richmond and Gold Coast, all of which will be played in Melbourne.



In positive news for the Saints faithful, it was confirmed on Monday evening that Darcy Wilson has committed to the club on a new two-year deal. The hard-running midfielder had attracted plenty of rival interest after a breakthrough season. The 20-year-old, who was drafted at pick 18 in the 2023 draft, will remain at the club until the end of the 2028 season. The Saints made a splash in last year’s player movement period, recruiting Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Sam Flanders and Liam Ryan, after making Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera the league’s first $2 million-a-season man. St Kilda’s big spending has so far delivered only a mediocre return, worsened by Flanders suffering a season-ending Achilles injury. De Koning also missed games with broken ribs and a punctured lung, but demonstrated what he could bring in a strong performance against the Roos on Sunday.



Lion straight to tribunal on misconduct charge Brisbane youngster Ty Gallop has been sent straight to the AFL tribunal for shoving Port Adelaide’s Mitch Georgiades’ head into the turf. Gallop has been charged with serious misconduct for the incident in the second quarter of Brisbane’s win over Port at the Gabba on Sunday. The 20-year-old rolled Georgiades in a heavy tackle but has come under scrutiny for his actions off the ball immediately after. As the Lions swept downfield, Gallop lifted Georgiades by the jumper before slamming him back into the turf head first.



Depending on how the tribunal sees the incident, Gallop could face multiple weeks on the sidelines. “It wasn’t a great look, but I’m on the other side of it,” Port Adelaide coach Josh Carr said. “They’re a team that plays tough and pushes the limits. We got the free kick, so we got rewarded. There’s not much more to say.” Carr said Georgiades was unaffected by the incident after the game.



Gallop’s choice to hit out at Georgiades was described as “a stupid action” by former Brisbane great Alastair Lynch. “We’ve been singing the praises of Ty Gallop over the last half a dozen weeks particularly,” Lynch said on Fox Footy. “But that’s just a stupid action. We don’t want to see that. Mitch has had some problems with concussion. AAP and Scott Spits Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.
